explanation: Spot on! Because skin layers absorb very slowly here, it's the perfect spot to watch for a localized immune reaction like a TB test. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T15#GNS122_U1_T15_h4)

question: When giving a routine subcutaneous insulin injection to an adult, how should you position the skin and needle?

options.A: Inject the medication directly into the dermis until a fluid bleb forms.
options.B: Push the needle straight down into the muscle at a 90-degree angle.
options.C: Stretch the skin flat and insert the needle at a 15-degree angle.
options.D: Pinch a skin fold and insert the needle at a 45 to 90-degree angle.

explanation: You got it! Pinching the fatty tissue makes sure your needle stays in the fat layer and doesn't accidentally dive into the muscle underneath. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T15#GNS122_U1_T15_h4)

question: Which muscle site is generally considered the safest and most reliable for giving an intramuscular injection to an adult?

options.A: Ventrogluteal
options.B: Rectus femoris
options.C: Dorsogluteal
options.D: Deltoid

explanation: Brilliant! The ventrogluteal site is clear of major nerves and big blood vessels, making it a nurse's best friend for adult IM shots. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T15#GNS122_U1_T15_h5)

question: What is the main benefit of using the Z-track technique when giving an intramuscular injection?

options.A: It seals the medication inside the muscle and prevents leakage into skin tissue.
options.B: It speeds up the absorption rate of irritating oily substances.
options.C: It allows the nurse to inject larger volumes of fluid into the deltoid.
options.D: It completely eliminates the pain associated with needle puncture.

explanation: Well done! Pulling the skin sideways before poking creates a zigzag path that traps irritating drugs safely down in the muscle. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T15#GNS122_U1_T15_h5)

question: What is the biggest clinical advantage of giving a medication straight into a vein (intravenously)?

options.A: It requires minimal monitoring compared to oral medications.
options.B: It prevents rapid allergic reactions from occurring.
options.C: It carries zero risk of localized tissue irritation.
options.D: It provides immediate systemic availability of the medication.

explanation: You're doing great! Since IV medications go right into the bloodstream, they start working instantly—a lifesaver in emergencies. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T15#GNS122_U1_T15_h6)

question: Why must you check if two drugs are compatible before adding an IV piggyback medicine into an existing line?

options.A: Hospital pharmacy software blocks incompatible infusions anyway.
options.B: Primary fluids neutralize the therapeutic effect of all antibiotics.
options.C: Incompatible drugs can form precipitates that block the catheter.
options.D: Mismatched drugs will automatically cause severe patient hypertension.

explanation: Spot on! Mixing the wrong drugs can cause chemical reactions that turn into solid gunk, clogging the line and endangering the patient. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T15#GNS122_U1_T15_h6)

question: A patient with a peripheral IV line says it hurts, and you notice the area is cool, pale, and swollen. What has likely happened?

options.A: Air embolism
options.B: Circulatory overload
options.C: Phlebitis
options.D: Infiltration

explanation: You got it! When the IV fluid slips out of the vein and leaks into the surrounding tissue, it makes the skin feel cool, tight, and swollen. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T15#GNS122_U1_T15_h7)

question: Your patient suddenly starts wheezing, struggling to breathe, and breaking out in hives right after an IV medication starts. What is your very first action?

options.A: Stop the infusion immediately.
options.B: Slow the infusion rate to a keep-vein-open speed.
options.C: Notify the attending physician before taking action.
options.D: Document the vital signs in the patient chart.

explanation: Brilliant nursing instinct! Always stop the flow first to keep any more of the allergen from entering their system. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T15#GNS122_U1_T15_h7)

question: When is the right time for a nurse to document a medication in the patient's chart?

options.A: Only if the patient experiences a negative side effect.
options.B: Before drawing up the medication in the treatment room.
options.C: Immediately after the medication is given.
options.D: At the end of the shift during the final handover report.

explanation: Exactly right! Documenting right away prevents accidental double-dosing by another nurse who might think the dose was missed. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T15#GNS122_U1_T15_h8)

question: Why is it important to check up on your patient after giving an injection or IV medication?

options.A: It ensures the medication achieved its intended effect and checks for adverse reactions.
options.B: It proves to the hospital pharmacy that the correct vial was opened.
options.C: It satisfies legal billing requirements for injectable supplies.
options.D: It replaces the need to check vital signs prior to administration.

explanation: You nailed it! Because injections work fast, following up helps you catch any early side effects and make sure the patient is feeling better. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T15#GNS122_U1_T15_h8)

question: What is the primary advantage of intravenous therapy over oral medication administration?

options.A: It prevents medications from being filtered by the kidneys.
options.B: It is completely painless and requires no technical skill.
options.C: It provides immediate systemic availability by bypassing the digestive tract.
options.D: It eliminates all potential risks of systemic infection.

explanation: Giving medications directly into a vein places them instantly into the bloodstream, avoiding the delay of digestion and liver processing. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T16#GNS122_U1_T16_h1)

question: When is a nurse most likely to initiate intravenous therapy for a patient?

options.A: When the patient needs a rapid correction of severe dehydration.
options.B: When the patient is eating normally and taking daily multivitamin pills.
options.C: When topical skin cream is prescribed for a localized rash.
options.D: When a mild headache needs to be relieved over an eight-hour period.

explanation: Severe dehydration requires quick fluid volume restoration directly into the blood vessels, which can only be achieved effectively through IV therapy. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T16#GNS122_U1_T16_h1)

question: Which vein is located in the antecubital fossa and is often used for emergency access or blood draws?

options.A: Digital dorsal vein
options.B: Median cubital vein
options.C: Temporal scalp vein
options.D: Great saphenous vein

explanation: The median cubital vein sits right in the bend of the elbow, making it large, prominent, and easy to access quickly. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T16#GNS122_U1_T16_h2)

question: Why is the antecubital fossa generally avoided for long-term peripheral IV maintenance?

options.A: Bending the elbow can easily kink and block the catheter.
options.B: Medications cannot reach the heart from upper arm veins.
options.C: Infusions run much slower through arm veins than hand veins.
options.D: The veins in this area have no nerve supply nearby.

explanation: Movement at the elbow joint puts constant stress on an IV catheter in the antecubital space, leading to infiltration or flow stoppage. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T16#GNS122_U1_T16_h2)

question: Which IV solution is classified as isotonic and commonly used for fluid resuscitation?

options.A: 0.9% Normal Saline
options.B: 5% Dextrose in water
options.C: 3.0% Sodium Chloride
options.D: 0.45% Sodium Chloride

explanation: Normal Saline at 0.9% concentration matches body fluid osmolarity, keeping red blood cells stable while expanding blood volume. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T16#GNS122_U1_T16_h3)

question: What happens to body cells when a hypotonic IV solution is infused into the vascular system?

options.A: Fluid is pulled out of the cells into the bloodstream, causing them to shrink.
options.B: Water molecules stay completely inside the blood vessels with no movement.
options.C: Fluid moves from the blood vessels into the cells, causing them to swell.
options.D: Red blood cells immediately break apart and release all their hemoglobin.

explanation: Hypotonic solutions have a lower concentration of solutes than blood, so water shifts toward areas of higher solute concentration inside the cells. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T16#GNS122_U1_T16_h3)

question: Where should a nurse begin looking when selecting a site for peripheral IV insertion?

options.A: As close to the shoulder joint as physically possible
options.B: Directly in the antecubital fossa of the dominant arm
options.C: On the most distal areas of the non-dominant hand or forearm
options.D: On the lower extremities near the ankle joints

explanation: Starting low on the non-dominant arm preserves higher vein sites for future use if the current line fails or needs replacement. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T16#GNS122_U1_T16_h4)

question: Why must a nurse check a female patient's surgical history before placing an IV in her arm?

options.A: To confirm she is not currently allergic to standard soap.
options.B: To avoid placing an IV on the same side as a prior mastectomy.
options.C: To make sure she has never received a blood transfusion before.
options.D: To ensure her blood pressure can be measured safely on that arm.

explanation: Lymph node removal during a mastectomy impairs lymphatic drainage, making that arm vulnerable to swelling and severe infection if punctured. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T16#GNS122_U1_T16_h4)

question: What is the primary indicator that the needle has successfully entered the lumen of the vein during insertion?

options.A: The surrounding skin turns pale and cold to the touch.
options.B: The patient reports a warm, soothing sensation in the hand.
options.C: A flashback of blood appears in the catheter hub chamber.
options.D: The tourniquet drops off the patient's arm automatically.

explanation: Blood entering the flash chamber confirms that the needle tip is inside the blood vessel before advancing the plastic cannula. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T16#GNS122_U1_T16_h5)

question: What unit of measurement is typically used when programming an electronic infusion pump?

options.A: Drops per minute (gtt/min)
options.B: Milligrams per minute (mg/min)
options.C: Milliliters per hour (mL/hr)
options.D: Liters per 24 hours (L/day)

explanation: Electronic infusion pumps are calibrated to deliver exact volumetric amounts calculated in milliliters per hour. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T16#GNS122_U1_T16_h6)

question: Why is a microdrip tubing set (60 gtt/mL) often chosen for infants or sensitive pediatric patients?

options.A: It eliminates the need to use an electronic infusion pump entirely.
options.B: It pumps fluids at a much faster speed than standard gravity tubing.
options.C: It allows for much smaller, more precise adjustments in fluid delivery.
options.D: It prevents air bubbles from ever entering the patient's bloodstream.

explanation: Microdrip sets produce tiny drops, making it easier to deliver precise fluid volumes and prevent accidental fluid overload in small patients. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T16#GNS122_U1_T16_h6)

question: Which complication involves a vesicant medication leaking into the surrounding tissue and causing severe tissue damage?

options.A: Simple infiltration
options.B: Fluid overload
options.C: Air embolism
options.D: Extravasation

explanation: Extravasation specifically refers to the leakage of harsh, blistering drugs (vesicants) that destroy local tissue if not managed quickly. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T16#GNS122_U1_T16_h7)

question: What is the very first action a nurse should take when suspecting an IV site has infiltrated?

options.A: Stop the infusion and remove the catheter immediately.
options.B: Flush the catheter with sterile saline to clear any local blockage.
options.C: Apply a hot compress directly over the swollen site while the line runs.
options.D: Slow the infusion rate down by half and monitor for one hour.

explanation: Stopping the infusion prevents any more fluid from entering the damaged tissue space, protecting the patient from further injury. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T16#GNS122_U1_T16_h7)

question: How often should an IV insertion site covered with a transparent dressing be visually inspected by the nurse?

options.A: Whenever the patient complains of severe pain
options.B: Only once every seven days
options.C: Only when changing the IV solution bag
options.D: During every routine shift assessment

explanation: Frequent visual checks through transparent dressings allow nurses to catch early signs of redness, swelling, or infiltration. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T16#GNS122_U1_T16_h8)

question: Why should a nurse apply pressure to an IV site immediately after withdrawing the catheter?

options.A: To ensure the plastic catheter tip remains intact inside the arm.
options.B: To push any remaining trapped air bubbles back up into the vein.
options.C: To stimulate rapid skin healing and eliminate scarring completely.
options.D: To stop bleeding and prevent hematoma formation at the site.

explanation: Applying direct pressure helps seal the puncture wound in the blood vessel wall, stopping external bleeding and preventing internal bruising. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T16#GNS122_U1_T16_h8)

question: What makes an IV fluid 'isotonic'?

options.A: It draws fluid out of the blood vessels and into the tissue cells
options.B: It contains large protein molecules that cannot cross membranes
options.C: It causes body cells to swell by forcing water inside them
options.D: It has the same particle concentration as blood plasma

explanation: You've got this! Isotonic fluids match the natural concentration of our blood, meaning they safely boost fluid volume without causing water to rush into or out of our cells. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T17#GNS122_U1_T17_h1)

question: Why would a doctor order a hypotonic fluid like 0.45% Normal Saline?

options.A: To maintain a stable vein without altering any fluid balance
options.B: To rapidly replace large volumes of blood loss from trauma
options.C: To treat severe cellular dehydration by moving water into tissues
options.D: To pull excess fluid out of swollen brain cells and tissues

explanation: Think of hypotonic fluids as having fewer particles than blood. When a patient is super dehydrated, these fluids move out of the veins and into thirsty cells to plump them back up! [learn more](GNS122_U1_T17#GNS122_U1_T17_h1)

question: What is the safest way to check a patient's identity before starting an IV?

options.A: Look at the medication chart resting on the bedside table
options.B: Ask the client what room they are currently staying in
options.C: Check the client's identification band using two unique identifiers
options.D: Call out the client's full name and wait for a head nod

explanation: Safety first! Always use two patient identifiers (like name and hospital number on the ID band) to make sure you are giving the right treatment to the right person. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T17#GNS122_U1_T17_h2)

question: A patient with heart failure needs an IV infusion. What is your most important pre-infusion check?

options.A: Choosing a vein located in the dominant hand for comfort
options.B: Selecting the largest gauge needle available for rapid infusion
options.C: Warming the intravenous fluid bag to body temperature first
options.D: Listening to the client's lung sounds and checking baseline vital signs

explanation: Great clinical thinking! Heart failure patients struggle to handle extra fluid. Checking their lungs and vitals first gives you a baseline so you can catch early signs of fluid overload. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T17#GNS122_U1_T17_h2)

question: When inserting a peripheral IV catheter, what angle should your needle enter the skin?

options.A: 75 to 90 degrees
options.B: 5 to 10 degrees
options.C: 45 to 60 degrees
options.D: 15 to 30 degrees

explanation: An angle of 15 to 30 degrees is the sweet spot! It lets you slide right through the skin and gently catch the superficial vein without poking through the back wall. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T17#GNS122_U1_T17_h3)

question: Why must you let the skin antiseptic dry completely before starting an IV stick?

options.A: To allow the chemical to fully destroy microorganisms on the skin
options.B: To ensure the vein stays plump and easy to palpate
options.C: To prevent the sticky dressing from sliding off wet skin
options.D: To stop the client from feeling a sharp burning sensation

explanation: Patience pays off! Antiseptics like chlorhexidine need a little contact and drying time to actually kill the germs on the skin before you puncture it. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T17#GNS122_U1_T17_h3)

question: What does the 'drop factor' on an IV tubing package tell you?

options.A: The number of drops delivered in one milliliter of fluid
options.B: The maximum speed the fluid can flow through the line
options.C: The total number of milliliters the tubing can hold
options.D: The hours the administration set can remain sterile

explanation: You've got this. Drop factor tells you the size of the drops the tubing makes, which you need to know when calculating manual drip rates (gtt/min). [learn more](GNS122_U1_T17#GNS122_U1_T17_h4)

question: An order reads: 1,000 mL normal saline over 8 hours. Your tubing drop factor is 15 gtt/mL. What is the flow rate?

options.A: 63 gtt/min
options.B: 15 gtt/min
options.C: 31 gtt/min
options.D: 125 gtt/min

explanation: Math made simple! Multiply total volume (1000) by drop factor (15) to get 15,000 drops, then divide by total minutes (480 mins). That gives you roughly 31 drops per minute. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T17#GNS122_U1_T17_h4)

question: How often should you change a clean, intact transparent IV dressing?

options.A: Every 24 hours
options.B: Every 7 days
options.C: Only when the IV line is removed
options.D: Every 14 days

explanation: Standard hospital guidelines recommend changing transparent peripheral IV dressings every 7 days unless they get dirty, loose, or wet. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T17#GNS122_U1_T17_h5)

question: Why is it important to regularly check the connection joints of an IV setup?

options.A: To ensure the gravity roller clamp is set to the maximum speed
options.B: To check if the plastic tubing needs to be warmed with a heating pad
options.C: To make sure the manufacturer label matches the client's chart
options.D: To prevent accidental disconnection, fluid leakage, and bacterial entry

explanation: Keeping connections tight keeps the system sterile! It stops messy leaks and prevents nasty bacteria from sneaking into your patient's bloodstream. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T17#GNS122_U1_T17_h5)

question: What is the main difference between infiltration and extravasation?

options.A: Extravasation makes the skin feel very cold, whereas infiltration makes it feel hot
options.B: Infiltration only happens in the legs, while extravasation happens in the arms
options.C: Extravasation involves tissue-damaging vesicant drugs that can cause necrosis
options.D: Infiltration requires immediate surgical removal of the vein tissue

explanation: Both mean fluid leaked out of the vein, but extravasation is extra scary because the leaked drug is a 'vesicant' that can actually destroy the surrounding tissue and cause severe sores. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T17#GNS122_U1_T17_h6)

question: Your IV patient suddenly feels short of breath, has crackles in their lungs, and high blood pressure. What do you do first?

options.A: Slow the infusion rate, elevate the head of the bed, and notify the provider
options.B: Flush the line rapidly with a bolus of normal saline to check patency
options.C: Place the client flat on their left side and prepare for emergency intubation
options.D: Remove the IV cannula immediately and apply a cold ice pack to the limb

explanation: Classic signs of fluid overload! Slowing the fluids and sitting the patient up helps them breathe easier while you alert the doctor. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T17#GNS122_U1_T17_h6)

question: Why must you always inspect the tip of an IV catheter after you remove it?

options.A: To determine what gauge size was used for the infusion
options.B: To measure the exact length of the vein inside the client's arm
options.C: To ensure the catheter tip broke off completely or remained intact
options.D: To check if any blood clots formed inside the plastic tubing

explanation: Always double-check that tiny plastic tip! Ensuring it's in one piece means no broken plastic fragment floated off into the patient's bloodstream. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T17#GNS122_U1_T17_h7)

question: What is the correct technique for pulling out a peripheral IV catheter?

options.A: Twist the hub rapidly while pulling outward with force
options.B: Lift the tip upward quickly at a 90-degree angle
options.C: Flush the line with saline right before pulling it out
options.D: Pull it out smoothly and parallel to the skin surface

explanation: Keep it smooth! Pulling the catheter out parallel to the skin prevents it from scraping or tearing the delicate inside lining of the vein. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T17#GNS122_U1_T17_h7)

question: Why do hospitals nowadays rarely give whole blood to patients?

options.A: Whole blood carries no oxygen-carrying capacity
options.B: Patients usually only need specific blood components
options.C: Whole blood spoils within two hours of collection
options.D: Processing whole blood is too expensive for hospitals

explanation: Great job thinking like a clinician! Blood is separated into parts so patients get precisely what they lack—like just red cells or platelets—rather than getting components they don't need. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T18#GNS122_U1_T18_h1)

question: Why is double-checking the patient's ID band considered the absolute most important rule before a blood transfusion?

options.A: It ensures the hospital billing department charges the correct patient
options.B: It guarantees the blood donor receives proper compensation
options.C: It prevents clerical errors that can cause fatal incompatible reactions
options.D: It speeds up the time it takes to deliver blood from the lab

explanation: Spotting identity mistakes saves lives! Giving blood to the wrong person is a major cause of dangerous reactions, making this check vital. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T18#GNS122_U1_T18_h1)

question: Which blood type is known as the universal red cell donor because almost anyone can safely receive it in emergencies?

options.A: Type AB positive
options.B: Type B negative
options.C: Type A positive
options.D: Type O negative

explanation: You've got this! Type O negative red cells have no main antigens, so they won't trigger an attack in most recipients. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T18#GNS122_U1_T18_h2)

question: What is the main reason lab scientists perform a crossmatch before releasing blood?

options.A: To check for hidden antibodies and ensure true compatibility between donor and recipient
options.B: To determine the patient's exact height and weight for dosage calculations
options.C: To sterilize the blood product before it leaves the blood bank
options.D: To measure the exact volume of red blood cells in the donor bag

explanation: Crossmatching is like a test-drive in a test tube! It mixes donor cells with patient serum to catch any immune clashes early. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T18#GNS122_U1_T18_h2)

question: When should you take a patient's baseline vital signs when getting ready to give a blood transfusion?

options.A: Immediately before starting the transfusion
options.B: Only when the patient complains of fever
options.C: Six hours after the transfusion finishes
options.D: The evening before the procedure is scheduled

explanation: Taking vitals right before the infusion gives you a clear starting point so you can easily spot if anything changes later. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T18#GNS122_U1_T18_h3)

question: How many nurses must check the blood bag details against the patient's ID band?

options.A: Two licensed nurses
options.B: Only one registered nurse
options.C: Any available hospital staff member
options.D: A nurse and a laboratory technician

explanation: Two pairs of eyes are better than one! Having two qualified nurses check together is a mandatory safety net. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T18#GNS122_U1_T18_h3)

question: Which IV fluid is the ONLY one safe to use alongside blood products?

options.A: Ringer's Lactate Solution
options.B: 0.9% Normal Saline
options.C: 5% Dextrose in Water
options.D: Half-Normal Saline

explanation: Normal saline is isotonic and friendly to red blood cells, preventing them from bursting or clumping like other fluids might. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T18#GNS122_U1_T18_h4)

question: Why do nurses prefer using a large-bore cannula (like an 18-gauge) for blood transfusions?

options.A: It prevents the physical damage and destruction of red blood cells
options.B: It prevents the IV site from swelling or leaking into the tissues
options.C: It allows the nurse to infuse multiple medications at the same time
options.D: It reduces the need to check vital signs during the first fifteen minutes

explanation: Think of it like a wide pipe versus a tiny straw—narrow needles can squeeze and break fragile red blood cells, causing damage. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T18#GNS122_U1_T18_h4)

question: How fast should you run a blood transfusion during the very first fifteen minutes?

options.A: As fast as the gravity pump can squeeze
options.B: Completely shut off until vitals stabilize
options.C: Exactly 500 milliliters per hour
options.D: Slowly, around 50 to 60 drops per minute

explanation: Starting slow is a smart safety habit! If a reaction starts, a slow rate means less bad blood enters the body before you catch it. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T18#GNS122_U1_T18_h5)

question: Within how many hours must a single unit of packed red blood cells be completely infused?

options.A: Twelve hours
options.B: Four hours
options.C: Thirty minutes
options.D: Twenty-four hours

explanation: Keep an eye on the clock! Blood must finish within four hours so bacteria don't start multiplying in room temperature. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T18#GNS122_U1_T18_h5)

question: When is the best time to check the second set of vital signs after starting a blood transfusion?

options.A: After thirty minutes
options.B: At the very end of the bag
options.C: After two hours
options.D: After fifteen minutes

explanation: The 15-minute mark is crucial because most serious acute reactions happen right at the beginning of the infusion. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T18#GNS122_U1_T18_h6)

question: Your patient suddenly complains of lower back pain and chills mid-transfusion. What is your immediate nursing action?

options.A: Ignore the symptoms unless the blood pressure drops significantly
options.B: Stop the transfusion immediately and keep the vein open with saline
options.C: Leave the room quickly to fetch the attending physician
options.D: Slow the infusion rate down and give prescribed paracetamol

explanation: Trust your instincts! Back pain and chills are classic warning signs of a hemolytic reaction—stop the infusion right away. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T18#GNS122_U1_T18_h6)

question: Which symptom strongly points to an acute hemolytic transfusion reaction?

options.A: Lower back or flank pain
options.B: Gradual weight loss over days
options.C: Excessive daytime sleepiness
options.D: Severe localized skin dryness

explanation: When red cells break down inside the body, the kidneys take a hit, which often shows up as sharp lower back or flank pain. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T18#GNS122_U1_T18_h7)

question: What usually causes Transfusion-Associated Circulatory Overload (TACO)?

options.A: A mismatched ABO blood type between donor and recipient
options.B: Bacterial contamination of the red blood cells during storage
options.C: An allergic response to donor plasma proteins in the blood bag
options.D: Infusing blood too rapidly for the patient's cardiovascular system to handle

explanation: TACO happens when fluid goes in faster than a patient's heart can pump it, causing fluid backup in the lungs. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T18#GNS122_U1_T18_h7)

question: What fluid should you use to flush the IV tubing after a blood transfusion is complete?

options.A: Plain Tap Water
options.B: 0.9% Normal Saline
options.C: 5% Dextrose Water
options.D: Sterile Water for Injection

explanation: A normal saline flush nicely clears out any remaining blood products from the line without harming the patient's cells. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T18#GNS122_U1_T18_h8)

question: Which of these details is NOT necessary to write down in your notes after a blood transfusion?

options.A: The name of the blood donor's family members
options.B: The product serial number and volume given
options.C: The start and stop times of the infusion
options.D: The patient's post-transfusion vital signs

explanation: Donor privacy is key! Blood banks keep donor details strictly confidential, so they never appear in your patient's chart. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T18#GNS122_U1_T18_h8)

question: What does fluid balance mean in patient care?

options.A: Fluid intake is greater than output
options.B: Urine output equals total blood volume
options.C: Fluid intake equals fluid output
options.D: IV fluids match oral fluid intake

explanation: Fluid balance is achieved when the total volume of fluid entering the body matches the total volume leaving it. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T19#GNS122_U1_T19_h1)

question: Why is fluid balance monitoring especially critical for a patient with heart failure?

options.A: They lose all body fluids through sweating
options.B: Their hearts cannot pump excess fluid effectively
options.C: Their kidneys stop producing urine entirely
options.D: They always have high oral fluid intake

explanation: Compromised heart function makes it hard to handle extra fluid, quickly leading to dangerous fluid overload. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T19#GNS122_U1_T19_h1)

question: Which patient group requires strict fluid intake and output monitoring?

options.A: Patients taking diuretic medications
options.B: Patients waiting for outpatient eye surgery
options.C: Patients with mild, healing skin scratches
options.D: Patients admitted for routine physical exams

explanation: Diuretics alter fluid excretion, making it necessary to track how much urine the patient passes. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T19#GNS122_U1_T19_h2)

question: What is the primary goal of keeping a strict fluid chart on a surgical ward?

options.A: Preventing the patient from needing IV access
options.B: Proving the patient is drinking enough plain water
options.C: Calculating the exact daily hospital food costs
options.D: Detecting early signs of fluid overload or dehydration

explanation: Careful tracking lets nurses spot dangerous imbalances before they cause severe harm. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T19#GNS122_U1_T19_h2)

question: Which item should be counted as part of a patient's fluid intake?

options.A: An intramuscular pain injection
options.B: An intravenous blood transfusion
options.C: A solid tablet pain medication
options.D: A dry solid piece of toast

explanation: Blood products and IV fluids introduce liquid directly into the vascular system and must be counted as intake. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T19#GNS122_U1_T19_h3)

question: A patient drinks a mug of tea, receives an IV antibiotic piggyback, and eats a plate of rice. What counts as fluid intake?

options.A: The tea and the IV antibiotic
options.B: Only the IV antibiotic
options.C: Only the mug of tea
options.D: The tea, IV antibiotic, and rice

explanation: Liquids consumed orally and fluids given intravenously are recorded as intake, while solid food is excluded. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T19#GNS122_U1_T19_h3)

question: Which type of fluid output is typically easiest to measure accurately in a hospital ward?

options.A: Urine collected in a graduated container
options.B: Moisture lost through normal breathing
options.C: Fluid lost from weeping skin wounds
options.D: Sweat lost during a mild afternoon fever

explanation: Urine can be easily captured and measured using marked collection containers or catheter drainage bags. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T19#GNS122_U1_T19_h4)

question: Why are normal losses from breathing and light sweating called insensible fluid losses?

options.A: They only happen when the patient is unconscious
options.B: They do not affect the body's overall fluid balance
options.C: They cannot be measured directly with standard equipment
options.D: They are completely harmless to the human body

explanation: Insensible losses evaporate continuously into the air and through the skin without leaving a pool of liquid to measure. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T19#GNS122_U1_T19_h4)

question: What is the correct way to read fluid volume in a graduated cylinder?

options.A: Looking down from a standing position
options.B: Holding the cylinder up to a bright light
options.C: At eye level on a flat surface
options.D: Tilting the container at a 45-degree angle

explanation: Reading at eye level on a flat surface prevents parallax errors and ensures the measurement is correct. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T19#GNS122_U1_T19_h5)

question: How do nurses accurately measure fluid output from a heavy surgical dressing or pad?

options.A: Estimating the stain size using a common ruler
options.B: Squeezing the fluid out into a measuring cup
options.C: Asking the patient how much fluid they think leaked
options.D: Weighing the wet item and subtracting the dry weight

explanation: Weight is the most reliable way to quantify fluid soaked into solid materials, where one gram roughly equals one milliliter. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T19#GNS122_U1_T19_h5)

question: What standard unit of measurement is used on a hospital fluid intake and output chart?

options.A: Kilograms
options.B: Liters
options.C: Milliliters
options.D: Ounces

explanation: Milliliters provide the precise detail needed to track small fluid shifts safely. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T19#GNS122_U1_T19_h6)

question: A patient drinks a six-ounce cup of juice. How many milliliters should the nurse record on the chart?

options.A: 60 milliliters
options.B: 180 milliliters
options.C: 300 milliliters
options.D: 120 milliliters

explanation: Multiplying six ounces by thirty milliliters per ounce gives a total volume of 180 milliliters. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T19#GNS122_U1_T19_h6)

question: What does a positive fluid balance indicate for a patient over a twenty-four-hour period?

options.A: Output was greater than intake
options.B: The patient lost too much body weight
options.C: Intake and output were perfectly even
options.D: Intake was greater than output

explanation: A positive balance means more fluid entered the body than was eliminated, leaving a surplus behind. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T19#GNS122_U1_T19_h7)

question: A patient has a total fluid intake of 2,200 milliliters and a total output of 1,500 milliliters. What is their net balance?

options.A: Negative 700 milliliters
options.B: Positive 3,700 milliliters
options.C: Negative 3,700 milliliters
options.D: Positive 700 milliliters

explanation: Subtracting 1,500 output from 2,200 intake leaves a remaining surplus of 700 milliliters. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T19#GNS122_U1_T19_h7)

question: Which nursing action compromises the accuracy of a fluid balance chart?

options.A: Waiting until the end of the shift to guess and write down intake amounts
options.B: Involving the patient and family in reporting oral drinks
options.C: Converting all cup and bowl volumes into milliliters promptly
options.D: Notifying the doctor immediately about a sudden drop in urine output

explanation: Relying on memory causes missed entries and incorrect data that jeopardize patient safety. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T19#GNS122_U1_T19_h8)

question: Why is it vital to educate family members about the fluid chart when they are visiting?

options.A: Family members must empty the bedpans during visiting hours
options.B: Education keeps visitors from drinking the patient's water
options.C: Visitors often give the patient drinks that need to be recorded
options.D: Visitors are legally required to sign off on the hospital chart

explanation: Family members frequently bring water, juice, or tea, and nurses must capture these amounts to keep the record accurate. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T19#GNS122_U1_T19_h8)

question: What is the primary organ responsible for the first-pass effect of oral medications?

options.A: The pancreas
options.B: The stomach
options.C: The liver
options.D: The kidneys

explanation: Blood from the digestive tract flows directly to the liver through the portal system, where drugs undergo significant metabolism before reaching the rest of the body. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T2#GNS122_U1_T2_h1)

question: Why are oral medication doses often higher than intravenous doses of the same drug?

options.A: Oral medications dissolve much slower in the bloodstream than IV fluids
options.B: The stomach acid completely destroys most active drug ingredients
options.C: Part of the drug is broken down by the liver before reaching the bloodstream
options.D: The intestines absorb only a tiny fraction of swallowed medicines

explanation: The first-pass effect breaks down a portion of the oral drug in the liver, meaning a higher dose is needed to achieve the same therapeutic effect as an IV dose. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T2#GNS122_U1_T2_h1)

question: What is a major advantage of the oral route of drug administration?

options.A: It is convenient and economical for the patient
options.B: It is completely safe for unconscious patients
options.C: It bypasses the liver completely
options.D: It works faster than intravenous injections

explanation: Swallowing pills requires no special sterile equipment and can easily be managed by conscious patients, making it cost-effective and convenient. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T2#GNS122_U1_T2_h2)

question: When should a nurse avoid giving medications by the oral route?

options.A: When the drug is prescribed in liquid form
options.B: When the patient is eating a normal meal
options.C: When the patient has a mild headache
options.D: When the patient is vomiting or unconscious

explanation: Unconscious or vomiting patients cannot swallow safely, placing them at high risk of choking or aspirating medication into their lungs. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T2#GNS122_U1_T2_h2)

question: Why are some oral tablets manufactured with an enteric coating?

options.A: To protect the stomach lining and prevent the drug from dissolving too early
options.B: To combine two different drugs into a single dose
options.C: To help the medicine dissolve instantly in the mouth
options.D: To make the pill taste sweet for young children

explanation: Enteric-coated drugs are designed to pass through the acidic stomach unharmed and only dissolve once they reach the small intestine. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T2#GNS122_U1_T2_h3)

question: A patient asks if they can crush a sustained-release tablet because they have trouble swallowing large pills. What is the best nursing action?

options.A: Contact the prescriber or pharmacist to find an alternative liquid form
options.B: Dissolve the whole pill in a glass of warm water
options.C: Crush the pill thoroughly and mix it with applesauce
options.D: Cut the pill in half using a tablet cutter

explanation: Crushing sustained-release or enteric-coated medications destroys their special delivery mechanism, leading to a dangerous surge of the drug all at once. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T2#GNS122_U1_T2_h3)

question: What is the primary action a nurse should perform before preparing any medication?

options.A: Check the patient's room temperature
options.B: Ask the family member what drugs the patient takes
options.C: Verify the order against the medication administration record
options.D: Wash the medication trolley with bleach

explanation: Comparing the medication order against the official administration record prevents medication errors and ensures patient safety. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T2#GNS122_U1_T2_h4)

question: Why should a nurse assess a patient's swallowing ability before giving oral pills?

options.A: To prevent choking and potential aspiration into the lungs
options.B: To see if the patient has any food allergies
options.C: To check how fast the liver will metabolize the drug
options.D: To determine if the patient prefers liquid or solid medicines

explanation: Swallowing difficulties place patients at high risk of aspirating foreign objects or liquids into the respiratory tract. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T2#GNS122_U1_T2_h4)

question: How many unique patient identifiers should a nurse check before giving medication?

options.A: Only one
options.B: At least two
options.C: Exactly four
options.D: None if the nurse knows the patient well

explanation: Using at least two patient identifiers, such as checking the hospital band and asking the patient's name, ensures the correct person receives the medication. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T2#GNS122_U1_T2_h5)

question: Which scenario represents a violation of the 'right time' medication principle?

options.A: Crushing a simple uncoated tablet for a patient who cannot swallow pills
options.B: Giving a routine morning antibiotic two hours late without a valid reason
options.C: Documenting the medication immediately after the patient swallows it
options.D: Checking the patient's identification band before opening the package

explanation: Administering medications significantly outside their scheduled time frame can cause blood levels to drop too low or spike too high. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T2#GNS122_U1_T2_h5)

question: What position should a patient be in when receiving oral medications?

options.A: Upright sitting position
options.B: Flat on their back
options.C: Lying on their left side
options.D: Bent over at the waist

explanation: An upright or elevated sitting position uses gravity to help the patient swallow safely and prevents choking. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T2#GNS122_U1_T2_h6)

question: A nurse hands a patient their morning pills, but the patient is busy talking on the phone and asks the nurse to leave the cup on the bedside table. What should the nurse do?

options.A: Place the pills in the patient's water cup so they dissolve for later
options.B: Take the pills away and document that the patient refused the medication
options.C: Leave the pills on the table and remind the nurse's assistant to check later
options.D: Stay with the patient, wait until they finish the call, and watch them take the pills

explanation: Medications should never be left unattended at the bedside because the patient might forget them, take them incorrectly, or someone else might take them. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T2#GNS122_U1_T2_h6)

question: What term describes the use of multiple medications simultaneously, which is common in older adults?

options.A: Enteric coating
options.B: Polypharmacy
options.C: Aspiration risk
options.D: First-pass effect

explanation: Polypharmacy refers to the concurrent use of multiple drugs by a patient, which frequently happens in geriatric care and raises the risk of drug interactions. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T2#GNS122_U1_T2_h7)

question: Why are pediatric medication doses usually calculated based on the child's body weight?

options.A: Weight calculations are only used for intravenous drugs, not oral ones
options.B: Children's body composition and organ maturity differ greatly from adults
options.C: Children refuse to swallow pills that weigh more than a certain amount
options.D: Hospital pharmacies only stock liquid medicines in weight-based bottles

explanation: Because children process drugs differently due to developing organs and varying body mass, doses must be individualized by weight to prevent toxicity. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T2#GNS122_U1_T2_h7)

question: When should a nurse document that a medication has been given to a patient?

options.A: Immediately after the patient swallows the medication
options.B: Before pouring the medication from the stock bottle
options.C: At the end of the entire nursing shift
options.D: Whenever the nurse has spare time during the day

explanation: Documenting right after administration prevents accidental double-dosing and ensures an accurate, up-to-date medical record. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T2#GNS122_U1_T2_h8)

question: What is the main purpose of post-administration monitoring after giving an oral drug?

options.A: To update the hospital kitchen about the patient's dietary intake
options.B: To clean the medication cup and return it to the storage room
options.C: To calculate how much money the patient owes for the prescription
options.D: To evaluate if the drug worked and watch for any adverse reactions

explanation: Monitoring ensures the medication produces the desired therapeutic outcome and allows the nurse to catch side effects or allergic reactions early. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T2#GNS122_U1_T2_h8)

question: What is the main reason a nurse dilutes a medicated lotion?

options.A: To change the color of the cream
options.B: To decrease its active concentration
options.C: To make the container last longer
options.D: To speed up the drying process

explanation: Dilution lowers the percentage of the active drug so it is gentler on sensitive skin. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T20#GNS122_U1_T20_h1)

question: Why can altering a ready-made topical cream cause problems?

options.A: It changes the expiration date to the exact same day
options.B: It breaks down the product stability and preservatives
options.C: It automatically turns the lotion into a liquid
options.D: It causes the active ingredient to evaporate instantly

explanation: Mixing products messes up the chemical balance and can make it easier for bacteria to grow. Don't worry, you'll get the hang of product safety in no time! [learn more](GNS122_U1_T20#GNS122_U1_T20_h1)

question: Which body area absorbs topical medications the fastest, often requiring a lower concentration?

options.A: The face and skin folds
options.B: The soles of the feet
options.C: The palms of the hands
options.D: The thick skin of the back

explanation: Thin skin areas absorb medications much quicker, increasing the risk of irritation if the drug is too strong. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T20#GNS122_U1_T20_h2)

question: A patient with a healing skin rash is stepped down to a milder lotion. What is the goal of this change?

options.A: To remove the need for any further skin assessments
options.B: To completely stop all moisture from reaching the skin
options.C: To maintain skin healing without causing local side effects
options.D: To increase the absorption speed of the original drug

explanation: We use weaker strengths as healing progresses to protect the skin safely without over-treating it. Great job keeping the patient's comfort in mind! [learn more](GNS122_U1_T20#GNS122_U1_T20_h2)

question: What is the main job of a vehicle when diluting a lotion?

options.A: To act as a safe base that mixes well with the active drug
options.B: To completely neutralize the active drug's healing properties
options.C: To add a strong fragrance to cover up chemical odors
options.D: To change a liquid medication into a hard tablet

explanation: Think of the vehicle as a friendly carrier base that helps you spread the active medicine evenly without fuss. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T20#GNS122_U1_T20_h3)

question: What happens when you mix two bases that don't go together?

options.A: The mixture separates and delivers an uneven dose
options.B: The mixture instantly cures all skin infections
options.C: The chemical formula permanently turns into a solid block
options.D: The active medication becomes twice as strong

explanation: If bases don't match, they split apart, meaning some parts of the cream will have too much drug and others too little. You've got this! [learn more](GNS122_U1_T20#GNS122_U1_T20_h3)

question: When preparing a weaker cream from a stronger stock, what is your very first step?

options.A: Identify the starting strength and your target strength
options.B: Measure the patient's daily fluid intake and output
options.C: Throw away half of the total stock bottle immediately
options.D: Add water directly into the manufacturer's original tube

explanation: Always check where you are starting (stock strength) and where you want to end up before doing any math! [learn more](GNS122_U1_T20#GNS122_U1_T20_h4)

question: After figuring out how much active medication you need for a dilution, how do you find out how much plain base to add?

options.A: Subtract the active medication volume from the total target volume
options.B: Use the exact same amount of stock cream as the final volume
options.C: Multiply the active medication volume by the target percentage
options.D: Add equal parts of water regardless of the final volume needed

explanation: Simply take your total target amount, subtract the active cream you measured, and fill the remaining space with your plain base. Simple and easy! [learn more](GNS122_U1_T20#GNS122_U1_T20_h4)

question: Why do nurses use geometric dilution when mixing creams?

options.A: To ensure an even and thorough blend of the active drug
options.B: To remove all the natural oils from the base vehicle
options.C: To speed up the drying time of the lotion on the skin
options.D: To make the final mixture change color as it mixes

explanation: Mixing equal amounts gradually keeps the active drug from clumping up in one spot. It's a neat little trick of the trade! [learn more](GNS122_U1_T20#GNS122_U1_T20_h5)

question: Which of these tools do you need on your clean workspace when mixing a topical dilution?

options.A: A standard household kitchen spoon
options.B: A clean mixing tile and spatula
options.C: A sterile surgical scalpel
options.D: A glass measuring cup for oral liquids

explanation: A clean flat tile and a spatula give you a nice, sanitary surface to blend your creams smoothly. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T20#GNS122_U1_T20_h5)

question: What vital information must go on the label of a freshly diluted lotion?

options.A: New concentration and expiration date
options.B: The name of the pharmacy technician who delivered it
options.C: The manufacturer's original batch number only
options.D: The patient's room number and diagnosis

explanation: Always label the new strength and expiry date so no one accidentally applies the wrong dose. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T20#GNS122_U1_T20_h6)

question: Why does a freshly mixed diluted lotion expire much faster than the original factory product?

options.A: Mixing breaks down preservatives and introduces potential microbes
options.B: The active drug evaporates completely within twenty-four hours
options.C: The packaging material reacts poorly to room lighting
options.D: Air pressure inside the room changes the chemical balance

explanation: Opening and mixing a product outside the factory opens the door to germs and weakens its built-in preservatives. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T20#GNS122_U1_T20_h6)

question: In which direction should you smooth a topical lotion onto a patient's skin?

options.A: Strictly from the bottom of the limb upward
options.B: In a crisscross pattern across the rash
options.C: In the direction of hair growth
options.D: In tight circular motions against the hair

explanation: Smoothing lotions in the direction of hair growth keeps hair follicles happy and prevents painful inflammation. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T20#GNS122_U1_T20_h7)

question: What should you do to the skin before putting on a newly diluted medicated lotion?

options.A: Apply a thick layer of oil to seal the pores
options.B: Clean and dry the skin gently
options.C: Scrub the area firmly with an antiseptic pad
options.D: Warm the skin with a heating pad for ten minutes

explanation: A gentle wash removes dirt without upsetting the skin barrier. Nice and easy! [learn more](GNS122_U1_T20#GNS122_U1_T20_h7)

question: What is the big danger if you fail to mix a diluted lotion thoroughly?

options.A: Extending the expiration date by several months
options.B: Turning the entire mixture into a watery liquid
options.C: Creating concentrated hot spots that irritate the skin
options.D: Changing the color of the cream to bright yellow

explanation: If you don't mix it well, pockets of high-strength medicine can hide in the cream and sting the patient's skin. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T20#GNS122_U1_T20_h8)

question: Which sign tells you a mixed lotion should be thrown away immediately?

options.A: A label showing it was mixed three days ago
options.B: Visible separation or discoloration
options.C: A smooth and uniform texture throughout
options.D: A slight cooling sensation upon skin contact

explanation: If the cream separates or changes color, it means it has gone bad and is no longer safe to use. You're doing great! [learn more](GNS122_U1_T20#GNS122_U1_T20_h8)

question: What happens to the solid particles in a drug suspension over time?

options.A: Solid particles are dispersed and tend to settle
options.B: Solid particles are fully dissolved in the liquid
options.C: Active ingredients are bound permanently to the bottle
options.D: The mixture remains completely clear at all times

explanation: Think of muddy water! Suspensions have tiny bits of medicine floating around that love to sink to the bottom if left alone. That's why we always shake them first! [learn more](GNS122_U1_T21#GNS122_U1_T21_h1)

question: Why is it risky to give a patient an unmixed suspension right from the bottle?

options.A: The liquid will foam up and block the patient's airway
options.B: The patient might get a weak dose first and a toxic dose last
options.C: The medicine will taste too sweet and cause vomiting
options.D: The solid particles will react chemically with stomach acid

explanation: Spot on! Since the medicine settles at the bottom, an unmixed bottle means watery liquid at first (weak dose) and a sludgy finish at the end (too strong!). [learn more](GNS122_U1_T21#GNS122_U1_T21_h1)

question: When giving a thick oral suspension through a feeding tube, why do we dilute it first?

options.A: To make the medication taste much sweeter
options.B: To destroy harmful bacteria growing in the liquid
options.C: To prevent the thick liquid from clogging the tube
options.D: To speed up how fast the drug enters the bloodstream

explanation: You got it! Thick syrups and suspensions love to gum up feeding tubes. Diluting keeps everything flowing smoothly so the patient gets their full feed and meds. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T21#GNS122_U1_T21_h2)

question: How does diluting a medication help when giving tiny doses to an infant?

options.A: It completely eliminates all potential drug side effects
options.B: It makes measuring a larger volume more accurate
options.C: It prevents the infant from developing a drug allergy
options.D: It shortens the half-life of the drug in the body

explanation: Measuring tiny drops like 0.2 mL can be nerve-wracking. Diluting lets you draw up a slightly bigger, much safer-to-measure amount! [learn more](GNS122_U1_T21#GNS122_U1_T21_h2)

question: What is an essential safety habit after calculating a children's drug dose?

options.A: Throw away half of the calculated medication
options.B: Heat the liquid to body temperature before giving
options.C: Ask another nurse to double-check the math
options.D: Store the leftover mixture in a dark refrigerator

explanation: Two pairs of eyes are always better than one, especially with kids' doses! A quick double-check keeps everyone safe and builds your clinical confidence. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T21#GNS122_U1_T21_h3)

question: A doctor orders 250 mg of a suspension. The bottle label says 125 mg per 5 mL. How much should you measure?

options.B: 10 mL
options.C: 5 mL
options.D: 2.5 mL

explanation: Nice calculation! Dose ordered (250) divided by stock dose (125) equals 2. Multiply that by 5 mL, and you get 10 mL. You're getting the hang of this! [learn more](GNS122_U1_T21#GNS122_U1_T21_h3)

question: What is the very first thing you should do before preparing to measure a medication?

options.A: Shake the empty measuring cup vigorously
options.B: Pour the medication directly down the drain
options.C: Heat the glass bottle in a microwave oven
options.D: Perform hand hygiene and put on gloves

explanation: Safety first! Standard infection control always starts with clean hands before touching any patient supplies or medications. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T21#GNS122_U1_T21_h4)

question: Why must you shake a suspension bottle vigorously right before pouring a dose?

options.A: To cool down the liquid inside the glass container
options.B: To evenly redistribute settled solid drug particles
options.C: To check if the outer safety seal is broken
options.D: To create air bubbles that make the drug taste better

explanation: Shaking mixes the active medicine back into the liquid so the patient gets the right dose, not just flavored water! [learn more](GNS122_U1_T21#GNS122_U1_T21_h4)

question: Which of these habits helps keep oral syringes clean and free of germs?

options.A: Rinsing the dirty syringe in a shared sink basin
options.B: Storing open syringes in a warm pocket all day
options.C: Avoiding touching the syringe tip to any surface
options.D: Touching the tip directly to the patient's tongue

explanation: Keep that tip sterile! Touching it to counters or fingers can introduce unwanted bacteria right back into the medicine bottle. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T21#GNS122_U1_T21_h5)

question: What can happen if you mix certain suspensions with the wrong type of liquid?

options.A: The liquid immediately changes into a bright gas
options.B: The drug becomes twice as potent instantly
options.C: The active drug may precipitate or break down
options.D: The medication turns into a solid plastic block

explanation: Chemical reactions can ruin a drug! Mixing incompatible fluids can cause the medicine to clump up, fall apart, or lose its healing power. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T21#GNS122_U1_T21_h5)

question: What key tip should you teach a mother giving an oral suspension to her toddler at home?

options.A: Store the open bottle on a sunny kitchen windowsill
options.B: Shake the bottle well immediately before every single dose
options.C: Mix the entire bottle with juice and keep it on the counter
options.D: Stop the medication as soon as the child feels better

explanation: Empowering mothers with good education is key! Reminding them to shake the bottle every time ensures the child gets the exact medicine they need. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T21#GNS122_U1_T21_h6)

question: Where is the safest place in an infant's mouth to squirt liquid medication?

options.A: Between the infant's cheek and gum in the side of the mouth
options.B: Underneath the infant's tongue like a sublingual tablet
options.C: Mixed into a large bowl of hot porridge for breakfast
options.D: Directly down the center of the infant's throat

explanation: Smart nursing trick! Pushing liquid into the side of the cheek prevents choking and gagging, making medicine time much calmer for baby and nurse. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T21#GNS122_U1_T21_h6)

question: What crucial detail must you write on a newly mixed (reconstituted) suspension bottle?

options.A: The patient's room number and diagnosis
options.B: The exact date and time the medication expires
options.C: The name of the pharmacy supplier
options.D: The manufacturer's original stock number

explanation: Always label your mixtures! Reconstituted drugs spoil fast once water is added, so tracking the expiry date keeps your patient safe. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T21#GNS122_U1_T21_h7)

question: Why do freshly mixed (reconstituted) suspensions expire much faster than dry powders?

options.A: The active drug evaporates into the air inside the room
options.B: The plastic bottle begins to melt in the refrigerator
options.C: Water activates chemical breakdown and microbial growth
options.D: Refrigeration destroys the chemical bonds of the powder

explanation: Water wakes everything up! Once water is added, it triggers chemical breakdown and creates a cozy home for bacteria to multiply. That's why they don't last long. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T21#GNS122_U1_T21_h7)

question: What is the primary reason for diluting a highly concentrated intravenous medication?

options.A: To change the chemical class of the drug
options.B: To make the medication expire much slower
options.C: To eliminate the need for sterile technique
options.D: To reduce irritation to the blood vessels

explanation: High concentrations of certain drugs can damage vein walls and cause severe pain or tissue injury. Diluting them lowers this risk. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T22#GNS122_U1_T22_h1)

question: Why are certain medications supplied to the hospital ward in powdered form instead of ready-to-use liquids?

options.A: Powders do not require any mathematical calculations to mix
options.B: Powders have a much longer shelf-life before reconstitution
options.C: Powders can be swallowed directly if the injection fails
options.D: Powders automatically dissolve in normal room air moisture

explanation: Many active drug compounds break down quickly in liquid form. Manufacturers supply them as powders to maintain stability until right before use. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T22#GNS122_U1_T22_h1)

question: What does it mean when a medication and a diluent are incompatible and form a precipitate?

options.A: Solid particles form and turn the mixture cloudy
options.B: The temperature of the syringe drops drastically
options.C: The mixture changes into a harmless gas bubbles
options.D: The volume of the liquid increases on its own

explanation: Precipitation creates solid particles or crystals in the fluid, which can cause dangerous blockages if injected into the body. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T22#GNS122_U1_T22_h2)

question: Where should a nurse look first to confirm which diluent is safe for a specific powdered medication?

options.A: The nursing station whiteboard schedule for the current shift
options.B: The patient's daily food and fluid intake preference chart
options.C: The general hospital cleaning and sanitation protocol manual
options.D: The official drug manufacturer package insert or pharmacy reference

explanation: The manufacturer package insert or hospital pharmacy guide provides precise instructions on approved diluents and safe mixing ratios. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T22#GNS122_U1_T22_h2)

question: What does 'displacement volume' mean when reconstituting a powdered medication in a vial?

options.A: The leftover medicine discarded after the injection is given
options.B: The speed at which the plunger pushes the fluid out
options.C: The amount of liquid lost through evaporation during mixing
options.D: The extra space taken up by the dry powder inside the liquid

explanation: Dry powder adds physical volume to the vial when mixed with a liquid, which can change the final concentration if not accounted for. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T22#GNS122_U1_T22_h3)

question: A doctor orders 250 mg of a drug. The vial contains 500 mg of powder. The instructions state to add 2 mL of sterile water to yield 500 mg per 2 mL. How many milliliters should the nurse withdraw?

options.A: 1 mL
options.B: 4 mL
options.C: 0.5 mL
options.D: 2 mL

explanation: If 500 mg is in 2 mL, then half the dose (250 mg) is found in half the volume, which is 1 mL. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T22#GNS122_U1_T22_h3)

question: Why must a nurse use a filter needle when drawing medication from a glass ampoule?

options.A: To make the plunger move more smoothly inside the barrel
options.B: To filter out bacteria present in the room air
options.C: To change the chemical pH of the liquid medicine
options.D: To prevent tiny glass shards from entering the syringe

explanation: Snapping the neck of a glass ampoule creates microscopic shards. A filter needle traps these fragments so they are not injected into the patient. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T22#GNS122_U1_T22_h4)

question: What is the correct action to take if a sterile syringe needle accidentally brushes against the outside of the nurse's clean uniform?

options.A: Use the needle anyway since the uniform was freshly laundered
options.B: Discard the needle and syringe immediately and get new ones
options.C: Wipe the needle with an alcohol swab and continue using it
options.D: Dip the needle into boiling water for ten seconds before use

explanation: Uniforms are not sterile. Any contact with non-sterile surfaces contaminates the equipment, requiring immediate replacement to prevent infection. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T22#GNS122_U1_T22_h4)

question: What happens if a nurse shakes a vial of reconstituted medication too vigorously?

options.A: The active ingredients in the medication instantly multiply
options.B: The medicine changes color to indicate it is ready
options.C: Excessive foam and bubbles form, making accurate measurement difficult
options.D: The glass vial shatters due to rapid temperature changes

explanation: Vigorous shaking whips air into the liquid, creating foam and bubbles that distort volume measurements inside the syringe. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T22#GNS122_U1_T22_h5)

question: Why is air injected into a closed medication vial before withdrawing the liquid?

options.A: To equalize pressure and make fluid withdrawal easier
options.B: To cool down the medication temperature inside the vial
options.C: To kill any bacteria that might be living in the drug
options.D: To dilute the medication before it enters the needle

explanation: Injecting air replaces the volume of liquid being removed, preventing a vacuum from forming inside the vial which makes drawing fluid difficult. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T22#GNS122_U1_T22_h5)

question: Which piece of information is NOT strictly required on a medication label immediately after dilution?

options.A: The exact dose and concentration prepared
options.B: The patient's favorite hobby or pastime
options.C: The generic or brand name of the drug
options.D: The initials of the nurse who mixed it

explanation: Personal hobbies are irrelevant to medication safety. Labels require identification of the drug, dose, patient, time, and preparer. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T22#GNS122_U1_T22_h6)

question: What is the primary danger of leaving a prepared, diluted injection unlabeled on a medication cart?

options.A: The medicine will automatically change into a solid block
options.B: The plastic barrel of the syringe will dissolve within minutes
options.C: Another healthcare worker might administer the wrong drug or dose
options.D: The expiration date of the diluent will immediately reset

explanation: Unlabeled medications invite administration errors, as staff cannot verify what substance, concentration, or patient the syringe belongs to. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T22#GNS122_U1_T22_h6)

question: Why do nurses need to master drug dosage calculations?

options.A: To prevent medication errors and keep patients safe
options.B: To save money on pharmacy supplies
options.C: To speed up morning rounds
options.D: To skip calling the doctor

explanation: Calculations act as your final safety net to make sure patients get the exact right dose—no more, no less. You've got this! [learn more](GNS122_U1_T23#GNS122_U1_T23_h1)

question: When should you, as the nurse, do your final dosage calculation?

options.A: Only when the pharmacist calls
options.B: Right before giving the drug
options.C: After a bad reaction happens
options.D: During your annual nursing review

explanation: Always double-check your math right before administration. It is your last chance to catch mistakes before the drug enters the patient's body. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T23#GNS122_U1_T23_h1)

question: In a fraction, what does the bottom number (the denominator) stand for?

options.A: The total number of equal parts making up the whole
options.B: The maximum adult dose limit
options.C: A metric conversion factor
options.D: The part ordered by the doctor

explanation: Think of a pizza! The denominator at the bottom tells you the total number of slices the whole pizza is cut into. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T23#GNS122_U1_T23_h2)

question: How should you write five-tenths as a decimal to avoid a dangerous dosing error?
explanation: Always put a leading zero before the decimal point (0.5 instead of .5). If you miss the dot on '.5', it looks like 5—and that's a massive overdose! [learn more](GNS122_U1_T23#GNS122_U1_T23_h2)

question: What is the standard metric unit for measuring liquid volume in the ward?

options.A: Drop
options.B: Grain
options.C: Pound
options.D: Milliliter

explanation: Liters and milliliters (mL) are our go-to units for measuring liquid medications and IV fluids every day. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T23#GNS122_U1_T23_h3)

question: Why do we love using the metric system in healthcare?

options.A: Only international companies use it
options.B: It means no math is ever needed
options.C: Patients never ask questions about it
options.D: It uses a simple base-ten scale that makes conversions safe and easy

explanation: Base-ten means you can convert units just by moving the decimal point. No complicated math required! [learn more](GNS122_U1_T23#GNS122_U1_T23_h3)

question: How many milligrams are in a single gram?

options.A: 100 milligrams
options.B: 1,000 milligrams
options.C: 10 milligrams
options.D: 1,000,000 milligrams

explanation: Remember that 'milli' means one-thousandth. So, it takes 1,000 milligrams to make one full gram. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T23#GNS122_U1_T23_h4)

question: Your patient weighs 154 pounds. What is their weight in kilograms?

options.A: 154 kg
options.B: 77 kg
options.C: 70 kg
options.D: 348 kg

explanation: Just divide pounds by 2.2! So, 154 ÷ 2.2 gives you 70 kg. Easy peasy. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T23#GNS122_U1_T23_h4)

question: What key detail does a drug label tell you about its strength?

options.A: The amount of active drug per tablet, capsule, or milliliter
options.B: The name of the drug rep
options.C: The patient's diagnosis
options.D: How much the hospital paid for it

explanation: The label strength tells you the concentration—how much medicine is actually packed into each pill or mL. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T23#GNS122_U1_T23_h5)

question: What should you do if a doctor's written order is messy or unclear?

options.A: Guess based on the diagnosis
options.B: Give half the dose just to be safe
options.C: Ask another patient in the ward
options.D: Call the prescriber directly to clarify

explanation: Never guess! Always contact the doctor who wrote the order to clear up any confusion before giving the drug. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T23#GNS122_U1_T23_h5)

question: In the classic formula (Desired over Have), what does the letter 'D' stand for?

options.A: Daily maximum limit
options.B: Drop factor of the IV set
options.C: Dilution volume
options.D: Desired dose ordered by the prescriber

explanation: 'D' is simply what the doctor Desires (ordered) for the patient to receive. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T23#GNS122_U1_T23_h6)

question: The doctor orders Paracetamol 500 mg. Pharmacy sends Paracetamol scored tablets of 250 mg each. How many tablets will you give?

options.A: 1 tablet
options.B: 0.5 tablets
options.C: 4 tablets
options.D: 2 tablets

explanation: Using Desired over Have: (500 mg / 250 mg) × 1 tablet = 2 tablets. Perfect! [learn more](GNS122_U1_T23#GNS122_U1_T23_h6)

question: Why do we calculate children's drug doses based on their body weight?

options.A: Kids can't swallow adult pills
options.B: Hospital insurance requires it for kids
options.C: Children process and clear drugs differently based on size
options.D: It helps check expiration dates

explanation: Children's bodies and organs are still developing, so weight-based dosing is vital to avoid accidental overdose. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T23#GNS122_U1_T23_h7)

question: A child weighs 20 kg. The safe dose is 5 mg/kg/day. What is the total daily dose?

options.A: 4 mg
options.B: 100 mg
options.C: 25 mg
options.D: 200 mg

explanation: Multiply weight by the dose per kg: 20 kg × 5 mg = 100 mg daily. You've got this math down! [learn more](GNS122_U1_T23#GNS122_U1_T23_h7)

question: What does 'drop factor' mean when setting up a gravity IV line?

options.A: How fast blood pressure drops
options.B: The number of drops in one milliliter for that specific tubing set
options.C: The maximum speed for potassium
options.D: The total time for an IV bag to empty

explanation: Check the IV tubing box! The drop factor tells you how many drops (gtt) make up 1 mL, like 15 gtt/mL. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T23#GNS122_U1_T23_h8)

question: An IV bag of 1,000 mL Normal Saline is ordered to run over 8 hours using a pump. What is the hourly rate?

options.A: 150 mL/hr
options.B: 80 mL/hr
options.C: 125 mL/hr
options.D: 100 mL/hr

explanation: Divide total volume by total hours: 1,000 mL ÷ 8 hours = 125 mL/hr. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T23#GNS122_U1_T23_h8)

question: Which of the following describes an independent double-check for high-risk medication calculations?

options.A: The doctor and patient calculate the pill count together at discharge
options.B: The pharmacist calculates the dose and the nurse administers it without review
options.C: One nurse calculates the dose twice on two different patient charts
options.D: Two nurses calculate the dose separately without discussing their numbers beforehand

explanation: Independent double-checks require two clinicians to work out the math separately to catch hidden errors before administration. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T23#GNS122_U1_T23_h9)

question: Which of these practices is DANGEROUS and should be avoided when writing dosages?

options.A: Writing out the word 'units' instead of abbreviations
options.B: Using a leading zero before a decimal (0.5 mg)
options.C: Using a trailing zero after a whole number (e.g., 5.0 mg)
options.D: Checking unfamiliar doses in a drug handbook

explanation: Never use trailing zeros! If the decimal point gets smudged, 5.0 mg can easily look like 50 mg. Keep it simple and safe (just write 5 mg). [learn more](GNS122_U1_T23#GNS122_U1_T23_h9)

question: Why do intramuscular injections get absorbed faster than subcutaneous ones?

options.A: Subcutaneous fat contains no blood vessels
options.B: Muscles produce enzymes that break down drugs
options.C: The needle used is always much thinner
options.D: Muscle tissue has a rich blood supply

explanation: Great job thinking about how drugs move in the body! Muscles have plenty of blood vessels, which helps medications rush quickly into the bloodstream. You've got this! [learn more](GNS122_U1_T3#GNS122_U1_T3_h1)

question: When would you choose an intramuscular injection instead of giving pills by mouth?

options.A: When the patient cannot take oral medications
options.B: When the patient wants to avoid any skin punctures
options.C: When the medication needs to work over a full week
options.D: When the drug is completely harmless to the stomach

explanation: Spot on! If a patient is vomiting or unable to swallow, going through the muscle is a safe and reliable backup plan. Keep up the good work! [learn more](GNS122_U1_T3#GNS122_U1_T3_h1)

question: What is the safest site for giving an intramuscular injection to an adult?

options.A: Dorsogluteal
options.B: Vastus lateralis
options.C: Deltoid
options.D: Ventrogluteal

explanation: You got it! The ventrogluteal site is clear of major nerves and blood vessels, making it the safest choice for adult IM injections. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T3#GNS122_U1_T3_h2)

question: You need to give a routine vaccine to a 12-month-old baby. Which site should you use?

options.A: Deltoid
options.B: Dorsogluteal
options.C: Vastus lateralis
options.D: Ventrogluteal

explanation: Brilliant! The vastus lateralis (outer thigh) is well-developed in infants and is the recommended spot for their routine immunizations. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T3#GNS122_U1_T3_h2)

question: What does a higher needle gauge number actually mean?

options.A: A longer needle shaft
options.B: A duller needle tip
options.C: A thinner needle diameter
options.D: A larger medication volume

explanation: It can feel confusing at first, but remember: the higher the gauge number, the thinner the needle! You're learning fast. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T3#GNS122_U1_T3_h3)

question: Why must you split a 5ml medication dose into two separate injection sites for an adult?

options.A: Single adult IM sites should not exceed three milliliters
options.B: Thick oils prevent the plunger from moving past three milliliters
options.C: Patients are allergic to volumes greater than two milliliters
options.D: All syringes break if filled past the halfway mark

explanation: That's right! Putting more than 3ml into one muscle site causes too much pressure, severe pain, and poor drug absorption. Splitting it keeps your patient comfortable. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T3#GNS122_U1_T3_h3)

question: Why do you need the patient's muscle to be relaxed before giving an IM injection?

options.A: It prevents the needle from bending inside the skin
options.B: It stops local bleeding from tiny blood vessels
options.C: It makes insertion easier and decreases pain
options.D: It speeds up the chemical breakdown of the drug

explanation: Exactly! A relaxed muscle lets the needle slide in smoothly, while a tense muscle makes it hurt more. A calm patient is a happy patient! [learn more](GNS122_U1_T3#GNS122_U1_T3_h4)

question: What should you do if the chosen injection site has an open sore or infection?

options.A: Warm the skin with a hot pack to improve blood flow
options.B: Choose a different healthy site for the injection
options.C: Use a longer needle to bypass the damaged area
options.D: Clean the sore with extra antiseptic before piercing

explanation: Always protect broken skin! Finding a healthy site prevents spreading infection and helps the medication absorb properly. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T3#GNS122_U1_T3_h4)

question: What is the main reason for using the Z-track technique during an IM injection?

options.A: To numb the skin surface without using ice packs
options.B: To push blood vessels completely away from the needle tip
options.C: To prevent irritating medication from leaking into subcutaneous tissue
options.D: To make the needle go twice as deep into the bone

explanation: You've got it! Pulling the skin aside creates a zigzag track that traps the medicine deep inside the muscle, protecting the upper skin layers from irritation or stains. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T3#GNS122_U1_T3_h5)

question: When do you release the pulled skin during a Z-track injection?

options.A: While the medication is still flowing from the syringe
options.B: Before the needle is inserted into the muscle
options.C: Immediately after pushing the needle through the skin
options.D: After the needle has been completely withdrawn

explanation: Spot on! Let go of the skin only after the needle is completely out so the track stays sealed. Great clinical thinking! [learn more](GNS122_U1_T3#GNS122_U1_T3_h5)

question: At what angle should you insert an intramuscular needle?

options.A: Fifteen degrees
options.B: Forty-five degrees
options.C: One hundred degrees
options.D: Ninety degrees

explanation: Fantastic! A straight-up 90-degree angle ensures the needle clears the fat layer and goes right into the muscle. [learn more](GNS122_U1_T3#GNS122_U1_T3_h6)

question: Why must you let the skin antiseptic dry completely before inserting the needle?

options.A: Antiseptic works only when it turns into a white powder
