question: Why is checking the net fluid balance important after a rectal washout?

options.A: To calculate the exact caloric intake of the patient
options.B: To make sure the patient is not retaining excessive fluid
options.C: To verify the total operating room expenses for the day
options.D: To determine how much medication to give orally

explanation: Comparing how much fluid went in versus how much came out helps you make sure the patient isn't holding onto too much water. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T13#GNS212_U1_T13_h6)

question: What is the most crucial detail to write in your nursing notes after a washout?

options.A: The favorite food of the patient's family
options.B: The volume and appearance of the fluid returned
options.C: The weather conditions outside the hospital
options.D: The exact brand name of the lubricant used

explanation: Always document what came out! Recording the amount and look of the return proves that the procedure worked and was safe. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T13#GNS212_U1_T13_h7)

question: What should you do if you notice fresh, bright red bleeding from the rectum after a washout?

options.A: Report the finding to the physician immediately
options.B: Document it as a completely normal expected result
options.C: Administer a stronger oral laxative dose to the patient
options.D: Wait twenty-four hours to see if it stops on its own

explanation: Bright red blood means there might be a small injury or tear in the lining. Always let the doctor know right away so it can be checked. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T13#GNS212_U1_T13_h7)

question: What is the name for the surgical opening of the large intestine onto the belly wall?

options.A: A catheter
options.B: A stoma
options.C: An incision
options.D: A fistula

explanation: Great job! A stoma is simply the surgically created opening of the bowel onto the tummy surface where waste leaves the body. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T14#GNS212_U1_T14_h1)

question: Why do doctors most commonly perform a colostomy?

options.A: To permanently cure long-term constipation without changing diet
options.B: To bypass or remove a diseased or damaged part of the bowel
options.C: To allow direct medicine administration into the bloodstream
options.D: To increase the length of the small intestine for better food absorption

explanation: Spot on! Conditions like severe infection, injury, or cancer mean we need to safely divert waste away from a sick section of the large intestine. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T14#GNS212_U1_T14_h1)

question: Which type of colostomy usually gives the most firm and solid stool?

options.A: Transverse colostomy
options.B: Sigmoid colostomy
options.C: Loop colostomy
options.D: Ascending colostomy

explanation: You got it! Because a sigmoid colostomy sits near the very end of the colon, the body has absorbed lots of water, leaving solid stool. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T14#GNS212_U1_T14_h2)

question: What decides how thick or watery a colostomy stool will be?

options.A: The anatomical location of the stoma along the large intestine
options.B: The amount of physical exercise the patient does every day
options.C: The time of day the patient eats their main meal
options.D: The exact brand of the appliance pouch the patient wears

explanation: Exactly! Stool gets thicker the longer it travels through the colon because more water is absorbed along the way. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T14#GNS212_U1_T14_h2)

question: What is the normal, healthy look of a newly made intestinal stoma?

options.A: Pink to brick-red
options.B: Bright yellow or green
options.C: Dark purple to black
options.D: Pale white or gray

explanation: Correct! A healthy stoma is packed with tiny blood vessels, which gives it a nice moist, pink to brick-red color. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T14#GNS212_U1_T14_h3)

question: During a routine check, what does a pale, dusky, or blue-purple stoma tell you?

options.A: Inadequate blood supply to the stoma tissue
options.B: Normal healing after belly surgery
options.C: Too much fluid intake by the patient
options.D: A properly sealed ostomy appliance

explanation: Spot on. Color changes like blue, purple, or paleness mean blood flow is blocked or low—this is a true surgical emergency! [learn more](GNS212_U1_T14#GNS212_U1_T14_h3)

question: Why must the hole on the skin barrier be measured to fit just a tiny bit larger than the stoma?

options.A: To allow for the natural shrinking of the stoma over many years
options.B: To prevent the barrier from rubbing against and injuring the stoma tissue
options.C: To give extra space for air to circulate under the pouch
options.D: To make it easier to empty liquid waste from the bottom

explanation: You nailed it! Cutting the opening slightly larger protects the delicate stoma tissue from painful friction while keeping the skin safe. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T14#GNS212_U1_T14_h4)

question: You are getting ready to put a new colostomy bag on a patient. What is the right first step for the skin?

options.A: Rub a thick layer of oily moisturizing lotion to soften the skin
options.B: Scrub the area hard with an alcohol-based antiseptic
options.C: Dust the moist skin heavily with a scented powder
options.D: Clean the skin gently with warm water and pat it completely dry

explanation: Correct! The skin needs to be clean and totally dry so the adhesive barrier can stick securely without leaking. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T14#GNS212_U1_T14_h4)

question: Which foods are most likely to cause a blockage in a patient with a colostomy?

options.A: Corn, nuts, and popcorn
options.B: Cooked carrots and soft pumpkin
options.C: Applesauce and plain yogurt
options.D: Plain rice and boiled potatoes

explanation: Spot on! Foods with tough hulls, skins, or hard fibrous bits don't digest easily and can get stuck right inside the stoma. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T14#GNS212_U1_T14_h5)

question: Which of these foods should a patient expect to cause extra gas and strong odor?

options.A: Plain steamed rice
options.B: Boiled white chicken
options.C: Beans and onions
options.D: White toast and butter

explanation: You got it! Certain sulfur-rich or fermentable foods naturally lead to more tummy gas and stronger stoma smells. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T14#GNS212_U1_T14_h5)

question: What do we call a colostomy problem where the bowel telescopes out and the stoma becomes way too long?

options.A: Retraction
options.B: Hernia
options.C: Necrosis
options.D: Prolapse

explanation: Correct! A prolapse happens when extra bowel pushes out through the stoma site, making it stick out much further than normal. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T14#GNS212_U1_T14_h6)

question: What is a parastomal hernia in a patient with a colostomy?

options.A: Total loss of blood flow leading to dark, dead tissue at the stoma tip
options.B: Chemical skin burns caused by leaked digestive juices
options.C: Complete blockage of the bowel by tough food particles
options.D: A loop of intestine pushing through a weakened belly wall muscle near the stoma

explanation: Spot on! A parastomal hernia is a weak spot in the muscle around the stoma that lets tummy contents bulge out. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T14#GNS212_U1_T14_h6)

question: Why do we encourage a new colostomy patient to start practicing bag changes early?

options.A: To prove the patient doesn't need emotional counseling anymore
options.B: To make the surgical belly cut heal much faster
options.C: To help the hospital nurses finish their heavy daily chores
options.D: To build self-confidence and lower worry about caring for themselves at home

explanation: You nailed it! Practicing with a nurse nearby helps patients beat their fears and master the skills they need to be independent. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T14#GNS212_U1_T14_h7)

question: What emotional feeling do patients adjusting to a new stoma most commonly experience?

options.A: Complete indifference to physical changes
options.B: Immediate excitement to rush back to work
options.C: Angry behavior toward medical staff
options.D: Body image disturbance and anxiety

explanation: Spot on. Adjusting to a changed body appearance and worrying about leaks or smells can easily cause stress and emotional upset. You're doing great! [learn more](GNS212_U1_T14#GNS212_U1_T14_h7)

question: What is the main job of the nephrons in the kidneys?

options.A: Transporting urine directly to the urethra
options.B: Storing urine until it leaves the body
options.C: Pumping blood through the lower back
options.D: Filtering the blood to form urine

explanation: You've got this! Nephrons are the tiny working units inside your kidneys that clean your blood and make urine. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T15#GNS212_U1_T15_h1)

question: What is the main difference between the ureters and the urethra?

options.A: Ureters store urine, while the urethra filters waste products from the bloodstream
options.B: Ureters and urethra perform the exact same task on opposite sides of the pelvis
options.C: Ureters carry urine from kidneys to the bladder, while the urethra carries urine outside the body
options.D: Ureters pump urine out of the body, while the urethra connects the kidneys directly to the outside

explanation: Think of ureters as the pipes coming down from the kidneys to the bladder, and the urethra as the final exit tube to the outside world! [learn more](GNS212_U1_T15#GNS212_U1_T15_h1)

question: What do we call pain or a burning feeling when passing urine?

options.A: Retention
options.B: Dysuria
options.C: Incontinence
options.D: Hematuria

explanation: Dysuria is just the medical word for painful or burning urination. Great term to keep in your clinical vocabulary bag! [learn more](GNS212_U1_T15#GNS212_U1_T15_h2)

question: A patient suddenly feels a strong need to pee and leaks a little before reaching the toilet. What is this called?

options.A: Urinary incontinence
options.B: Hematuria
options.C: Renal failure
options.D: Urinary retention

explanation: Incontinence simply means losing control of urine flow. You will see this a lot in clinical rotations! [learn more](GNS212_U1_T15#GNS212_U1_T15_h2)

question: When checking for urinary retention, what does a nurse feel for in the lower belly?

options.A: A firm, rounded bladder above the pubic bone
options.B: Soft, empty folds of skin near the belly button
options.C: Warm fluid moving freely inside the intestines
options.D: A hard, pulsing mass on the left side

explanation: When urine gets trapped (retention), the bladder fills up and feels like a firm dome right above the pubic bone. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T15#GNS212_U1_T15_h3)

question: Why do doctors order a urine culture after a test shows an infection?

options.A: To find the exact type of bacteria and the best antibiotic to treat it
options.B: To check if the kidneys are filtering red blood cells properly
options.C: To measure the exact total volume of urine produced in twenty-four hours
options.D: To scan the bladder walls for structural tears or tumors

explanation: A regular test tells us there's an infection, but a culture helps us pick the exact right drug to knock it out! [learn more](GNS212_U1_T15#GNS212_U1_T15_h3)

question: Tracking a patient's fluid intake and output mainly helps you evaluate what?

options.A: Lung capacity and oxygen levels
options.B: Muscle strength in the lower limbs
options.C: Kidney function and hydration status
options.D: The patient's daily calorie intake

explanation: Checking what goes in versus what comes out is a brilliant way to see if the kidneys are doing their job and if the patient is well-hydrated. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T15#GNS212_U1_T15_h4)

question: A patient on a bedpan is struggling to urinate while lying flat. What should you try first?

options.A: Assist the patient into a more natural, upright sitting position
options.B: Restrict all fluid intake for the rest of the day
options.C: Insert an indwelling catheter immediately without further delay
options.D: Administer a strong diuretic medication by mouth

explanation: Gravity and a normal sitting posture help relax the muscles, making it much easier to pass urine naturally. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T15#GNS212_U1_T15_h4)

question: Where should a urinary drainage bag always hang relative to the patient's bladder?

options.A: Below the level of the bladder
options.B: Flat on the floor next to the bed
options.C: Above the level of the bladder
options.D: Level with the patient's chest

explanation: Always keep it lower than the bladder! Gravity keeps the urine flowing away from the body and stops nasty germs from creeping back up. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T15#GNS212_U1_T15_h5)

question: Which of these is unsafe when caring for a patient with an indwelling catheter?

options.A: Keeping the drainage bag below the level of the bladder
options.B: Cleaning the perineal area and catheter tubing daily
options.C: Disconnecting the tubing frequently to let the patient walk easier
options.D: Removing the catheter as soon as it is no longer needed

explanation: Never break that closed system! Opening the tubing lets bacteria waltz right into the urinary tract. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T15#GNS212_U1_T15_h5)

question: What is the main goal of teaching Kegel exercises to someone with urinary incontinence?

options.A: To strengthen the pelvic floor muscles supporting the bladder
options.B: To relax the abdominal wall during a physical exam
options.C: To stretch the ureters and widen the urinary tract
options.D: To increase total daily urine production in the kidneys

explanation: Kegels tone up those pelvic floor muscles, giving the patient much better control over when they go. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T15#GNS212_U1_T15_h6)

question: How does bladder retraining help a patient with urge incontinence?

options.A: It numbs the bladder nerves permanently using special exercises
options.B: It trains the bladder to hold increasing amounts of urine by voiding on a set timetable
options.C: It empties the bladder continuously so the patient never feels any sensation
options.D: It stops the kidneys from producing urine during the night hours

explanation: Following a set bathroom schedule helps calm the bladder down and slowly helps it hold more urine over time. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T15#GNS212_U1_T15_h6)

question: What is the primary definition of urinary retention?

options.A: The inability to completely empty the bladder
options.B: The involuntary leakage of urine during coughing
options.C: The frequent passing of very small urine volumes
options.D: The total absence of urine production by kidneys

explanation: Urinary retention specifically refers to the body's inability to expel urine stored in the bladder, leading to incomplete emptying. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T16#GNS212_U1_T16_h1)

question: How does urinary retention differ fundamentally from urinary incontinence?

options.A: Retention requires dialysis, while incontinence requires immediate surgery
options.B: Retention involves urine accumulation, while incontinence involves involuntary leakage
options.C: Retention causes painful urination, while incontinence is always painless
options.D: Retention affects only females, while incontinence affects only males

explanation: While both are common lower urinary tract disorders, retention is characterized by holding onto urine the body wants to expel, whereas incontinence is the uncontrolled loss of urine. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T16#GNS212_U1_T16_h1)

question: A common mechanical obstruction causing urinary retention in older men is...

options.A: detrusor muscle weakness
options.B: anticholinergic medication use
options.C: benign prostatic hyperplasia
options.D: neurogenic bladder disease

explanation: Enlargement of the prostate gland physically squeezes the urethra, making it difficult for urine to pass out of the bladder. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T16#GNS212_U1_T16_h2)

question: Why do certain drugs like antihistamines trigger urinary retention?

options.A: They cause the kidneys to produce excessive amounts of urine
options.B: They irritate the mucosal lining of the bladder wall
options.C: They impair the contraction of the detrusor muscle
options.D: They physically block the opening of the ureters

explanation: Many medications have anticholinergic properties that prevent the bladder muscle from squeezing strongly enough to empty properly. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T16#GNS212_U1_T16_h2)

question: What is a defining feature of acute urinary retention?

options.A: Continuous dribbling of large urine volumes
options.B: Sudden onset with severe suprapubic pain
options.C: Gradual accumulation of urine without any pain
options.D: Completely normal bladder fullness on palpation

explanation: Acute retention hits abruptly and causes intense discomfort because the bladder distends rapidly over a short period. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T16#GNS212_U1_T16_h3)

question: Why do patients with chronic urinary retention often experience overflow incontinence?

options.A: Frequent antibiotic use irritates the bladder lining and causes leakage
options.B: The kidneys suddenly start producing more urine than the bladder can hold
options.C: The urethral sphincter completely relaxes due to chronic nerve damage
options.D: The overstretched bladder leaks when intravesical pressure exceeds sphincter resistance

explanation: When a chronically full bladder reaches its limit, small amounts of urine escape past the tight sphincter, mimicking simple incontinence. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T16#GNS212_U1_T16_h3)

question: What physical finding is most characteristic of a severely distended bladder?

options.A: A dull, rounded mass in the suprapubic region
options.B: A soft, flat abdomen with no tenderness on palpation
options.C: Sharp rebound tenderness in the right lower quadrant
options.D: Hyperactive bowel sounds heard over the lower quadrants

explanation: A full bladder pushes upward out of the pelvis and presents as a palpable, dull-sounding mass just above the pubic bone. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T16#GNS212_U1_T16_h4)

question: A male patient post-surgery cannot urinate for six hours and has lower belly pain. What is your immediate nursing assessment step?

options.A: Administer a strong oral diuretic medication as prescribed
options.B: Document the finding as normal post-operative urinary hesitancy
options.C: Palpate and perkuss the suprapubic area for bladder distention
options.D: Encourage the patient to drink two liters of water immediately

explanation: Checking for a palpable bladder confirms whether urine is actually accumulating before taking further clinical action. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T16#GNS212_U1_T16_h4)

question: What non-invasive device is commonly used at the bedside to measure bladder volume?

options.A: Digital sphygmomanometer
options.B: Portable bladder ultrasound scanner
options.C: Peak flow respiratory meter
options.D: Standard multi-lead ECG machine

explanation: A bladder scanner calculates urine volume inside the bladder safely and quickly without inserting any tubes. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T16#GNS212_U1_T16_h5)

question: Why are serum creatinine and urea tests ordered for a patient with severe urinary retention?

options.A: To measure the exact volume of urine left inside the bladder
options.B: To calculate the correct dosage of antibiotics needed for treatment
options.C: To check if bladder backpressure has started harming the kidneys
options.D: To determine the specific bacterial infection causing the blockage

explanation: Longstanding high pressure in the urinary tract travels upward to the kidneys, impairing their filtration ability and elevating blood waste levels. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T16#GNS212_U1_T16_h5)

question: What is the immediate priority treatment for acute urinary retention?

options.A: Immediate surgical removal of the prostate gland
options.B: Bladder decompression via catheterization
options.C: Continuous bladder irrigation with sterile water
options.D: Administration of high-dose intravenous diuretics

explanation: Relieving the agonizing pressure by draining accumulated urine through a catheter is the urgent first step. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T16#GNS212_U1_T16_h6)

question: How do alpha-blockers help manage urinary retention caused by an enlarged prostate?

options.A: They dissolve the fibrous tissue obstructing the urethral lumen
options.B: They relax the smooth muscle fibers in the prostate and bladder neck
options.C: They stop the kidneys from making more urine during the night
options.D: They paralyze the bladder wall to stop painful muscle spasms

explanation: Alpha-blockers ease the squeeze around the urethra, allowing urine to flow more freely without immediate surgery. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T16#GNS212_U1_T16_h6)

question: Why should a nurse avoid draining a massive volume of urine all at once?

options.A: Total drainage stops the kidneys from producing any further urine
options.B: It forces air bubbles into the bladder and causes severe pain
options.C: Rapid decompression can cause bleeding and sudden blood pressure drops
options.D: It will immediately cause the catheter balloon to burst inside

explanation: Sudden reduction of intravesical pressure causes mucosal vessel rupture and rapid fluid shifts, risking shock and severe bleeding. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T16#GNS212_U1_T16_h7)

question: You have inserted a catheter for acute retention and 1200 mL drains rapidly. What is your best action based on safety guidelines?

options.A: Inject sterile water into the balloon to secure the tubing in place
options.B: Clamp the tubing temporarily to control the rate of bladder decompression
options.C: Remove the catheter immediately and notify the doctor of the high volume
options.D: Administer a rapid intravenous fluid bolus to prevent dehydration

explanation: Gradual drainage prevents sudden pressure changes within the bladder and protects the patient from hemorrhage and shock. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T16#GNS212_U1_T16_h7)

question: What is a severe systemic complication of untreated urinary retention?

options.A: Essential hypertension
options.B: Urosepsis
options.C: Peripheral neuropathy
options.D: Pulmonary edema

explanation: Stagnant, retained urine serves as a breeding ground for bacteria, which can easily invade the bloodstream and cause life-threatening sepsis. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T16#GNS212_U1_T16_h8)

question: Why is keeping the urinary drainage bag below the level of the bladder crucial?

options.A: It prevents backflow of contaminated urine into the bladder
options.B: It speeds up the rate of urine production by the kidneys
options.C: It keeps the catheter balloon inflated inside the bladder
options.D: It stops the patient from feeling the urge to urinate

explanation: Gravity ensures urine flows downward away from the body; lifting the bag above the bladder pushes bacteria straight back inside. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T16#GNS212_U1_T16_h8)

question: What is the primary clinical definition of urinary incontinence?

options.A: The involuntary loss of urine
options.B: Painful urination during the night
options.C: The complete inability to produce urine
options.D: An infection of the urinary bladder

explanation: Urinary incontinence is specifically defined as the involuntary leakage or loss of urine. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T17#GNS212_U1_T17_h1)

question: Why do many elderly patients in Nigeria often fail to report urinary incontinence early?

options.A: Hospitals do not treat urinary tract issues
options.B: The symptoms disappear without medical treatment
options.C: Diagnostic tests are too expensive to perform
options.D: They consider it a normal part of aging

explanation: Many individuals delay seeking help because they mistakenly believe leaking urine is an inevitable part of growing older. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T17#GNS212_U1_T17_h1)

question: Which part of the nervous system helps the bladder relax so it can store urine?

options.A: Somatic nervous system
options.B: Central nervous system
options.C: Sympathetic nervous system
options.D: Parasympathetic nervous system

explanation: The sympathetic nervous system promotes detrusor muscle relaxation and sphincter contraction so the bladder can hold urine safely. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T17#GNS212_U1_T17_h2)

question: What happens in the bladder and urinary sphincter when a person urinates normally?

options.A: Both the detrusor and sphincter relax completely
options.B: Detrusor relaxation and sphincter contraction
options.C: Detrusor contraction and sphincter relaxation
options.D: Both the detrusor and sphincter contract together

explanation: Urine leaves the body when the bladder muscle contracts while the outlet sphincter relaxes to open the passage. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T17#GNS212_U1_T17_h2)

question: A patient leaks urine when coughing or lifting heavy market loads. What type of incontinence is this?

options.A: Stress urinary incontinence
options.B: Overflow urinary incontinence
options.C: Urge urinary incontinence
options.D: Functional urinary incontinence

explanation: Stress incontinence occurs when physical pressure from coughing or lifting overcomes weak pelvic floor muscles. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T17#GNS212_U1_T17_h3)

question: What is the underlying mechanism responsible for overflow urinary incontinence?

options.A: Sudden bladder spasms without warning
options.B: Physical inability to walk to the toilet
options.C: Weakened pelvic floor support from childbirth
options.D: An overdistended bladder that fails to empty

explanation: Overflow incontinence occurs when urinary retention fills the bladder past capacity, causing continuous minor leakage. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T17#GNS212_U1_T17_h3)

question: Which condition is a major contributing factor to urinary incontinence in aging men?

options.A: Frequent pregnancies
options.B: Prostatic enlargement
options.C: Pelvic floor relaxation
options.D: Estrogen deficiency

explanation: Enlargement of the prostate gland obstructs the urinary outlet in men, frequently causing overflow or urge incontinence. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T17#GNS212_U1_T17_h4)

question: How can chronic constipation contribute to urinary incontinence?

options.A: Hardened stool blocks the flow of urine in the urethra
options.B: The straining weakens the abdominal wall muscles permanently
options.C: Constipation causes severe dehydration and concentrated urine
options.D: Stool pressure in the rectum irritates the adjacent bladder

explanation: An impacted bowel exerts physical pressure against the urinary bladder, triggering involuntary bladder contractions. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T17#GNS212_U1_T17_h4)

question: What is the primary purpose of a voiding diary during clinical assessment?

options.A: To measure the exact weight of the patient daily
options.B: To record fluid intake, leakage frequency, and triggers
options.C: To track the patient's daily diet and nutritional status
options.D: To calculate the total kidney filtration rate over time

explanation: A voiding diary helps nurses and doctors identify patterns, fluid habits, and specific triggers associated with leakage episodes. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T17#GNS212_U1_T17_h5)

question: Why is a urinalysis routinely performed during the evaluation of urinary incontinence?

options.A: To measure the exact bladder muscle thickness
options.B: To rule out active urinary tract infections
options.C: To assess the strength of the pelvic floor
options.D: To determine the patient's neurological status

explanation: Urinary tract infections can cause acute irritation and symptoms that mimic or worsen incontinence, so infection must be excluded. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T17#GNS212_U1_T17_h5)

question: What is the main goal of teaching a patient Kegel exercises?

options.A: To relax the abdominal wall
options.B: To empty the bowel completely
options.C: To reduce nighttime fluid intake
options.D: To strengthen pelvic floor muscles

explanation: Kegel exercises specifically target and strengthen the pelvic floor muscles to improve urinary sphincter control. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T17#GNS212_U1_T17_h6)

question: How does a timed voiding schedule help a patient with urge incontinence?

options.A: It eliminates the need for pelvic floor muscle training
options.B: It prevents the bladder from filling past the trigger point
options.C: It stretches the urethra to make passing urine easier
options.D: It completely stops the kidneys from producing urine

explanation: Scheduled voiding empties the bladder at regular intervals before unmanaged urgency and involuntary leakage can occur. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T17#GNS212_U1_T17_h6)

question: Which class of medication is commonly prescribed to calm an overactive bladder muscle?

options.A: Anticholinergics
options.B: Diuretics
options.C: Anticoagulants
options.D: Antibiotics

explanation: Anticholinergic drugs reduce bladder contractions and help manage symptoms of urge urinary incontinence. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T17#GNS212_U1_T17_h7)

question: Why is topical estrogen sometimes prescribed for postmenopausal women with incontinence?

options.A: To increase the total volume of urine produced daily
options.B: To improve the health of urethral and vaginal tissues
options.C: To prevent the development of kidney stones
options.D: To stimulate voluntary contractions of the abdominal wall

explanation: Estrogen deficiency causes thinning of urogenital tissues, and topical application helps restore structural support and tissue health. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T17#GNS212_U1_T17_h7)

question: What skin problem often happens when urine stays in contact with the skin for too long?

options.A: Increased production of subcutaneous fat
options.B: Complete loss of skin sensation
options.C: Permanent thickening of the epidermis
options.D: Moisture-associated skin breakdown

explanation: Constant exposure to urine irritates the skin, leading to rashes, sores, and moisture-associated skin breakdown. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T17#GNS212_U1_T17_h8)

question: What should be the nurse's main focus when dealing with the emotional impact of incontinence?

options.A: Reducing social stigma and supporting patient dignity
options.B: Focusing solely on surgical treatment options
options.C: Ensuring the patient stays indoors at all times
options.D: Reporting the condition to public health authorities

explanation: Because patients often experience shame and isolation, nursing care must prioritize emotional support and dignity. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T17#GNS212_U1_T17_h8)

question: What triggers urine leakage in a patient with stress incontinence?

options.A: Physical pressure from activity
options.B: Complete blockage of the urethra
options.C: A severe urinary tract infection
options.D: Sudden bladder muscle spasms

explanation: Physical activities that increase intra-abdominal pressure force urine out when pelvic support is weak. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T18#GNS212_U1_T18_h1)

question: How does stress incontinence differ from urge incontinence?

options.A: It only affects male patients rather than female patients
options.B: It occurs exclusively during sleep instead of waking hours
options.C: It is caused by physical pressure rather than sudden bladder muscle contractions
options.D: It involves complete inability to produce urine rather than leakage

explanation: Stress incontinence is a mechanical problem of support, while urge incontinence involves involuntary bladder muscle contractions. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T18#GNS212_U1_T18_h1)

question: Which muscle group forms the primary supportive sling for the pelvic organs?

options.A: Internal sphincter
options.B: Levator ani muscles
options.C: Abdominal rectus
options.D: Detrusor muscle

explanation: The levator ani group provides the main structural floor supporting the bladder and urethra. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T18#GNS212_U1_T18_h2)

question: What is the primary function of the urethral sphincters in urinary continence?

options.A: To remain contracted and keep the urinary channel closed at rest
options.B: To generate the force needed to empty the bladder completely
options.C: To transmit nerve signals from the spinal cord to the brain
options.D: To produce hormones that regulate daily urine production volume

explanation: Sphincters act as tight valves that maintain closure until purposeful urination occurs. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T18#GNS212_U1_T18_h2)

question: What is urethral hypermobility in the context of stress incontinence?

options.A: Complete rigidity of the urinary sphincter muscle fibers
options.B: Excessive downward movement of the bladder neck during pressure
options.C: Involuntary spasms of the bladder wall muscle
options.D: Rapid bacterial infection traveling up the urinary tract

explanation: Hypermobility means the support structures have slackened, allowing the urethra to drop abnormally during strain. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T18#GNS212_U1_T18_h3)

question: Why does weakening of the pelvic floor lead directly to urine leakage?

options.A: It blocks the normal flow of blood to the bladder walls
options.B: It causes the bladder to shrink to a much smaller size
options.C: It prevents proper pressure transmission to close the urethra
options.D: It stops the kidneys from filtering waste products properly

explanation: Without a firm backstop from supportive tissues, increased abdominal pressure pushes urine out past the unsupported urethra. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T18#GNS212_U1_T18_h3)

question: Which factor is a primary cause of pelvic floor trauma leading to stress incontinence?

options.A: A sedentary lifestyle
options.B: High daily water intake
options.C: Consuming too much caffeine
options.D: Vaginal childbirth

explanation: The stretching and physical strain of vaginal delivery frequently damages pelvic support tissues and nerves. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T18#GNS212_U1_T18_h4)

question: How does chronic coughing contribute to the development of stress incontinence?

options.A: By placing repetitive downward strain on the pelvic floor muscles
options.B: By increasing overall daily urine production in the kidneys
options.C: By irritating the inner lining of the urinary bladder
options.D: By weakening the nerve connections in the lower spinal cord

explanation: Repeated forceful coughs repeatedly stress and fatigue the pelvic support structures until they weaken. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T18#GNS212_U1_T18_h4)

question: What is the purpose of a bladder diary during clinical assessment?

options.A: To measure exact muscle strength in the pelvic floor
options.B: To record daily fluid intake and episodes of leakage
options.C: To check blood pressure changes during urination
options.D: To test for bacterial infections in the urine sample

explanation: A bladder diary tracks patterns of fluid consumption and incontinence events over multiple days. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T18#GNS212_U1_T18_h5)

question: How is a basic cough stress test performed during a physical exam?

options.A: The nurse listens to the abdomen with a stethoscope while coughing
options.B: The patient coughs with a full bladder while observing for leakage
options.C: The patient drinks large volumes of water until coughing starts
options.D: The patient holds their breath while running on a treadmill

explanation: Observing immediate urine loss during a cough confirms the mechanical nature of stress incontinence. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T18#GNS212_U1_T18_h5)

question: What is the primary goal of teaching Kegel exercises to a patient?

options.A: To reduce nighttime urine production by the kidneys
options.B: To relax the abdominal wall during deep breathing exercises
options.C: To strengthen the pelvic floor muscles supporting the urethra
options.D: To expand the total physical capacity of the bladder muscle

explanation: Kegels build strength in the levator ani muscles to improve structural support around the urethra. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T18#GNS212_U1_T18_h6)

question: Which instruction is most important when teaching a patient how to perform Kegel exercises?

options.A: Hold your breath tightly for one full minute during each contraction
options.B: Perform the exercises only while standing up in front of a mirror
options.C: Drink two glasses of water immediately before starting your routine
options.D: Avoid contracting your abdominal, thigh, or buttock muscles at the same time

explanation: Isolating the pelvic floor ensures the correct muscle group is being strengthened without substituting other muscle groups. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T18#GNS212_U1_T18_h6)

question: What is the most common surgical procedure performed for stress urinary incontinence?

options.A: Artificial kidney transplant
options.B: Complete bladder removal
options.C: Prostate gland resection
options.D: Mid-urethral sling placement

explanation: Mid-urethral slings provide a supportive hammock under the urethra to prevent downward displacement during pressure. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T18#GNS212_U1_T18_h7)

question: Why might a doctor prescribe topical estrogen to a postmenopausal patient with stress incontinence?

options.A: To stimulate rapid weight loss and reduce abdominal pressure
options.B: To improve the health and elasticity of the urethral tissues
options.C: To increase the total volume of urine held in the kidneys
options.D: To cause temporary paralysis of the bladder wall muscles

explanation: Estrogen helps maintain mucosal thickness and vascularity in the urogenital tissues, supporting closure. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T18#GNS212_U1_T18_h7)

question: Which of the following is NOT a common complication associated with chronic untreated stress incontinence?

options.A: Severe perineal skin breakdown
options.B: Complete permanent kidney failure
options.C: Recurrent urinary tract infections
options.D: Social withdrawal and isolation

explanation: Stress incontinence affects lower urinary tract support, not kidney filtration function, so kidney failure is not a typical complication. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T18#GNS212_U1_T18_h8)

question: What is a key nursing priority when educating a patient recovering from a mid-urethral sling procedure?

options.A: Telling them pelvic floor exercises are no longer necessary
options.B: Instructing them to stop drinking all fluids for three months
options.C: Encouraging heavy lifting immediately to test the new sling
options.D: Teaching them to watch for signs of urinary retention or infection

explanation: Postoperative monitoring for normal voiding and infection prevention is essential after urinary tract surgery. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T18#GNS212_U1_T18_h8)

question: What is the primary function of a medical bougie?

options.A: To widen strictures and guide tube placement
options.B: To irrigate blocked surgical drains continuously
options.C: To measure core body temperature accurately
options.D: To suture internal tissues during open surgery

explanation: Bougies are slender, flexible instruments designed to navigate narrow tracts, stretch strictures, and act as guides for larger therapeutic tubes. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T19#GNS212_U1_T19_h1)

question: Why must nurses understand the physical differences between bougies and dilators?

options.A: To bill the patient accurately for disposable hospital supplies
options.B: To select the correct instrument and prevent mucosal trauma
options.C: To calculate exact drug dosages based on instrument length
options.D: To sterilize the equipment using high-pressure steam autoclaves

explanation: Knowing the flexibility and rigidity of these devices ensures appropriate clinical application and protects fragile internal tissues from injury. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T19#GNS212_U1_T19_h1)

question: Which type of bougie relies on heavy internal filling to assist with gravity-driven passage?

options.A: Hurst bougie
options.B: Savary-Gillard dilator
options.C: Maloney bougie
options.D: Urethral sound

explanation: Maloney bougies contain mercury or tungsten inside to provide weighted momentum during esophageal dilation. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T19#GNS212_U1_T19_h2)

question: What is the specific advantage of using a wire-guided Savary-Gillard dilator?

options.A: It delivers continuous electrical current to cauterize bleeding tissue
options.B: It safely tracks over a guidewire through tight strictures
options.C: It allows direct visualization through an attached miniature camera
options.D: It relies entirely on gravity without requiring manual pressure

explanation: Wire-guided systems reduce the risk of creating false passages by following the precise path established by a secure guidewire. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T19#GNS212_U1_T19_h2)

question: A common gastrointestinal indication for using an esophageal dilator is:

options.A: Gastric ulceration
options.B: Peptic stricture
options.C: Acute appendicitis
options.D: Internal hemorrhoids

explanation: Chronic acid exposure leads to scar tissue formation and narrowing, known as a peptic stricture, which requires mechanical dilation. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T19#GNS212_U1_T19_h3)

question: A patient with chronic urethral strictures is admitted with painful urination and poor urine stream. What primary problem does dilation address?

options.A: Excessive production of concentrated urine
options.B: Obstruction to normal urinary elimination
options.C: Weakness of the external urinary sphincter
options.D: Bacterial colonization of the urinary bladder

explanation: Urethral strictures mechanically block urine flow, and dilating the tract relieves this obstruction to restore normal voiding. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T19#GNS212_U1_T19_h3)

question: What is the primary reason an adult patient must remain NPO before an esophageal dilation procedure?

options.A: To ensure accurate blood glucose level readings
options.B: To prevent pulmonary aspiration during the procedure
options.C: To prevent allergic reactions to local anesthetics
options.D: To allow complete absorption of oral medications

explanation: An empty stomach significantly reduces the risk of regurgitation and aspiration of gastric contents during upper GI instrumentation. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T19#GNS212_U1_T19_h4)

question: Which nursing action is most critical during the immediate pre-procedure phase for a dilation?

options.A: Placing the patient in a prone position for airway drainage
options.B: Inserting a large-bore peripheral intravenous line in the foot
options.C: Administering a full dose of broad-spectrum oral antibiotics
options.D: Verifying informed consent and checking baseline vital signs

explanation: Confirming consent ensures legal and ethical readiness, while baseline vitals provide essential reference points for monitoring procedural tolerance. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T19#GNS212_U1_T19_h4)

question: What type of lubricant should the nurse prepare for inserting medical bougies or dilators?

options.A: Sterile mineral oil
options.B: Silicone-based gel
options.C: Petroleum-based ointment
options.D: Water-soluble lubricant

explanation: Water-soluble lubricants facilitate smooth insertion without damaging delicate medical polymers or leaving irritating oily residues inside tracts. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T19#GNS212_U1_T19_h5)

question: Why is continuous pulse oximetry essential during an esophageal dilation procedure under sedation?

options.A: To determine when the local anesthetic has completely worn off
options.B: To measure the exact depth of the stricture inside the esophagus
options.C: To calculate the total volume of blood lost during insertion
options.D: To detect early signs of hypoxia or respiratory depression

explanation: Sedation combined with upper GI manipulation places the patient at risk for airway compromise, making oxygen saturation monitoring vital. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T19#GNS212_U1_T19_h5)

question: What is the most serious potential complication following an esophageal or urethral dilation procedure?

options.A: Temporary hair loss
options.B: Peripheral edema
options.C: Tissue perforation
options.D: Hypertensive crisis

explanation: Mechanical stretching of tight strictures carries an inherent risk of tearing or perforating the mucosal wall, which is a surgical emergency. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T19#GNS212_U1_T19_h6)

question: A patient complains of sudden, severe chest pain and develops a fever two hours after an esophageal dilation. What should the nurse suspect?

options.A: Acute anxiety attack
options.B: Esophageal perforation
options.C: Normal post-procedure soreness
options.D: Mild local anesthetic reaction

explanation: Severe chest pain and fever post-procedure are classic indicators of a tear or perforation requiring urgent medical evaluation. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T19#GNS212_U1_T19_h6)

question: Which instruction is most appropriate for a patient discharged after an esophageal dilation?

options.A: Progress slowly from clear liquids to soft foods as tolerated
options.B: Avoid drinking any fluids for at least forty-eight hours
options.C: Resume a regular spicy solid diet immediately upon arrival home
options.D: Lie flat in bed for two hours after every meal

explanation: Gradual dietary advancement prevents irritation and ensures the newly dilated esophagus can comfortably handle food intake. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T19#GNS212_U1_T19_h7)

question: Why is it important to provide written discharge instructions to patients after a dilation procedure?

options.A: Patients may forget verbal instructions due to residual sedation or stress
options.B: Insurance companies mandate written proof of completed nursing care
options.C: It replaces the need for any verbal explanation by the nursing staff
options.D: Hospital policies require a signed paper copy for medical billing

explanation: Anxiety and lingering medication effects impair memory retention, making written guides essential for safe home recovery. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T19#GNS212_U1_T19_h7)

question: What is the primary purpose of a nasogastric tube?

options.A: To provide continuous oxygen to the lungs
options.B: To deliver liquid nutrients directly into the stomach
options.C: To drain excess urine from the bladder
options.D: To remove harmful toxins from the bloodstream

explanation: A nasogastric tube is passed through the nose into the stomach to supply food and medications when a patient cannot swallow safely. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T2#GNS212_U1_T2_h1)

question: Why do we prefer feeding through a stomach tube rather than an IV drip when the patient's digestive system is working?

options.A: It keeps the gut healthy and stops bad bacteria from moving around
options.B: It is completely painless and requires no monitoring
options.C: It completely eliminates the risk of aspiration
options.D: It takes only a few minutes to set up every morning

explanation: Using the normal digestive tract keeps the gut lining strong and stops dangerous bacteria from escaping into the bloodstream. You've got this! [learn more](GNS212_U1_T2#GNS212_U1_T2_h1)

question: What position should your patient be in when you are inserting a nasogastric tube?

options.A: Lying on the left side (Sims position)
options.B: Sitting upright in high Fowler's position
options.C: Head tilted downward (Trendelenburg)
options.D: Flat on the back (supine)

explanation: Sitting the patient straight up aligns their throat nicely, making it much easier and safer to slide the tube down. Great job! [learn more](GNS212_U1_T2#GNS212_U1_T2_h2)

question: A patient needs a nasogastric tube but has a history of a severe skull fracture at the base of the head. What should you do?

options.A: Perform the insertion quickly while the patient is asleep
options.B: Proceed with normal insertion using extra lubrication
options.C: Consult the doctor because putting a tube through the nose is risky here
options.D: Insert the tube through the mouth instead without checking

explanation: A basilar skull fracture means the bone near the brain is damaged, so passing a tube through the nose could accidentally enter the brain. Always check with your senior or doctor! [learn more](GNS212_U1_T2#GNS212_U1_T2_h2)

question: What kind of lubricant should you put on a nasogastric tube before sliding it in?

options.A: Sterile mineral oil
options.B: Antiseptic surgical gel
options.C: Water-soluble lubricant
options.D: Petroleum jelly ointment

explanation: We use a water-soluble jelly so that if a tiny bit accidentally goes into the lungs, the body absorbs it safely without causing pneumonia. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T2#GNS212_U1_T2_h3)

question: Why do nurses use a pH testing strip when checking a newly placed nasogastric tube?

options.A: To test how acidic the fluid pulled from the tube is
options.B: To check the expiry date of the food formula
options.C: To check if the patient has a stomach ulcer
options.D: To measure the sugar level in the feed

explanation: Stomach acid is very sour! Testing the pH of fluid from the tube helps us confirm the tip is safely inside the acidic stomach, not the lungs. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T2#GNS212_U1_T2_h3)

question: When measuring for a nasogastric tube using the NEX method, what does the letter 'E' stand for?

options.A: Earlobe
options.B: Epiglottis
options.C: Esophagus
options.D: Eyebrow

explanation: NEX stands for Nose to Earlobe to Xiphoid process. It's the classic bedside trick to guess how far the tube needs to go! [learn more](GNS212_U1_T2#GNS212_U1_T2_h4)

question: What should you do immediately if your patient starts coughing violently and turning blue while you are passing a tube?

options.A: Ask the patient to take a deep breath and swallow
options.B: Push the tube down faster to clear the way
options.C: Stop pushing and pull the tube right back out
options.D: Inject water to wash it down

explanation: Coughing and turning blue (cyanosis) means the tube has mistakenly slipped into the windpipe instead of the food pipe. Pull it back out immediately and let them catch their breath! [learn more](GNS212_U1_T2#GNS212_U1_T2_h4)

question: What is considered the absolute best (gold standard) way to confirm a nasogastric tube is in the right spot?

options.A: Measuring the length of tubing left outside the nose
options.B: Listening for air sounds over the belly with a stethoscope
options.C: Checking for water drops inside the clear plastic tube
options.D: Abdominal X-ray

explanation: An X-ray gives us clear visual proof that the tip is sitting comfortably in the stomach before we start any feeding. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T2#GNS212_U1_T2_h5)

question: Which pH test result tells you that the nasogastric tube is successfully resting in the stomach?

options.A: A high reading of 9.0
options.B: An alkaline reading of 8.5
options.C: A reading of 4.0
options.D: A neutral reading of 7.0

explanation: Stomach contents are acidic, so a low pH (like 4.0 or lower) is a strong sign that your tube is in the right place. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T2#GNS212_U1_T2_h5)

question: How much water is normally used to flush a nasogastric tube before and after giving feeds?

options.A: 200 milliliters
options.B: 30 milliliters
options.C: 5 milliliters
options.D: 500 milliliters

explanation: A quick flush of about 30 mL of clean water keeps the tube clear of leftover formula and prevents blocks without flooding the patient. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T2#GNS212_U1_T2_h6)

question: Why must the head of the bed stay raised for at least 30 minutes after a tube feeding?

options.A: To let gravity keep the food down and prevent it from flowing into the lungs
options.B: To help the stomach absorb food much faster
options.C: To keep the patient awake and chatty
options.D: To ensure the nurse can easily check the vital signs

explanation: Keeping the bed elevated uses gravity to stop the food from flowing back up into the throat and causing aspiration pneumonia. Safety first! [learn more](GNS212_U1_T2#GNS212_U1_T2_h6)

question: What is the best way to stop a nasogastric tube from getting blocked?

options.A: Changing the tube to a smaller size every week
options.B: Adding cooking oil to every feed
options.C: Flushing it with warm water before and after feeds and drugs
options.D: Blowing air down the tube twice a shift

explanation: Regular water flushes wash away sticky food and medicine residue before they can dry up and clog your tube. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T2#GNS212_U1_T2_h7)

question: A patient on continuous tube feeding has a red, sore spot right on the edge of their nostril. What should you do?

options.A: Clean the skin, apply a protective cream, and tape the tube to a slightly different spot
options.B: Put thick gauze padding under the tube
options.C: Leave the tape loose so the tube rubs freely
options.D: Pull the tube out permanently and stop feeding

explanation: Protecting the skin and shifting the pressure point gives the sore spot a chance to heal while keeping the patient fed. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T2#GNS212_U1_T2_h7)

question: What instruction should you give your patient right before you pull out a nasogastric tube?

options.A: Cough gently to clear the throat
options.B: Swallow hard several times
options.C: Blow air out forcefully through the mouth
options.D: Take a deep breath and hold it

explanation: Holding the breath closes the windpipe, keeping the lungs safe from breathing in any leftover fluid as the tube slides out. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T2#GNS212_U1_T2_h8)

question: Why should you always look closely at the tip of the nasogastric tube right after removing it?

options.A: To measure the patient's stomach length
options.B: To check how much stomach acid is left on it
options.C: To make sure the whole tube came out in one piece and nothing broke off inside
options.D: To check if the patient chewed on the plastic

explanation: Checking the removed tube ensures no broken bits were left behind in the patient's stomach or food pipe. A quick glance saves a lot of trouble! [learn more](GNS212_U1_T2#GNS212_U1_T2_h8)

question: What is the approximate length of the adult female urethra?

options.A: 18 to 20 cm
options.B: 25 to 30 cm
options.C: 3.8 to 5 cm
options.D: 10 to 12 cm

explanation: The female urethra is significantly shorter than the male urethra, typically measuring between 3.8 and 5 centimeters. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T20#GNS212_U1_T20_h1)

question: Why does the male urethra present a greater challenge during catheterisation compared to the female urethra?

options.A: It connects directly to the ureters without a bladder
options.B: It has multiple sections and natural curves
options.C: It possesses a much wider diameter throughout
options.D: It is surrounded by a weaker sphincter muscle

explanation: The male urethra is longer and includes prostatic, membranous, and penile sections with curves that require careful maneuvering during catheter passage. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T20#GNS212_U1_T20_h1)

question: Which catheter type is designed for continuous bladder irrigation following urological surgery?

options.A: Single-lumen catheter
options.B: Intermittent catheter
options.C: Three-way catheter
options.D: Straight rubber catheter

explanation: A three-way indwelling catheter contains an extra channel dedicated to continuous fluid infusion for bladder irrigation and blood clot removal. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T20#GNS212_U1_T20_h2)

question: A patient admitted with severe postpartum urinary retention requires bladder drainage without a prolonged indwelling device. What is the most appropriate equipment?

options.A: Three-way Foley catheter
options.B: Suprapubic catheter
options.C: Intermittent catheter
options.D: Condom catheter

explanation: Intermittent catheters are inserted for immediate drainage and removed right away, avoiding the infection risks associated with long-term indwelling tubes. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T20#GNS212_U1_T20_h2)

question: What allergy must be specifically checked before inserting a standard indwelling urinary catheter?

options.A: Penicillin
options.B: Paracetamol
options.C: Latex
options.D: Sulfonamide

explanation: Many conventional catheters are manufactured from latex, making pre-procedural allergy screening vital to prevent severe hypersensitivity reactions. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T20#GNS212_U1_T20_h3)

question: What is the primary purpose of explaining the catheterisation procedure to the patient beforehand?

options.A: To obtain legal permission from the hospital director
options.B: To reduce anxiety and encourage patient cooperation
options.C: To assess the patient's baseline renal function
options.D: To eliminate the need for sterile gloves during setup

explanation: Clear explanation promotes relaxation of the pelvic floor muscles, which makes urethral identification and catheter passage much easier. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T20#GNS212_U1_T20_h3)

question: Why must the catheter be advanced a few centimeters further after urine first appears?

options.A: To ensure the balloon is fully inside the bladder before inflation
options.B: To prevent the drainage bag from filling up too quickly
options.C: To stretch the urethral sphincter for permanent dilation
options.D: To anchor the drainage tubing directly against the meatus

explanation: Inflating the retention balloon inside the urethra instead of the bladder causes severe trauma and intense pain for the patient. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T20#GNS212_U1_T20_h4)

question: During catheterisation of a male patient, resistance is met at the external sphincter. What action should the nurse take?

options.A: Apply maximum physical force to push past the obstruction
options.B: Inflate the retention balloon immediately at that exact spot
options.C: Withdraw the equipment and abandon all future attempts
options.D: Ask the patient to take slow deep breaths and gently pause

explanation: Deep breathing helps relax the pelvic floor and external sphincter, allowing the catheter to pass smoothly without forcing tissue. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T20#GNS212_U1_T20_h4)

question: Where must the urine collection bag be positioned relative to the patient's bladder?

options.A: Hanging from the headboard
options.B: Directly level with the hips
options.C: Below the level of the bladder
options.D: Above the mattress surface

explanation: Gravity drainage requires the bag to remain lower than the bladder to prevent contaminated urine from flowing backward into the urinary tract. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T20#GNS212_U1_T20_h5)

question: What is the primary reason for securing the catheter tubing to the patient's thigh?

options.A: To prevent accidental disconnection of the drainage bag
options.B: To minimize urethral trauma caused by traction and movement
options.C: To stop spontaneous deflation of the retention balloon
options.D: To accelerate the normal rate of glomerular filtration

explanation: Securing the tubing stops piston-like movement of the catheter inside the urethra, which reduces inflammation, erosion, and irritation. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T20#GNS212_U1_T20_h5)

question: How should a nurse manage sudden painful bladder spasms in a patient with a patent catheter?

options.A: Administer prescribed antispasmodic medications
options.B: Pull the catheter outward until resistance is met
options.C: Clamp the drainage tubing for four hours at a time
options.D: Inflate the retention balloon with extra sterile water

explanation: Bladder spasms are contractions of the detrusor muscle triggered by the foreign body; antispasmodics calm the muscle without altering the device. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T20#GNS212_U1_T20_h6)

question: Which finding is most characteristic of a catheter-associated urinary tract infection?

options.A: Fever and cloudy urine
options.B: Increased urine specific gravity
options.C: Dark amber concentrated output
options.D: High systemic blood pressure

explanation: Infection in the urinary tract typically manifests with systemic signs like fever alongside turbid, foul-smelling urine. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T20#GNS212_U1_T20_h6)

question: What tool is required to deflate the retention balloon prior to catheter removal?

options.A: A sterile clamp or hemostat
options.B: An intravenous infusion cannula
options.C: A luer-lock syringe without a needle
options.D: A surgical scalpel blade

explanation: A needleless syringe is inserted into the inflation valve to extract the sterile water used to keep the balloon inflated. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T20#GNS212_U1_T20_h7)

question: A patient has not voided eight hours after catheter removal and reports lower abdominal discomfort. What is the appropriate nursing action?

options.A: Re-insert a new indwelling catheter immediately without checking
options.B: Encourage the patient to restrict all fluid intake for the day
options.C: Administer a potent diuretic medication orally
options.D: Assess for bladder distention and notify the physician

explanation: Post-catheter urinary retention is a common complication requiring clinical assessment and possible re-catheterisation or bladder scanning. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T20#GNS212_U1_T20_h7)

question: What primary feature keeps an indwelling urinary catheter secured inside the bladder?

options.A: A retention balloon filled with sterile water
options.B: A suction mechanism connected to the drainage bag
options.C: An external adhesive tape attached to the thigh
options.D: A flexible wire mesh anchored to the urethral wall

explanation: Inflating the internal balloon with sterile water prevents the catheter from slipping out of the bladder prematurely. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T21#GNS212_U1_T21_h1)

question: A patient admitted to the surgical ward requires hourly urine output tracking. Why is an indwelling catheter chosen over intermittent catheterization?

options.A: Patients find indwelling tubes much more comfortable than periodic drainage
options.B: Indwelling catheters completely eliminate the risk of urinary tract infections
options.C: Continuous drainage allows real-time monitoring without repeated urethral trauma
options.D: Intermittent catheters cannot be used in male surgical patients

explanation: Continuous urine output monitoring in unstable patients requires an open, uninterrupted drainage pathway to assess kidney perfusion accurately. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T21#GNS212_U1_T21_h1)

question: What is the approximate length of the adult female urethra?

options.A: 18 to 20 centimeters
options.B: 25 to 30 centimeters
options.C: 3 to 5 centimeters
options.D: 10 to 12 centimeters

explanation: The female urethra is short, measuring roughly 3 to 5 cm, which also places women at a higher risk for bacterial ascent. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T21#GNS212_U1_T21_h2)

question: A student nurse preparing to catheterize an elderly female patient cannot locate the urinary meatus due to tissue changes. What action should the nurse take next?

options.A: Reposition the patient into a Sims or lateral position for better exposure
options.B: Force the catheter upward until urine returns spontaneously
options.C: Insert the catheter blindly into the largest visible opening in the area
options.D: Abandon the procedure entirely without notifying the primary team

explanation: Altering the patient's position can bring hidden anatomical landmarks into view safely without risking accidental vaginal catheterization. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T21#GNS212_U1_T21_h2)

question: What does a French (Fr) scale measurement represent regarding a urinary catheter?

options.A: The volume capacity of the retention balloon
options.B: The external diameter of the catheter tube
options.C: The maximum pressure threshold of the valve
options.D: The total length of the drainage tubing

explanation: The French scale measures catheter caliber, with larger numbers indicating thicker tube diameters. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T21#GNS212_U1_T21_h3)

question: Why is a coude tip catheter specifically chosen for an older male patient with prostatic enlargement?

options.A: The integrated balloon requires no fluid for bladder retention
options.B: The wider lumen prevents clots from blocking the drainage channels
options.C: The soft silicone material dissolves automatically after two weeks
options.D: The curved tip helps navigate past the obstructed prostatic urethra

explanation: The upward curve of a coude tip glides smoothly over an enlarged prostate gland where straight catheters usually get stuck. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T21#GNS212_U1_T21_h3)

question: What critical allergy must a nurse screen for before opening a standard catheterization kit?

options.A: Dietary proteins and gluten
options.B: Oral antibiotics and analgesics
options.C: Latex and antiseptic solutions
options.D: Intravenous fluids and saline

explanation: Standard trays often contain latex catheters and iodine-based antiseptics, both of which can provoke severe allergic responses. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T21#GNS212_U1_T21_h4)

question: Why is it important to perform a bladder scan or abdominal palpation prior to catheterization?

options.A: To confirm the actual presence of urine retention before invasive manipulation
options.B: To stimulate voluntary micturition and avoid the procedure entirely
options.C: To measure the exact length of the urethral canal accurately
options.D: To determine if the patient has a systemic urinary tract infection

explanation: Assessing bladder volume prevents unnecessary catheterization in patients whose bladders are actually empty. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T21#GNS212_U1_T21_h4)

question: When should the retention balloon be inflated during an indwelling catheter insertion?

options.A: Immediately upon touching the external urinary meatus
options.B: After urine flow is observed and the catheter is advanced further
options.C: After the drainage bag is completely filled with urine
options.D: Before inserting any portion of the tube into the urethral canal

explanation: Inflating the balloon inside the urethra causes severe trauma; it must rest entirely inside the bladder cavity first. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T21#GNS212_U1_T21_h5)

question: A nurse inserts a catheter into a female patient, sees urine flow, and immediately inflates the balloon. The patient cries out in sharp pain. What mistake occurred?

options.A: The drainage bag was placed above the level of the bladder
options.B: A Coude tip catheter was selected instead of a straight one
options.C: The catheter was not advanced far enough before balloon inflation
options.D: The antiseptic solution used was far too cold for the patient

explanation: Seeing urine confirms the tip is in the bladder neck, but advancing further ensures the balloon clears the urethral sphincter before inflation. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T21#GNS212_U1_T21_h5)

question: Where must the urine collection bag be positioned relative to the patient's bladder?

options.A: Elevated on an IV pole during ambulation
options.B: Level with the patient's hips when sitting
options.C: Always below the level of the bladder
options.D: Hanging directly on the bed mattress surface

explanation: Gravity drainage fails and urine flows backward into the bladder if the collection bag is raised above bladder level. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T21#GNS212_U1_T21_h6)

question: Why should nurses avoid applying antibacterial ointments around the catheter insertion site?

options.A: Creams instantly block the drainage eyes and cause acute retention
options.B: Lipid-based substances neutralize the effect of the sterile water balloon
options.C: Antimicrobial creams dissolve the silicone material of the catheter
options.D: Ointments trap moisture and can promote fungal or bacterial growth

explanation: Moisture barrier accumulation around the meatus creates an ideal breeding ground for pathogens rather than protecting against infection. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T21#GNS212_U1_T21_h6)

question: What is the single most effective measure for preventing catheter-associated urinary tract infections?

options.A: Applying antibiotic cream to the meatus twice daily
options.B: Performing daily bladder washouts with sterile saline
options.C: Changing the entire drainage bag every twenty-four hours
options.D: Prompt removal of the catheter when clinically unnecessary

explanation: Limiting the duration of catheterization drastically reduces the window for bacterial colonization and biofilm formation. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T21#GNS212_U1_T21_h7)

question: Why is routine prophylactic bladder irrigation discouraged in patients with indwelling catheters?

options.A: Irrigation fluids instantly trigger severe bladder spasms and bleeding
options.B: Continuous flushing prevents the kidneys from producing normal urine
options.C: Saline solutions dissolve the rubber material of the drainage bag
options.D: Breaking the closed system increases the risk of introducing bacteria

explanation: Opening sealed drainage junctions defeats the closed-system barrier designed to keep external microbes out of the urinary tract. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T21#GNS212_U1_T21_h7)

question: A patient with an indwelling catheter has had no urine output for three hours and reports lower abdominal fullness. What is the nurse's first action?

options.A: Immediately deflate the balloon and remove the catheter
options.B: Administer a potent loop diuretic intravenously
options.C: Disconnect the drainage bag to flush the catheter with tap water
options.D: Inspect the tubing for kinks, twists, or external pressure

explanation: Checking for simple mechanical obstructions like a kinked line or a patient lying on the tubing is always the first troubleshooting step. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T21#GNS212_U1_T21_h8)

question: What is the typical underlying cause of urine leaking around the insertion site of an indwelling catheter?

options.A: A failure to inflate the retention balloon with enough sterile water
options.B: Excessive daily fluid intake overwhelming the drainage bag capacity
options.C: The collection bag hanging too low below the level of the mattress
options.D: Bladder spasms causing the detrusor muscle to contract around the tube

explanation: Involuntary bladder contractions squeeze urine out past the catheter walls, resulting in bypassing or leakage around the meatus. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T21#GNS212_U1_T21_h8)

question: What crucial step must be performed before pulling out an indwelling urinary catheter?

options.A: Apply antiseptic ointment directly to the external meatus
options.B: Flush the drainage lumen with sterile water to clear sediment
options.C: Completely deflate the retention balloon by withdrawing all fluid
options.D: Clamp the drainage tubing for two hours prior to extraction

explanation: Failing to remove all water from the balloon turns the catheter into a makeshift obstacle that severely tears the urethra during extraction. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T21#GNS212_U1_T21_h9)

question: A patient's catheter is removed at 0800. By 1500, the patient feels lower abdominal discomfort and has not voided. What is the appropriate nursing assessment?

options.A: Encourage the patient to wait overnight before reporting symptoms
options.B: Administer an oral laxative to stimulate pelvic nerve pathways
options.C: Reinsert a new indwelling catheter immediately without evaluation
options.D: Assess for urinary retention using bladder palpation or scanning

explanation: Patients should void within 6 to 8 hours post-removal; failing this requires checking for urinary retention and potential bladder distension. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T21#GNS212_U1_T21_h9)

question: Why do surgeons place a surgical drain?

options.A: To close deep wounds faster
options.B: To prevent fluid from building up and causing infection
options.C: To stop the need for antibiotics
options.D: To help the body reabsorb blood

explanation: Drains stop blood, serum, or pus from pooling, which lowers the chance of bacteria growing. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T22#GNS212_U1_T22_h1)

question: When is a prophylactic drain used?

options.A: After an infection has already started
options.B: Before surgery to empty the bowel
options.C: To treat a confirmed internal abscess
options.D: During surgery to stop expected fluid buildup

explanation: Prophylactic drains are placed when a surgeon expects extra fluid or blood after an operation. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T22#GNS212_U1_T22_h1)

question: Which of these is an example of an open drainage system?

options.A: Chest drainage unit
options.B: Penrose drain
options.C: Jackson-Pratt drain
options.D: Hemovac reservoir

explanation: A Penrose drain is an open system that lets fluid drain straight onto dressings outside the body. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T22#GNS212_U1_T22_h2)

question: Why are closed drainage systems preferred over open systems?

options.A: They lower the risk of germs traveling back into the body
options.B: They let fluid evaporate through the plastic
options.C: They mean nurses never need to check them
options.D: They do not rely on gravity

explanation: Sealed tubing stops environmental germs from easily moving backward into body tissues. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T22#GNS212_U1_T22_h2)

question: What is the main job of a nasogastric tube attached to suction?

options.A: Emptying fluid and gas from the stomach
options.B: Giving high-protein liquid feeds
options.C: Delivering medicine to the lungs
options.D: Checking continuous blood pressure

explanation: Suction through an NG tube clears out stomach contents to stop bloating, nausea, and vomiting. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T22#GNS212_U1_T22_h3)

question: Why must a urine bag always hang lower than the patient's bladder?

options.A: To stop urine from flowing backward into the bladder
options.B: To keep pressure high in the tube
options.C: To help the kidneys make urine faster
options.D: To make it easier for the nurse to read without bending

explanation: Gravity keeps urine moving away from the body. Raising the bag causes urine to flow backward, which can lead to an infection. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T22#GNS212_U1_T22_h3)

question: What does a sudden stop in fluid from a surgical drain usually mean?

options.A: The suction has naturally increased
options.B: The patient is completely healed
options.C: The tube is blocked or kinked
options.D: The body has stopped making fluid

explanation: A sudden drop in output is usually caused by a physical blockage in the tube rather than an overnight cure. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T22#GNS212_U1_T22_h4)

question: What should you do right away if bright red blood suddenly fills a surgical drain?

options.A: Clamp the drain so no more blood leaves
options.B: Lower the collection bag to the floor
options.C: Call the surgical team about possible bleeding
options.D: Flush the tube with sterile normal saline

explanation: Bright red bleeding points to active bleeding inside that needs quick medical attention. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T22#GNS212_U1_T22_h4)

question: Why do you need to squeeze bulb-style suction drains before putting the cap back on?

options.A: To create the suction needed to pull out fluid
options.B: To clean the inside of the chamber
options.C: To keep the plastic from cracking
options.D: To push trapped air out through the drain site

explanation: Compressing the bulb and sealing it creates a vacuum that gently pulls fluid from the surgical site. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T22#GNS212_U1_T22_h5)

question: Why is it important to pin or secure drainage tubing to the patient's clothing?

options.A: To help fluid flow upward
options.B: To keep the collection bag hidden
options.C: To stop the drain from being accidentally pulled out
options.D: To warm up the fluid inside

explanation: Securing the tube gives it some slack so moving around doesn't yank the drain out of the wound. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T22#GNS212_U1_T22_h5)

question: Which action is dangerous if a surgical drain is accidentally pulled out partway?

options.A: Pushing the tubing back into the wound
options.B: Checking the patient's vital signs
options.C: Putting a sterile dressing over the opening
options.D: Calling the doctor

explanation: Pushing a slipped tube back inside carries skin germs straight into the sterile wound. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T22#GNS212_U1_T22_h6)

question: A patient's suction drain stops working, and the area becomes tight and painful. What should you check first?

options.A: Turn the suction pressure all the way up
options.B: Remove the drain right away
options.C: Check the tubing for kinks or blood clots
options.D: Wash out the wound with tap water

explanation: Kinks and clots are the most common reasons a drain suddenly stops working. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T22#GNS212_U1_T22_h6)

question: Why is a patient asked to hold their breath or bear down when a drain is being removed?

options.A: To stop air from entering the empty tract
options.B: To make urine flow faster
options.C: To numb the skin
options.D: To relax the stomach muscles

explanation: This breathing technique changes pressure in the body, lowering the risk of air getting into the tissue space. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T22#GNS212_U1_T22_h7)

question: What kind of dressing is usually put on right after a drain is taken out?

options.A: A sterile dressing that seals the wound
options.B: A tight plaster cast
options.C: Wet gauze soaked in sterile water
options.D: A loose elastic bandage

explanation: An airtight dressing covers the opening to stop fluid leaks and keep bacteria out. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T22#GNS212_U1_T22_h7)

question: What is the primary purpose of performing bladder irrigation?

options.A: To measure accurate daily fluid intake levels
options.B: To stimulate normal kidney function and urine output
options.C: To maintain catheter patency and remove clots
options.D: To permanently cure chronic urinary tract infections

explanation: Irrigation flushes out debris and blood clots that could otherwise block urine flow through the catheter. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T23#GNS212_U1_T23_h1)

question: Why is bladder irrigation frequently ordered following prostate surgery?

options.A: It speeds up the healing of abdominal skin incisions
options.B: Anesthetics permanently paralyze the urinary sphincter muscles
options.C: Surgical patients lose the ability to produce natural urine
options.D: Post-operative bleeding can form clots and block the catheter

explanation: Surgeries near the prostate often cause bleeding, making regular clearing necessary to prevent dangerous urinary retention. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T23#GNS212_U1_T23_h1)

question: Which clinical condition is a clear indication for bladder irrigation?

options.A: Severe chronic kidney disease with low output
options.B: Mild dehydration in an elderly patient
options.C: An uncomplicated lower urinary tract infection
options.D: Presence of gross hematuria with clot formation

explanation: Blood clots pose a major risk of catheter blockage, making irrigation necessary to clear the pathway. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T23#GNS212_U1_T23_h2)

question: Why is recent urinary tract trauma a contraindication for bladder irrigation?

options.A: It instantly causes permanent kidney failure in patients
options.B: Fluid pressure can worsen injuries and spread infection
options.C: The bladder muscle cannot hold any liquid volume
options.D: Sterile water reacts dangerously with exposed blood

explanation: Introducing fluid and pressure into a traumatized tract can tear fragile tissues and introduce bacteria deeper. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T23#GNS212_U1_T23_h2)

question: What is a major disadvantage of using an open bladder irrigation system?

options.A: It requires specialized triple-lumen catheters every time
options.B: Increased risk of introducing bacteria into the urinary tract
options.C: Patients experience much more severe abdominal pain
options.D: The procedure takes significantly longer to complete

explanation: Disconnecting the catheter junction exposes the sterile interior to airborne and contact contaminants. [learn more](GNS212_U1_T23#GNS212_U1_T23_h3)
