explanation: Suctioning is primarily performed to clear trapped mucus and fluids when a patient cannot cough them out independently. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T12#GNS212_U2_T12_h1)

question: Why is suction applied intermittently rather than continuously during airway clearance?

options.A: To allow the suction machine time to build up mechanical pressure
options.B: To make sure the sterile catheter stays clean on the inside
options.C: To prevent severe damage to the airway lining and low oxygen levels
options.D: To give the nurse enough time to measure the suction gauge

explanation: Continuous suctioning pulls too much air out of the lungs and aggressively grips the delicate tissue inside the airway. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T12#GNS212_U2_T12_h1)

question: A patient with an endotracheal tube needs suctioning when which sign appears?

options.A: Warm, dry skin with pink nail beds
options.B: Audible or visible secretions in the airway tube
options.C: Deep, quiet breathing sounds in all lung fields
options.D: A normal, steady heart rate and blood pressure

explanation: Seeing or hearing mucus rattling in the tube tells the nurse the airway is partially blocked and needs clearing. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T12#GNS212_U2_T12_h2)

question: Which condition is a clear contraindication for routine nasotracheal suctioning?

options.A: Severe bleeding disorders or severe nasal trauma
options.B: Needing a routine check of vital signs every four hours
options.C: A mild low-grade fever without respiratory changes
options.D: Being sleepy but easily waking up when spoken to

explanation: Passing a catheter through a damaged or bleeding nose can cause dangerous hemorrhage and further trauma. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T12#GNS212_U2_T12_h2)

question: What is the typical safe suction pressure range for an adult patient?

options.A: 500 to 600 mmHg
options.B: 10 to 20 mmHg
options.C: 80 to 120 mmHg
options.D: 200 to 300 mmHg

explanation: Pressures between 80 and 120 mmHg are strong enough to remove thick mucus without causing excessive trauma to the airway lining. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T12#GNS212_U2_T12_h3)

question: You are preparing a suction catheter for an adult patient with an artificial airway. What is the rule of thumb for selecting the catheter size?

options.A: It must be the largest possible size that fits through the opening
options.B: It should always be a uniform size 14 French regardless of the tube
options.C: It should fill the entire inside of the tube to grab all the mucus
options.D: It should take up no more than half the inner diameter of the airway

explanation: Leaving enough open space around the catheter prevents a vacuum from forming inside the lungs, which would dangerously drop oxygen levels. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T12#GNS212_U2_T12_h3)

question: Why is a patient hyperoxygenated right before undergoing tracheobronchial suctioning?

options.A: To force thick mucus plugs to dissolve and loosen up inside the lungs
options.B: To build up an oxygen reserve and prevent dangerous drops during the procedure
options.C: To test if the oxygen tank and flowmeter are working properly
options.D: To help the patient fall into a deep sleep so they feel no discomfort

explanation: Because the suction catheter temporarily removes air from the airway, extra oxygen beforehand protects the patient from sudden hypoxia. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T12#GNS212_U2_T12_h4)

question: What is an important step when preparing a conscious patient for suctioning?

options.A: Explaining what will happen to reduce anxiety and fear
options.B: Administering a strong sleeping pill before starting
options.C: Telling them not to cough under any circumstances
options.D: Asking them to hold their breath until the procedure ends

explanation: Clear communication helps calm the patient, ensuring better cooperation and less panic during a vulnerable moment. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T12#GNS212_U2_T12_h4)

question: What is the maximum recommended time for a single suction pass?

options.A: 3 to 5 minutes
options.B: 1 to 2 minutes
options.C: 30 to 45 seconds
options.D: 10 to 15 seconds

explanation: Limiting passes to 10 to 15 seconds prevents the patient from running out of oxygen and developing dangerous heart rhythms. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T12#GNS212_U2_T12_h5)

question: When should suction be applied as you insert the catheter into the artificial airway?

options.A: Never apply suction while inserting the catheter
options.B: Apply continuous suction the entire time you push it in
options.C: Apply suction only when the catheter hits the back of the throat
options.D: Apply suction in short bursts on the way down

explanation: Applying suction during insertion damages the delicate lining of the airway and removes helpful air; suction is only applied while withdrawing. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T12#GNS212_U2_T12_h5)

question: Why might a patient experience a sudden dangerous drop in heart rate during suctioning?

options.A: A sudden spike in blood pressure from anxiety
options.B: Too much clean air rushing into the stomach
options.C: Stimulation of the vagus nerve in the airway
options.D: An allergic reaction to the sterile glove powder

explanation: The vagus nerve runs close to the airway and triggers a slowing of the heart rate when irritated by the suction catheter. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T12#GNS212_U2_T12_h6)

question: During suctioning, your patient's oxygen saturation drops rapidly and their heart rate becomes irregular. What is your very first action?

options.A: Document the normal finding and check the patient again in one hour
options.B: Quickly insert the catheter deeper to grab the remaining thick mucus
options.C: Turn up the wall suction pressure to finish the procedure faster
options.D: Stop suctioning immediately and provide oxygen via manual resuscitator

explanation: Safety comes first: stop the trauma, remove the negative pressure, and give the patient oxygen to recover. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T12#GNS212_U2_T12_h6)

question: Which detail is essential to include when charting after suctioning a patient?

options.A: Color, consistency, and amount of the removed secretions
options.B: The exact brand name of the sterile gloves used
options.C: The name of the company that manufactured the suction machine
options.D: The room temperature at the moment of the procedure

explanation: Recording the characteristics of mucus gives vital clues about infection, hydration status, and overall lung health. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T12#GNS212_U2_T12_h7)

question: What is the best way to evaluate if the suctioning procedure was successful?

options.A: Ask the doctor to review the nursing notes at the end of the shift
options.B: Measure the weight of the empty suction canister on a scale
options.C: Listen to the patient's lung sounds and check oxygen levels
options.D: Confirm that the patient has fallen asleep comfortably

explanation: Checking lung sounds and oxygen saturation directly shows whether airway clearance improved breathing function. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T12#GNS212_U2_T12_h7)

question: What is the main job of an Automated External Defibrillator (AED)?

options.A: Delivering a shock to restart a stopped heart
options.B: Monitoring blood pressure during cardiac arrest
options.C: Providing continuous mechanical chest compressions
options.D: Treating chaotic heart rhythms with a controlled shock

explanation: An AED targets lethal heart rhythms like ventricular fibrillation by delivering an electrical shock to restore a normal rhythm. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T2#GNS212_U2_T2_h1)

question: Why is it so important to use an AED quickly during sudden cardiac arrest?

options.A: It prevents permanent damage to the skeletal muscles
options.B: Delayed treatment causes irreversible kidney failure first
options.C: The battery life of the AED drains very quickly
options.D: Survival rates drop rapidly with every passing minute

explanation: Brain and heart tissue quickly die from lack of oxygen when the heart stops, making rapid intervention essential for survival. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T2#GNS212_U2_T2_h1)

question: Which heart rhythms will a standard AED actually deliver a shock for?

options.A: Atrial fibrillation and sinus bradycardia
options.B: Ventricular fibrillation and pulseless ventricular tachycardia
options.C: Asystole and pulseless electrical activity
options.D: Supraventricular tachycardia and heart block

explanation: AEDs are specifically programmed to detect and treat VF and pulseless VT. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T2#GNS212_U2_T2_h2)

question: A patient with chest pain and a strong pulse faints briefly and wakes up. What should you do with the AED?

options.A: Check the patient's blood pressure before opening the device
options.B: Attach the AED immediately just in case the heart stops
options.C: Place the adult electrode pads directly over the clothing
options.D: Do NOT apply the AED pads because the patient has a pulse

explanation: An AED is only indicated when the patient is pulseless, unconscious, and not breathing normally. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T2#GNS212_U2_T2_h2)

question: Which part of the AED actually sends the electrical current into the patient's skin?

options.A: The voice prompt speaker
options.B: The internal lithium battery
options.C: The adhesive electrode pads
options.D: The external plastic casing

explanation: Electrode pads contain conductive gel and metal plates that interface directly with the skin to transmit the shock. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T2#GNS212_U2_T2_h3)

question: What is the purpose of the voice instructions and lights on an AED?

options.A: Guiding the rescuer step-by-step through the resuscitation process
options.B: Recording the exact time of arrival at the emergency scene
options.C: Measuring the depth of chest compressions delivered by the nurse
options.D: Testing the respiratory rate of the patient before pad placement

explanation: Clear audio and visual instructions help reduce panic and ensure proper protocol is followed by the rescuer. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T2#GNS212_U2_T2_h3)

question: What is the very first thing you should do after the AED delivers a shock?

options.A: Remove the electrode pads from the skin
options.B: Check the patient's pupils for light reaction
options.C: Turn off the AED to save battery life
options.D: Resume chest compressions and CPR

explanation: Current resuscitation guidelines emphasize starting chest compressions right away after a shock is delivered. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T2#GNS212_U2_T2_h4)

question: A patient's chest is soaking wet with sweat during an emergency. What should you do before putting on the pads?

options.A: Skip the AED entirely and rely solely on hand compressions
options.B: Dry the chest quickly with a towel before applying pads
options.C: Pour alcohol over the chest to evaporate the moisture
options.D: Apply the pads directly over the water to save time

explanation: Moisture can create a conductive bridge for the electrical current, causing the shock to arc across the skin rather than passing through the heart. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T2#GNS212_U2_T2_h4)

question: Where should you place an AED pad if the patient has a visible pacemaker lump on their chest?

options.A: On the patient's back instead of the front chest wall
options.B: Directly on top of the pacemaker bulge for better contact
options.C: On the upper abdomen below the lower rib cage
options.D: At least one inch away from the implanted device

explanation: Placing pads directly over a pacemaker can block the shock delivery and damage the generator. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T2#GNS212_U2_T2_h5)

question: You see a medicated patch on a patient's chest right where an AED pad needs to go. What should you do?

options.A: Apply the pad to the back instead of moving the patch
options.B: Ignore the patch because medications do not affect AEDs
options.C: Place the AED pad directly over the transdermal patch
options.D: Remove the patch wearing gloves and wipe the skin

explanation: Medication patches can block pad adhesion and cause skin burns or absorb chemicals improperly during a shock. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T2#GNS212_U2_T2_h5)

question: What does an AED message saying 'Check Pads' usually mean?

options.A: The patient has regained a normal pulse and breathing
options.B: Poor contact or loose connection between the skin and pads
options.C: The internal computer has experienced a fatal software error
options.D: The battery charge has completely depleted during the analysis

explanation: This message typically indicates air gaps under the pads, excessive hair, or a loose cable connection. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T2#GNS212_U2_T2_h6)

question: An infant needs a shock, but only adult AED pads are nearby. What should you do?

options.A: Cut the adult metal plates in half with heavy scissors
options.B: Apply both pads to the back of the infant side by side
options.C: Use the adult pads, making sure they do not touch each other
options.D: Refuse to use the AED because adult pads are dangerous for infants

explanation: If pediatric equipment is missing, standard pads can be used on infants, often placed front-and-back to prevent overlap. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T2#GNS212_U2_T2_h6)

question: Why should you leave the AED pads on the patient even after they start breathing and have a pulse again?

options.A: To prevent the skin from developing pressure sores
options.B: To monitor for sudden recurrence of a shockable rhythm
options.C: To measure ongoing urine output accurately
options.D: To keep the patient's chest warm during transport

explanation: Patients who achieve return of spontaneous circulation are at high risk of slipping back into ventricular fibrillation or tachycardia. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T2#GNS212_U2_T2_h7)

question: What important details must you tell the incoming medical team when handing over a revived patient?

options.A: Total downtime and number of shocks delivered
options.B: The exact brand of batteries inside the AED unit
options.C: The name of the manufacturer who built the pads
options.D: The serial number of the AED device used

explanation: Advanced providers need to know the duration of cardiac arrest and the interventions performed to guide ongoing post-resuscitation care. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T2#GNS212_U2_T2_h7)

question: In infants and young children, what is the main way the body keeps up cardiac output?

options.A: Vascular tone
options.B: Stroke volume
options.C: Plasma volume
options.D: Heart rate

explanation: A child's heart has a limited ability to pump more blood per beat, so it relies heavily on beating faster to increase cardiac output. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T3#GNS212_U2_T3_h1)

question: Why does a baby's large back of the head (occiput) make opening the airway tricky during resuscitation?

options.A: It narrows the internal jugular veins
options.B: It completely blocks the nasal passages
options.C: It forces the neck into passive flexion
options.D: It prevents adequate chest compressions

explanation: An infant's prominent head causes their neck to bend forward when they lie flat on their back, which can easily block their soft airway. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T3#GNS212_U2_T3_h1)

question: When using the Pediatric Assessment Triangle (PAT), which side looks at brain function and mental alertness?

options.A: Appearance
options.B: Blood pressure
options.C: Work of breathing
options.D: Circulation to skin

explanation: Appearance reflects how well the central nervous system is working, showing us the child's level of alertness and brain perfusion. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T3#GNS212_U2_T3_h2)

question: A toddler has nasal flaring and pulls in their chest muscles when breathing, but is alert with a normal skin color. Which part of the PAT is mainly affected?

options.A: Neurological status
options.B: Appearance
options.C: Work of breathing
options.D: Circulation to skin

explanation: Nasal flaring and pulling in of chest muscles are classic warning signs that the child is working much harder than usual to breathe. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T3#GNS212_U2_T3_h2)

question: What is the right chest compression-to-breath ratio when two rescuers are doing CPR on a child?
explanation: When two people are performing CPR on a child, they use 15 chest compressions followed by 2 rescue breaths. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T3#GNS212_U2_T3_h3)

question: How deep should you press the chest when doing CPR on an infant?

options.A: At least one-third the depth of the chest
options.B: Exactly one inch regardless of body size
options.C: Two full inches to reach the heart chambers
options.D: Half the depth of the infant chest wall

explanation: Compressing the chest by at least one-third of its total front-to-back depth ensures blood circulates effectively during an arrest. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T3#GNS212_U2_T3_h3)

question: Which method is the most reliable way to confirm a breathing tube (endotracheal tube) is in the right place?

options.A: Auscultation of breath sounds
options.B: Continuous waveform capnography
options.C: Absence of gastric gurgling
options.D: Bilateral symmetrical chest expansion

explanation: Capnography detects exhaled carbon dioxide, which is the gold standard for proving the tube went into the trachea and not the stomach. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T3#GNS212_U2_T3_h4)

question: What is a common problem when using a bag-valve-mask with too much force or pressure on a child?

options.A: Severe systemic hypertension
options.B: Spontaneous pneumoperitoneum
options.C: Immediate tracheal rupture
options.D: Gastric inflation

explanation: Blowing air in too hard or fast forces air into the stomach instead of the lungs, which can lead to vomiting. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T3#GNS212_U2_T3_h4)

question: Which breath sound points most clearly to an upper airway blockage in a child?

options.A: Crackles
options.B: Rhonchi
options.C: Wheezing
options.D: Stridor

explanation: Stridor is a harsh, high-pitched sound heard when breathing in, usually caused by narrowing in the upper airway. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T3#GNS212_U2_T3_h5)

question: Why does respiratory failure often lead directly to cardiac arrest in children?

options.A: Hypoxia and hypercarbia directly depress the myocardium
options.B: Systemic blood pressure rises too fast to sustain output
options.C: Pulmonary infections always spread directly to the heart
options.D: Children have an inherently fragile heart muscle

explanation: Running out of oxygen and building up carbon dioxide weakens the heart muscle over time until it stops beating. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T3#GNS212_U2_T3_h5)

question: What is the standard first dose of IV fluid given to a child in hypovolemic shock?

options.A: 5 mL/kg
options.B: 50 mL/kg
options.C: 10 mL/kg
options.D: 20 mL/kg

explanation: A rapid fluid bolus of 20 mL/kg of isotonic solution is the standard starting treatment to replace lost volume. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T3#GNS212_U2_T3_h6)

question: A child comes in with early septic shock, warm skin, and strong, bounding pulses. How is this type of shock described?

options.A: Obstructive shock
options.B: Hypovolemic shock
options.C: Distributive shock
options.D: Cardiogenic shock

explanation: Septic shock causes blood vessels to widen incorrectly, which often makes the skin feel warm at first. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T3#GNS212_U2_T3_h6)

question: What heart rhythm is most commonly seen when a child suffers cardiac arrest?

options.A: Ventricular fibrillation
options.B: Atrial fibrillation
options.C: Asystole
options.D: Pulseless ventricular tachycardia

explanation: Unlike adults who frequently have shockable rhythms, children in cardiac arrest most often present with asystole or PEA. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T3#GNS212_U2_T3_h7)

question: What is the recommended starting shock dose when using a defibrillator on a child with ventricular fibrillation?

options.A: 2 J/kg
options.B: 10 J/kg
options.C: 1 J/kg
options.D: 4 J/kg

explanation: The initial manual shock dose for a shockable rhythm in a pediatric patient is 2 Joules per kilogram. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T3#GNS212_U2_T3_h7)

question: Why should we avoid driving carbon dioxide levels too low with over-ventilation after resuscitating a child?

options.A: It rapidly destroys surfactant in damaged lung tissue
options.B: It prevents effective renal clearance of metabolic acids
options.C: It causes cerebral vasoconstriction and reduced brain perfusion
options.D: It immediately triggers malignant ventricular arrhythmias

explanation: Low carbon dioxide makes the blood vessels in the brain narrow down, which cuts off necessary blood flow after CPR. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T3#GNS212_U2_T3_h8)

question: What is a main goal for managing body temperature after a child is successfully resuscitated from cardiac arrest?

options.A: Maintaining core temperature above normal limits
options.B: Inducing mild hypothermia in all pediatric patients
options.C: Allowing natural febrile responses to clear pathogens
options.D: Preventing fever to protect against further brain injury

explanation: Fever puts extra stress on the brain when it is already recovering from lack of oxygen, so keeping the temperature normal is crucial. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T3#GNS212_U2_T3_h8)

question: What is the normal resting respiratory rate range for a healthy adult?

options.A: 24 to 30 breaths per minute
options.B: 32 to 40 breaths per minute
options.C: 12 to 20 breaths per minute
options.D: 8 to 10 breaths per minute

explanation: A normal adult respiratory rate at rest falls between 12 and 20 breaths per minute. Rates outside this range signal potential respiratory distress or metabolic derangements. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T4#GNS212_U2_T4_h1)

question: A patient uses neck muscles to breathe. What does this physical sign indicate?

options.A: Normal relaxation of the chest
options.B: High carbon dioxide excretion efficiency
options.C: Increased work of breathing
options.D: Adequate oxygen exchange in alveoli

explanation: Accessory muscle use in the neck and chest means the body is struggling to move air into the lungs. This sign alerts the nurse to impending respiratory fatigue. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T4#GNS212_U2_T4_h1)

question: A patient complaining of the subjective feeling of breathlessness has which condition?

options.A: Orthopnea
options.B: Eupnea
options.C: Dyspnea
options.D: Apnea

explanation: Dyspnea is the clinical term used when a patient describes feeling short of breath or unable to get enough air. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T4#GNS212_U2_T4_h2)

question: An adult patient with pneumonia becomes suddenly restless and confused. What should the nurse suspect first?

options.A: Excessive fluid intake
options.B: Normal reaction to hospital noise
options.C: Low blood oxygen levels
options.D: Improved lung expansion

explanation: Confusion and restlessness are classic early signs of hypoxia because the brain is sensitive to drops in blood oxygen. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T4#GNS212_U2_T4_h2)

question: Which bed position is best for an adult patient experiencing acute shortness of breath?

options.A: Flat supine
options.B: Trendelenburg
options.C: High-Fowler's
options.D: Prone position

explanation: The High-Fowler's position allows gravity to pull the diaphragm downward, expanding lung capacity and easing breathing effort. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T4#GNS212_U2_T4_h3)

question: Why is an unresponsive patient without trauma placed in the lateral recovery position?

options.A: To increase the respiratory rate automatically
options.B: To reduce blood pressure in the lower extremities
options.C: To prevent aspiration of fluids into the airway
options.D: To make chest compressions easier to perform

explanation: Lying on the side allows saliva, blood, or vomit to drain out of the mouth instead of pooling in the pharynx and entering the trachea. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T4#GNS212_U2_T4_h3)

question: What is the maximum recommended flow rate for a standard nasal cannula?

options.A: 15 liters per minute
options.B: 12 liters per minute
options.C: 20 liters per minute
options.D: 6 liters per minute

explanation: A nasal cannula is designed for low-flow oxygen ranging between 1 and 6 liters per minute. Higher rates dry out and irritate the nasal mucosa without adding significant oxygen benefit. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T4#GNS212_U2_T4_h4)

question: Which oxygen delivery device provides a precise and controlled fraction of inspired oxygen?

options.A: Nasal cannula
options.B: Non-rebreather mask
options.C: Venturi mask
options.D: Simple face mask

explanation: The Venturi mask uses specific jet adapters to mix room air and oxygen precisely, making it safe for patients who require controlled oxygen delivery. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T4#GNS212_U2_T4_h4)

question: Why are petroleum-based lubricants forbidden around active oxygen therapy?

options.A: They can ignite easily in an oxygen-rich environment
options.B: They cause immediate allergic reactions in the nose
options.C: They dissolve the plastic material of the oxygen mask
options.D: They block the flow of gas inside the tubing

explanation: Petroleum products react violently with high concentrations of oxygen and can catch fire spontaneously. Water-soluble lubricants are used instead. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T4#GNS212_U2_T4_h5)

question: How should a heavy portable oxygen gas cylinder be stored safely in a hospital ward?

options.A: Stored inside a closed wooden wardrobe
options.B: Leaned loosely against a bedside chair
options.C: Chained upright to a wall bracket or cart
options.D: Laid flat on the floor underneath the bed

explanation: Oxygen cylinders must be secured upright to prevent them from tipping over, which can break the valve and turn the tank into a dangerous projectile. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T4#GNS212_U2_T4_h5)

question: What is the primary purpose of using an incentive spirometer after abdominal surgery?

options.A: To deliver humidified medication directly into the bronchi
options.B: To promote deep breathing and prevent atelectasis
options.C: To measure the exact blood pressure of the lungs
options.D: To remove fluid accumulation from the pleural space

explanation: Incentive spirometry encourages sustained maximal inspiration, which opens alveoli and prevents small lung collapses known as atelectasis. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T4#GNS212_U2_T4_h6)

question: How does pursed-lip breathing help a patient with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease?

options.A: It forces more oxygen molecules into the bloodstream instantly
options.B: It relaxes the heart muscle to slow down the pulse rate
options.C: It creates backpressure to keep small airways open during exhalation
options.D: It increases the production of surfactant in the alveoli

explanation: Pursed-lip breathing slows down expiration and prevents the premature collapse of small bronchioles, allowing more trapped air to escape. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T4#GNS212_U2_T4_h6)

question: A patient has cold hands and a pulse oximeter reading of 82 percent, but breathing is easy and skin is pink. What should the nurse do first?

options.A: Start emergency mechanical ventilation immediately
options.B: Warm the patient's hand or move the sensor to an earlobe
options.C: Document that the patient is in severe respiratory failure
options.D: Increase the oxygen flow rate to maximum capacity

explanation: Poor peripheral perfusion caused by cold extremities impairs light absorption by pulse oximeters, leading to false low readings that require verification. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T4#GNS212_U2_T4_h7)

question: Which nursing action is most effective for preventing skin breakdown behind the ears from oxygen tubing?

options.A: Removing the oxygen delivery system entirely for several hours
options.B: Placing protective padding beneath the tubing over pressure points
options.C: Tightening the head strap securely to stop all movement
options.D: Applying heavy waterproof tape directly over the sensitive skin

explanation: Using soft padding cushions the skin from continuous friction and pressure caused by plastic tubing without interrupting vital oxygen therapy. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T4#GNS212_U2_T4_h7)

question: What is the primary advantage of delivering medication directly through the respiratory tract?

options.A: It eliminates all potential systemic side effects.
options.B: It requires higher doses than oral administration.
options.C: It bypasses first-pass liver metabolism completely.
options.D: It targets the lungs directly for faster local action.

explanation: Inhaled medications act directly on the respiratory tissue, providing a rapid therapeutic response where it is needed most. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T5#GNS212_U2_T5_h1)

question: Why are lower drug doses often sufficient with inhalation therapy compared to oral routes?

options.A: The medication is absorbed slowly through the stomach lining.
options.B: The rich blood supply of the alveoli absorbs the drug efficiently.
options.C: Digestive enzymes enhance the potency of the inhaled substance.
options.D: The liver activates the drug before it reaches the lungs.

explanation: The massive surface area and dense capillary network in the lungs allow direct and rapid uptake into the bloodstream. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T5#GNS212_U2_T5_h1)

question: Which inhalation device requires the patient to take a fast and deep breath to activate medication delivery?

options.A: Metered-Dose Inhaler
options.B: Dry Powder Inhaler
options.C: Ultrasonic nebulizer
options.D: Standard oxygen mask

explanation: DPIs depend on the patient's inspiratory flow to aerosolize and pull the dry powder out of the device. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T5#GNS212_U2_T5_h2)

question: A patient with severe hand-breath coordination issues will benefit most from using which device?

options.A: A standard Metered-Dose Inhaler without accessories
options.B: A Dry Powder Inhaler requiring deep inhalation
options.C: A Metered-Dose Inhaler attached to a spacer
options.D: A capsule-based breath-actuated dry powder system

explanation: Spacers trap the medication plume and reduce the need for precise hand-breath synchronization during administration. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T5#GNS212_U2_T5_h2)

question: The primary clinical indication for prescribing a bronchodilator via inhalation is to:

options.A: suppress an irritating dry cough reflex.
options.B: relieve acute bronchospasm and open airways.
options.C: treat systemic bacterial lung infections.
options.D: dry up excessive pulmonary secretions.

explanation: Bronchodilators relax the smooth muscles surrounding the bronchial tubes to ease airflow obstruction. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T5#GNS212_U2_T5_h3)

question: A patient admitted with an acute asthma attack requires immediate relief. The nurse expects to administer:

options.A: a daily dry powder prophylactic capsule.
options.B: an oral long-acting maintenance steroid.
options.C: a subcutaneous viscous antibiotic injection.
options.D: an inhaled short-acting beta-agonist.

explanation: Short-acting beta-agonists provide rapid bronchodilation to reverse acute airway narrowing during an asthma exacerbation. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T5#GNS212_U2_T5_h3)

question: What is the best body position for a patient receiving inhalation therapy?

options.A: Trendelenburg position
options.B: High Fowler's or sitting upright
options.C: Left lateral recumbent
options.D: Flat on the back

explanation: An upright posture allows full expansion of the thoracic cavity and optimal inhalation of the aerosolized drug. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T5#GNS212_U2_T5_h4)

question: Why is assessing a patient's manual dexterity important before prescribing an MDI?

options.A: It dictates the correct dosage of the prescribed drug.
options.B: It prevents allergic skin reactions to the plastic casing.
options.C: It ensures they can clean the machine parts independently.
options.D: It determines if they can press the canister while breathing in.

explanation: MDIs require simultaneous hand depression and inhalation, making dexterity a critical factor for successful use. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T5#GNS212_U2_T5_h4)

question: What action should a nurse instruct the patient to take immediately after inhaling a corticosteroid?

options.A: Drink a full glass of milk
options.B: Swallow remaining saliva immediately
options.C: Brush the tongue aggressively
options.D: Rinse the mouth with water and spit

explanation: Rinsing removes residual steroid particles from the oral cavity, preventing fungal infections like thrush. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T5#GNS212_U2_T5_h5)

question: Why is a breath-hold of ten seconds recommended after inhaling medication from an MDI?

options.A: It allows aerosolized drug particles to settle in the airways.
options.B: It clears trapped carbon dioxide from the alveoli.
options.C: It prevents the patient from coughing up the liquid.
options.D: It forces the heart rate to slow down safely.

explanation: Holding the breath gives the suspended medication droplets time to deposit onto the respiratory epithelium via gravity. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T5#GNS212_U2_T5_h5)

question: A patient complains of a fast, pounding heartbeat after repeated puffs of an emergency inhaler. This is likely due to:

options.A: an allergic reaction to the plastic mouthpiece.
options.B: sudden oxygen toxicity in the bloodstream.
options.C: an acute bacterial lung infection.
options.D: systemic absorption of a beta-agonist drug.

explanation: Beta-agonists can stimulate beta receptors in the heart, causing tachycardia and palpitations as a systemic side effect. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T5#GNS212_U2_T5_h6)

question: Which of the following is NOT a standard safety precaution when managing nebulizer therapy equipment?

options.A: Cleaning equipment between patients to prevent infection
options.B: Reusing disposable plastic tubing across multiple wards
options.C: Keeping emergency oxygen readily accessible nearby
options.D: Monitoring the patient for signs of medication tremors

explanation: Reusing single-patient disposable equipment across different wards creates a high risk for cross-contamination and nosocomial infection. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T5#GNS212_U2_T5_h6)

question: How should a patient clean their plastic spacer device for home care maintenance?

options.A: Boil it in hot water for twenty minutes daily.
options.B: Wash in warm soapy water and air dry.
options.C: Soak it overnight in a strong chlorine bleach solution.
options.D: Wipe the inside surface with a dry cotton swab.

explanation: Mild soap and water remove residue while air drying prevents static charge buildup that attracts powder to the walls. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T5#GNS212_U2_T5_h7)

question: What tool should a patient use at home to track day-to-day changes in their lung capacity?

options.A: A standard mercury sphygmomanometer
options.B: A bedside pulse oximeter monitor
options.C: A personal peak flow meter
options.D: A digital oral thermometer

explanation: A peak flow meter measures expiratory flow rates, helping patients detect airway narrowing before symptoms become severe. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T5#GNS212_U2_T5_h7)

question: What material is a traditional Nelson inhaler typically constructed from?

options.A: Flexible rubber
options.B: Stainless steel
options.C: Heavy ceramic
options.D: Clear plastics

explanation: Traditional Nelson inhalers are made of earthenware or heavy ceramic to help retain heat during the steam inhalation process. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T6#GNS212_U2_T6_h1)

question: How does the mechanism of a Nelson inhaler differ from an electric nebulizer?

options.A: It delivers dry medication straight into the lower lungs
options.B: It uses steam from boiling water instead of compressed air
options.C: It produces a cold mist rather than warm vapor
options.D: It requires an electrical power source to heat the water

explanation: The Nelson inhaler relies entirely on steam generated from hot water, whereas electric nebulizers use mechanical pressure to create a mist. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T6#GNS212_U2_T6_h1)

question: What is the function of the small air inlet on the Nelson inhaler cork?

options.A: To drain out condensed water after treatment
options.B: To allow fresh air to mix with rising steam
options.C: To pour the boiling water into the container
options.D: To attach the oxygen tubing during therapy

explanation: The air inlet lets room air mix with the hot vapor, which lowers the temperature to a safe level for inhalation. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T6#GNS212_U2_T6_h2)

question: Why is the mouthpiece on a Nelson inhaler angled upward?

options.A: To lock the cork securely into the ceramic body
options.B: To make cleaning the inside of the container easier
options.C: To direct vapor smoothly toward the mouth and nose
options.D: To prevent liquid water from spilling out during boiling

explanation: The angled mouthpiece guides the medicated steam directly toward the patient's upper airway without requiring awkward head positioning. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T6#GNS212_U2_T6_h2)

question: A patient presents to the clinic with severe sinus congestion and a blocked nose. What is the most appropriate nursing intervention?

options.A: Encourage deep breathing exercises without any equipment
options.B: Set up a Nelson inhaler with hot water and medicated tincture
options.C: Administer dry oxygen therapy via a simple face mask immediately
options.D: Prepare the patient for immediate endotracheal intubation

explanation: Sinus congestion responds well to warm, moist vapor therapy which helps open up the nasal passages and drain the sinuses. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T6#GNS212_U2_T6_h3)

question: How full should the nurse fill the Nelson inhaler pot with boiling water?

options.A: Filled to the halfway mark
options.B: About two-thirds full
options.C: Exactly one-quarter full
options.D: Filled completely to the brim

explanation: Filling the pot two-thirds full leaves enough space for steam accumulation and prevents boiling water from splashing out. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T6#GNS212_U2_T6_h4)

question: Why must the nurse test the vapor temperature before giving the inhaler to the patient?

options.A: To prevent accidental scalding of the facial skin and mucous membranes
options.B: To ensure the volatile medication has fully dissolved in the water
options.C: To verify that the water is still actively boiling inside the pot
options.D: To check if the cork is sealed tight enough to hold pressure

explanation: Testing the vapor protects the patient from thermal burns caused by steam that is excessively hot. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T6#GNS212_U2_T6_h4)

question: What is the recommended patient posture during Nelson inhaler treatment?

options.A: Flat supine position
options.B: Upright sitting position
options.C: Left lateral recumbent
options.D: Trendelenburg position

explanation: An upright posture ensures optimal lung expansion and prevents accidental spillage of hot water onto the patient. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T6#GNS212_U2_T6_h5)

question: How should the patient breathe while using the Nelson inhaler?

options.A: Breathe rapidly through both nostrils only
options.B: Take slow, deep breaths through the mouth
options.C: Take shallow breaths exclusively through the nose
options.D: Hold the breath for one minute at a time

explanation: Breathing slowly and deeply through the mouth allows the warm vapor to reach deep into the upper respiratory tract. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T6#GNS212_U2_T6_h5)

question: What is the most significant hazard associated with the use of a Nelson inhaler?

options.A: Thermal scalding from hot water or steam
options.B: Severe systemic toxicity from herbal drugs
options.C: Permanent loss of the sense of smell
options.D: Sudden collapse of the upper lung lobes

explanation: Because the device uses boiling water, burns and scalds represent the primary safety hazard during treatment. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T6#GNS212_U2_T6_h6)

question: A confused elderly patient is prescribed steam inhalation. What is the most critical safety action for the nurse?

options.A: Close the room windows completely to trap the steam
options.B: Increase the water temperature to shorten treatment time
options.C: Remain with the patient throughout the entire procedure
options.D: Allow the patient to hold the heavy ceramic pot independently

explanation: Confused patients are at high risk of knocking over boiling water, requiring constant nurse attendance for safety. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T6#GNS212_U2_T6_h6)

question: What substance is notorious for leaving a sticky residue inside the Nelson inhaler that requires thorough washing?

options.A: Tincture of Benzoin
options.B: Liquid paraffin oil
options.C: Plain distilled water
options.D: Normal saline solution

explanation: Tincture of Benzoin leaves a sticky resin residue on the ceramic walls that must be scrubbed clean after every use. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T6#GNS212_U2_T6_h7)

question: Why must the nurse take apart and air dry all components after cleaning?

options.A: To test if the mouthpiece is still securely attached
options.B: To make the cork fit more loosely for the next patient
options.C: To prevent bacterial growth and maintain proper hygiene
options.D: To prevent the ceramic body from cracking in storage

explanation: Thorough drying prevents moisture buildup, which serves as a breeding ground for harmful microorganisms between uses. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T6#GNS212_U2_T6_h7)

question: What physical form does medication take inside a functioning nebulizer chamber?

options.A: A clear sterile solution
options.B: A heated steam vapor
options.C: A fine mist aerosol
options.D: A compressed solid tablet

explanation: A nebulizer converts liquid medication into a fine mist aerosol so it can be inhaled deep into the airways. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T7#GNS212_U2_T7_h1)

question: Why is nebulization preferred over oral pills for acute bronchospasm?

options.A: It completely avoids any risk of side effects
options.B: It bypasses the need for oxygen gas sources
options.C: It delivers medicine straight to the airways quickly
options.D: It requires zero patient coordination to perform

explanation: Inhaled aerosol acts directly on the respiratory mucosa, providing a much faster therapeutic response than systemic routes. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T7#GNS212_U2_T7_h1)

question: Which clinical condition is a primary indication for routine nebulizer therapy?

options.A: Bacterial skin infection
options.B: Acute bronchospasm
options.C: Iron deficiency anemia
options.D: Peripheral vascular disease

explanation: Bronchodilators delivered via nebulizer quickly relax tightened airway muscles during asthma or COPD attacks. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T7#GNS212_U2_T7_h2)

question: A patient with thick, sticky mucus plugs in the bronchioles most likely needs which type of nebulized agent?

options.A: A long-acting vasopressor
options.B: A mucolytic solution
options.C: A concentrated electrolyte
options.D: A broad-spectrum antibiotic

explanation: Mucolytic medications break down chemical bonds in thick mucus, making secretions much easier to cough out. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T7#GNS212_U2_T7_h2)

question: What is the typical total fluid volume required inside a standard nebulizer cup?

options.A: 50 to 100 milliliters
options.B: 1 to 2 liters
options.C: 3 to 4 milliliters
options.D: 10 to 15 milliliters

explanation: A total volume of 3 to 4 mL ensures optimal aerosolization and efficient delivery within a reasonable timeframe. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T7#GNS212_U2_T7_h3)

question: Why might a nurse add normal saline to a nebulizer cup containing the medication?

options.A: To completely neutralize any toxic drug reactions
options.B: To heat up the aerosolized droplets for comfort
options.C: To clean the plastic tubing during the treatment
options.D: To reach the proper volume for effective misting

explanation: Small drug doses do not create enough liquid depth to mist properly without adding a diluent like normal saline. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T7#GNS212_U2_T7_h3)

question: Which baseline assessment is most critical before starting a nebulizer treatment?

options.A: Abdominal girth and bowel sounds
options.B: Lung sounds and respiratory rate
options.C: Deep tendon reflex strength
options.D: Visual acuity and pupillary response

explanation: Assessing breath sounds and breathing effort beforehand provides a baseline to judge if the medication works. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T7#GNS212_U2_T7_h4)

question: A patient is too confused to keep a mouthpiece in place during respiratory treatment. What should the nurse do?

options.A: Tape the patient's mouth shut around the tube
options.B: Force the patient to hold the mouthpiece tightly
options.C: Switch to an appropriately sized face mask
options.D: Cancel the treatment until the doctor arrives

explanation: A face mask accommodates patients who cannot actively cooperate with holding a mouthpiece during therapy. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T7#GNS212_U2_T7_h4)

question: What is the standard flow rate for compressed air or oxygen during a nebulizer treatment?

options.A: 1 to 2 liters per minute
options.B: 15 to 20 liters per minute
options.C: 6 to 8 liters per minute
options.D: 25 to 30 liters per minute

explanation: A flow rate of 6 to 8 L/min provides enough pressure to effectively aerosolize the liquid medication. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T7#GNS212_U2_T7_h5)

question: Why is the patient placed in an upright sitting position before treatment begins?

options.A: To prevent the machine from overheating during use
options.B: To allow rapid absorption of the drug through the skin
options.C: To stop the patient from falling asleep too quickly
options.D: To promote maximum lung expansion and air entry

explanation: An upright posture allows the diaphragm to descend fully, helping the aerosol reach deeper lung zones. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T7#GNS212_U2_T7_h5)

question: What indicates that a nebulizer treatment has finished completely?

options.A: The patient coughing up clear fluid
options.B: The machine starting to make a loud buzzing noise
options.C: Sputtering sounds from the nebulizer cup
options.D: The oxygen tank pressure dropping to zero

explanation: When the liquid medication is depleted, the cup begins to sputter, signaling the end of the treatment. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T7#GNS212_U2_T7_h6)

question: Why should the nurse encourage coughing after a successful bronchodilator and mucolytic treatment?

options.A: To prove the medication caused an allergic reaction
options.B: To expel loosened mucus from the airways
options.C: To test the vocal cords for normal function
options.D: To expand collapsed alveoli in the lung bases

explanation: Coughing helps clear out the secretions that were successfully thinned and mobilized by the aerosolized treatment. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T7#GNS212_U2_T7_h6)

question: Which side effect is commonly observed during or after nebulized beta-agonist therapy?

options.A: Extreme drop in blood pressure
options.B: Severe drowsiness and deep sleep
options.C: Complete loss of the voice
options.D: Increased heart rate and tremors

explanation: Beta-agonists stimulate beta receptors outside the lungs, frequently causing temporary tachycardia and jitteriness. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T7#GNS212_U2_T7_h7)

question: What should the nurse do immediately if a patient develops severe chest pain during a treatment?

options.A: Wait until the medication cup is completely empty
options.B: Encourage the patient to breathe faster
options.C: Increase the gas flow rate to help them breathe
options.D: Stop the nebulizer and inform the doctor

explanation: Chest pain or severe distress indicates an adverse reaction requiring immediate cessation of therapy and medical review. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T7#GNS212_U2_T7_h7)

question: How should nebulizer parts be dried after washing to prevent contamination?

options.A: Wiped dry with unwashed hands
options.B: Stored wet inside a sealed plastic bag
options.C: Air dried on a clean surface
options.D: Dried vigorously with a shared towel

explanation: Air drying prevents the introduction of lint and bacteria from towels into the washed equipment. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T7#GNS212_U2_T7_h8)

question: Why is strict cleaning of the nebulizer cup necessary between uses?

options.A: To keep the plastic from changing color over time
options.B: To prevent bacterial growth in the moist chamber
options.C: To ensure the air compressor motor runs quietly
options.D: To prevent the next dose from tasting too sweet

explanation: Moist environments inside nebulizer cups easily harbor pathogens that can cause secondary respiratory infections. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T7#GNS212_U2_T7_h8)

question: What is the primary therapeutic goal of a steam tent?

options.A: Deliver dry oxygen therapy
options.B: Increase systemic blood pressure
options.C: Loosen thick mucus secretions
options.D: Lower the patient body temperature

explanation: Warm moisture thinned respiratory secretions, making it easier for the patient to cough them out and breathe better. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T8#GNS212_U2_T8_h1)

question: A patient with acute bronchitis is most likely to benefit from a steam tent because it provides what?

options.A: Immediate reduction in chest wall pain
options.B: High concentrations of pure ozone
options.C: Direct moisture to irritated airways
options.D: Permanent relief from bacterial infection

explanation: The humidified air soothes inflamed mucosal linings and loosens trapped mucus in the bronchial tree. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T8#GNS212_U2_T8_h1)

question: Where should the boiling water container be positioned during steam tent setup?

options.A: At a safe distance outside the tent
options.B: Inside the canopy close to the pillow
options.C: Balanced on the edge of the bedside table
options.D: Directly on the patient mattress for warmth

explanation: Keeping the heat source outside prevents accidental spills and direct contact burns inside the enclosure. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T8#GNS212_U2_T8_h2)

question: Why is a waterproof sheet placed on the mattress before building a steam tent?

options.A: To absorb excess carbon dioxide gas
options.B: To anchor the metal canopy frame firmly
options.C: To reflect heat back toward the patient
options.D: To prevent moisture from soaking the bed

explanation: Heavy condensation forms during steam therapy, requiring waterproof barriers to keep the bedding dry and comfortable. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T8#GNS212_U2_T8_h2)

question: What position should a patient be placed in before starting steam tent therapy?

options.A: Upright or semi-Fowler's position
options.B: Trendelenburg position with feet elevated
options.C: Prone position facing the mattress
options.D: Flat on the back with no pillow

explanation: An upright posture promotes optimal lung expansion and prevents aspiration of loosened secretions. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T8#GNS212_U2_T8_h3)

question: Why must oil-based chest rubs be removed before applying steam therapy?

options.A: They cause the plastic canopy sheets to dissolve
options.B: They interfere with electronic thermometer readings
options.C: They can increase skin sensitivity under moist heat
options.D: They completely block the generation of water vapor

explanation: Occlusive ointments combined with trapped heat can lead to skin irritation, rashes, or minor burns. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T8#GNS212_U2_T8_h3)

question: What is the recommended maximum duration for a single steam tent session?

options.A: Entire duration of the night shift
options.B: 15 to 20 minutes
options.C: 1 to 2 hours straight
options.D: 30 to 45 seconds total

explanation: Short sessions prevent patient exhaustion, overheating, and potential respiratory fatigue. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T8#GNS212_U2_T8_h4)

question: Why must a nurse remain nearby while a patient is inside a steam tent?

options.A: To constantly add boiling water to the kettle
options.B: To monitor for distress and prevent accidents
options.C: To measure the exact humidity percentage hourly
options.D: To prevent visitors from opening the canopy

explanation: Enclosed steam environments carry risks of overheating and sudden respiratory changes that require immediate nursing action. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T8#GNS212_U2_T8_h4)

question: What action should the nurse take immediately after ending the steam therapy session?

options.A: Dry the patient skin and assist with a clean gown
options.B: Leave the wet canopy in place for natural drying
options.C: Administer a cold bath to lower body temperature
options.D: Force the patient to drink ice-cold water quickly

explanation: Removing moisture prevents chilling and skin breakdown after exposure to heavy humidity. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T8#GNS212_U2_T8_h5)

question: Why should the steam tent canopy be opened gradually rather than yanked away all at once?

options.A: Sudden drafts can trigger chills or bronchospasm
options.B: Slow opening stops condensation from dripping on beds
options.C: It prevents the plastic sheet from making loud noises
options.D: Rapid pressure drops cause immediate ear damage

explanation: Abrupt temperature changes on warm, moist skin can induce sudden airway constriction or discomfort. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T8#GNS212_U2_T8_h5)

question: Which detail is NOT necessary to include in the documentation of steam tent therapy?

options.A: Pre and post-procedure breath sounds
options.B: The brand name of the kettle used
options.C: Exact start and end times of the session
options.D: Patient tolerance and sputum production

explanation: Equipment brand names are irrelevant to clinical care notes, whereas patient assessment data and responses are mandatory. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T8#GNS212_U2_T8_h6)

question: What immediate action is required if a patient sustains a scald injury during steam therapy?

options.A: Cover the burn tightly with dry cotton bandages
options.B: Apply thick antiseptic ointments over the blisters
options.C: Wait until the end of the shift to report the burn
options.D: Remove the heat source and apply cool clean water

explanation: Immediate cooling stops the burning process in the tissue layers, minimizing damage before medical review. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T8#GNS212_U2_T8_h6)

question: What is the approximate oxygen concentration of normal room air?

options.A: 100 percent
options.B: 50 percent
options.C: 21 percent
options.D: 10 percent

explanation: Ambient room air naturally contains roughly 21% oxygen, which serves as the baseline when calculating supplemental oxygen needs. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T9#GNS212_U2_T9_h1)

question: A patient with severe fever and increased metabolic demand is most likely receiving oxygen to prevent what condition?

options.A: Hypercapnia
options.B: Hypertension
options.C: Hypoxia
options.D: Dehydration

explanation: High metabolic states increase tissue oxygen consumption, which can lead to cellular oxygen deficiency if not supplemented. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T9#GNS212_U2_T9_h1)

question: What device controls the liters per minute of gas delivered to the patient?

options.A: Flowmeter
options.B: Humidifier bottle
options.C: Connecting tubing
options.D: Nasal prongs

explanation: The flowmeter attaches to the oxygen source to precisely regulate the speed and volume of gas output. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T9#GNS212_U2_T9_h2)

question: When should a nurse attach a humidification bottle to the oxygen delivery setup?

options.A: Only for pediatric patients
options.B: When flow rates exceed 4 LPM
options.C: Only during nighttime administration
options.D: Whenever oxygen is set to 1 LPM

explanation: Higher flow rates dry out nasal mucosa quickly, making humidification necessary to prevent mucosal damage and irritation. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T9#GNS212_U2_T9_h2)

question: Why is the semi-Fowler's position preferred when preparing a patient for oxygen therapy?

options.A: It stops nasal secretions from bleeding
options.B: It prevents aspiration of saliva
options.C: It optimizes lung expansion and breathing
options.D: It allows easier intravenous line insertion

explanation: Elevating the head of the bed decreases abdominal pressure on the diaphragm, making chest expansion easier for the patient. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T9#GNS212_U2_T9_h3)

question: What physical check of the patient is essential before inserting nasal prongs?

options.A: Inspecting nasal patency and mucosa
options.B: Palpating abdominal tenderness
options.C: Checking pupil light reflex
options.D: Auscultating bowel sounds

explanation: The nurse must ensure the nostrils are clear and free from trauma or severe congestion so airflow is not blocked. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T9#GNS212_U2_T9_h3)

question: In which direction should the nasal cannula prongs curve when inserted into the nose?

options.A: Downward toward the throat
options.B: Backward toward the ears
options.C: Upward toward the forehead
options.D: Outward toward the cheeks

explanation: Curving the prongs downward matches the natural anatomical direction of the nasal passages for effective airflow. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T9#GNS212_U2_T9_h4)

question: What is the correct sequence before placing the cannula on the patient's face?

options.A: Add sterile water only after securing the chin slider
options.B: Secure tubing around ears before connecting to the wall
options.C: Place prongs first, then turn on the gas
options.D: Turn on the gas and set flow rate before placing prongs

explanation: Verifying gas flow before application ensures the patient receives oxygen immediately and confirms equipment functionality. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T9#GNS212_U2_T9_h4)

question: What approximate FiO2 is delivered by a nasal cannula running at 4 liters per minute?

options.A: 60 percent
options.B: 36 percent
options.C: 100 percent
options.D: 24 percent

explanation: Each liter per minute of flow generally adds roughly 4% to the baseline 21% room air, bringing 4 LPM to approximately 36%. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T9#GNS212_U2_T9_h5)

question: Why is running a nasal cannula at rates above 6 liters per minute generally discouraged?

options.A: It melts the plastic connecting tubing
options.B: It reverses airflow and pulls room air into the cylinder
options.C: It causes immediate oxygen toxicity in all patients
options.D: It causes severe mucosal drying without increasing FiO2 much

explanation: High flow rates dry out nasal tissues painfully and inefficiently, making a simple face mask a better choice for higher oxygen needs. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T9#GNS212_U2_T9_h5)

question: Where should the nurse inspect most frequently for pressure breakdown caused by oxygen tubing?

options.A: Behind the ears and over the cheekbones
options.B: Underneath the chin and neck folds
options.C: Around the sternum and clavicle
options.D: Across the bridge of the nose

explanation: Tubing rests directly against the ears and cheeks, making those contact points vulnerable to friction and skin breakdown. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T9#GNS212_U2_T9_h6)

question: A patient receiving nasal oxygen complains of a dry, parched mouth. Which intervention should the nurse prioritize?

options.A: Increase the oxygen flow rate by 2 LPM
options.B: Remove the cannula permanently to stop dryness
options.C: Apply petroleum jelly directly inside the nostrils
options.D: Provide regular oral hygiene and offer sips of water

explanation: Mouth breathing dries mucosal membranes, so frequent oral care and hydration relieve discomfort safely. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T9#GNS212_U2_T9_h6)

question: Which safety hazard is the primary concern when administering supplemental oxygen?

options.A: Risk of electrical shock from the wall
options.B: Risk of sudden fire combustion
options.C: Risk of freezing cold gas burns
options.D: Risk of toxic chemical fumes

explanation: Oxygen is an accelerant that violently fuels fires, making flame and spark prevention an absolute priority. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T9#GNS212_U2_T9_h7)

question: Which patient group requires special caution regarding high-flow oxygen administration due to risk of respiratory depression?

options.A: Patients with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease
options.B: Patients recovering from normal appendectomy
options.C: Patients with severe bone fractures
options.D: Patients with acute malaria

explanation: Some COPD patients breathe based on low blood oxygen levels rather than carbon dioxide levels, so high oxygen can depress their breathing drive. [learn more](GNS212_U2_T9#GNS212_U2_T9_h7)

question: How do digital (electronic) blood pressure machines mainly measure your blood pressure?

options.A: By placing a small fluid tube inside the artery
options.B: By sensing pulse waves (oscillations) in the cuff
options.C: By feeling the pulse at the wrist directly
options.D: By listening to Korotkoff sounds with a tiny microphone

explanation: Digital machines look for tiny changes or oscillations in pressure caused by your pulse, rather than listening for sounds like we do with a stethoscope. Spot on! [learn more](GNS212_U4_T1#GNS212_U4_T1_h1)

question: Why does a patient moving around during a digital blood pressure check often cause an error?

options.A: Movement stops the battery from sending power to the screen
options.B: Moving completely shuts off the air valve inside the cuff
options.C: Physical activity instantly drops the patient's actual blood pressure
options.D: Movement creates false pressure bumps that confuse the machine's computer

explanation: The machine looks for very steady, specific waves. Any extra shaking or moving creates chaotic signals that mess up the calculation. Keep your patient nice and still! [learn more](GNS212_U4_T1#GNS212_U4_T1_h1)

question: What is one of the best perks of using an electronic blood pressure machine over a manual one?

options.A: They are completely unaffected if the patient moves
options.B: They take very little training to use correctly
options.C: They give exact readings even during serious heart rhythm problems
options.D: They never need new batteries or servicing

explanation: Digital monitors do the heavy lifting for you! You don't need expert stethoscope listening skills to get a quick reading. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T1#GNS212_U4_T1_h2)

question: When would a manual blood pressure check with a stethoscope be a better choice than a digital machine?

options.A: When the patient is checking their own pressure at home
options.B: When the patient has a very irregular heartbeat
options.C: When the hospital ward is completely quiet
options.D: When you are in a rush during a busy shift

explanation: Digital machines struggle to calculate properly when the heart rhythm jumps all over the place. That's when your manual auscultation skills shine! [learn more](GNS212_U4_T1#GNS212_U4_T1_h2)

question: Where should you position the lower edge of the blood pressure cuff on the patient's arm?

options.A: About one inch above the inner elbow crease
options.B: Right up against the shoulder joint
options.C: Directly over the bony wrist
options.D: Halfway down the forearm

explanation: Placing it about an inch above the elbow crease ensures the inner bladder sits right over the brachial artery. Perfect placement! [learn more](GNS212_U4_T1#GNS212_U4_T1_h3)

question: You get a falsely high blood pressure reading because the cuff you used was way too small for the patient's arm. What should you do next?

options.A: Record the high reading as their true baseline blood pressure
options.B: Switch to measuring the blood pressure on their ankle instead
options.C: Just subtract ten points from the result and write that down
options.D: Grab a larger cuff and repeat the check after giving the patient a short rest

explanation: A wrong cuff size means the reading isn't reliable. Always re-measure with the correct size after letting the patient rest for a minute. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T1#GNS212_U4_T1_h3)

question: Why can crossing the legs during a blood pressure check lead to a falsely high reading?

options.A: It blocks blood flow completely in the arm's brachial artery
options.B: It increases physical tension and blood vessel resistance in the body
options.C: It stops the machine from pumping air into the cuff
options.D: It drains the battery of the electronic device faster

explanation: Crossed legs and slouching temporarily boost your vascular pressure. Always remind patients to uncross their legs and keep feet flat on the floor! [learn more](GNS212_U4_T1#GNS212_U4_T1_h4)

question: Which of these is a MISTAKE when getting a patient ready for a digital blood pressure check?

options.A: Making sure both of the patient's feet are flat on the floor
options.B: Asking the patient to stay quiet while the machine runs
options.C: Allowing the patient to keep a thick sweater on with the cuff rolled over it
options.D: Ensuring the patient rests quietly for five minutes beforehand

explanation: Always put the cuff directly on bare skin! Thick clothing or tight rolling can pinch the arm and mess up your numbers. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T1#GNS212_U4_T1_h4)

question: What is a major giveaway that a digital blood pressure cuff has an air leak?

options.A: The screen flashes bright red and rings a loud alarm
options.B: The battery icon shows full charge the whole time
options.C: The machine shows an error code or cannot finish pumping up
options.D: The device measures the blood pressure twice as fast as usual

explanation: If air is escaping, the machine can't build up the pressure it needs, so it will usually flash an error message at you. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T1#GNS212_U4_T1_h5)

question: Why do electronic blood pressure monitors need to be checked and calibrated regularly?

options.A: Internal sensors naturally drift and lose accuracy over time and with use
options.B: It's just a rule made by manufacturers to keep batteries from exploding
options.C: The internal software wipes its own memory clean every few weeks
options.D: Sensors magically improve their own accuracy without any human help

explanation: Just like weighing scales, electronic monitors can get a bit out of whack over time. Regular checks ensure our numbers stay trustworthy. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T1#GNS212_U4_T1_h5)

question: A digital monitor shows a very high blood pressure for a calm patient who feels totally fine. What is your best immediate nursing action?

options.A: Write down the machine's number and walk away to another room
options.B: Check the reading manually using a stethoscope and manual cuff
options.C: Rush to give the patient strong blood pressure-lowering drugs
options.D: Throw the electronic device away and never use it again

explanation: Machines can glitch! If a result doesn't match how the patient looks or feels, always double-check it manually before panicking or treating. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T1#GNS212_U4_T1_h6)

question: Why is teaching patients how to use home blood pressure monitors such an important nursing duty?

options.A: Patients need to know how to solder broken circuit boards at home
options.B: Good technique prevents false readings that could lead to wrong medication changes
options.C: It stops patients from ever coming back to the hospital clinic
options.D: Home machines are so complicated that only rocket scientists can run them

explanation: If a patient uses poor posture or a bad cuff size at home, their doctor might see bad data and change their prescriptions incorrectly. Your teaching makes a real difference! [learn more](GNS212_U4_T1#GNS212_U4_T1_h6)

question: What is the main reason nurses use portable monitors in the hospital?

options.A: To track vital signs while a patient is moving
options.B: To permanently store a patient's entire medical history
options.C: To deliver intravenous medications automatically
options.D: To replace all stationary equipment in the intensive care unit

explanation: Portable monitors are lifesavers when patients are walking around or being moved between wards. They let us keep a close eye on vitals on the go! [learn more](GNS212_U4_T10#GNS212_U4_T10_h1)

question: Why are portable monitors so great for catching sudden changes in a patient's condition?

options.A: They provide continuous, real-time physiological data outside the bedside
options.B: They eliminate the need for any manual vital sign documentation
options.C: They completely prevent the occurrence of false alarms
options.D: They automatically diagnose underlying diseases without nurse input

explanation: Because they track vitals continuously—even during transport—we can spot sudden warning signs immediately and act fast. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T10#GNS212_U4_T10_h1)

question: Which portable device does a patient wear to continuously send heart rhythm data to the nurse's station?

options.A: A standard mercury sphygmomanometer
options.B: A handheld blood glucose meter
options.C: A telemetry transmitter
options.D: A basic digital thermometer

explanation: Telemetry packs are worn by the patient to wirelessly beam their ECG rhythm straight to the central monitor. Very handy for cardiac patients! [learn more](GNS212_U4_T10#GNS212_U4_T10_h2)

question: How is a transport monitor different from a simple, pocket-sized pulse oximeter?

options.A: It does not require a power source or battery to function
options.B: It tracks multiple vital parameters simultaneously during critical movement
options.C: It can only measure the patient's body temperature
options.D: It is strictly used for outpatient home care without nursing oversight

explanation: While a pocket oximeter usually only checks oxygen levels, a transport monitor is built to track several vital signs at once during busy or critical moves. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T10#GNS212_U4_T10_h2)

question: When are you most likely to hook an inpatient up to a portable monitor?

options.A: During intrahospital transport to diagnostic imaging
options.B: While the patient is sleeping quietly in a stable hospital bed
options.C: During routine discharge education in the room
options.D: When filing physical paper records in the nurses' station

explanation: Whenever we roll a patient out of their room for an X-ray or scan (diagnostic imaging), we hook them up to a portable monitor to keep them safe on the journey. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T10#GNS212_U4_T10_h3)

question: A recovering heart patient is ready to take their first walk down the ward corridor. What should you do?

options.A: Attach a portable telemetry or wireless monitoring unit
options.B: Keep the patient attached to a heavy wall-mounted monitor with long cables
options.C: Wait until the patient returns to the bed to check vitals
options.D: Disconnect all monitoring devices to encourage normal movement

explanation: Early walks are great for recovery, but we always want a wireless or telemetry unit attached so we can safely watch out for any exercise-related heart issues. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T10#GNS212_U4_T10_h3)

question: What is an important quick check before you connect a portable monitor to a patient?

options.A: Disconnecting all wireless internet routers nearby
options.B: Resetting the device to factory default settings
options.C: Calibrating the internal clock to Greenwich Mean Time
options.D: Checking the battery charge and power status

explanation: Always make sure the battery is charged! The last thing you want is the monitor dying halfway down the hallway. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T10#GNS212_U4_T10_h4)

question: Why is it smart to adjust alarm limits on a portable monitor for each specific patient?

options.A: The machine will refuse to record data without personalized input
options.B: Standard defaults are illegal to use in modern hospitals
options.C: Customizing limits stops the battery from draining too quickly
options.D: Factory defaults may be unsafe or cause unnecessary alarm fatigue

explanation: Generic settings can either miss a real problem or beep constantly for no reason (alarm fatigue). Tailoring it to the patient keeps everyone sane and safe! [learn more](GNS212_U4_T10#GNS212_U4_T10_h4)

question: What should you do FIRST when a portable monitor suddenly lets out a loud, urgent alarm?

options.A: Document a cardiac arrest in the patient chart right away
options.B: Immediately silence the device and walk away to find a doctor
options.C: Turn off the monitor power switch to stop the annoying noise
options.D: Assess the patient's physical condition and check the sensor placement

explanation: Patient first, always! Check the patient and make sure the sensor hasn't just popped off before jumping to conclusions. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T10#GNS212_U4_T10_h5)

question: What is a very common cause of false alarms on a portable pulse oximeter while moving a patient?

options.A: Normal room lighting brightness
options.B: Fresh battery installation
options.C: High room humidity levels
options.D: Motion artifact and shivering

explanation: Movement or shivering shakes the sensor around (motion artifact), confusing the machine and leading to wild or false readings. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T10#GNS212_U4_T10_h5)

question: When is it time to clean and disinfect a portable monitor?

options.A: Whenever the battery runs completely flat
options.B: Only once a week during night shift
options.C: Only if visibly stained with blood
options.D: After every single patient use

explanation: Wiping down the equipment between patients stops germs from spreading and keeps our hospital environment safe. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T10#GNS212_U4_T10_h6)

question: What is your best first step if a portable monitor starts showing crazy, unreadable numbers?

options.A: Throw the equipment into the nearest biohazard bin
options.B: Inspect cable connections and sensor placement
options.C: Take the device apart with a screwdriver to check internal wires
options.D: Ignore the error message until the shift ends

explanation: Usually, erratic data just means a loose cable or a slipped sensor. Always check the physical setup first! [learn more](GNS212_U4_T10#GNS212_U4_T10_h6)

question: What is the main job of wearable health devices in clinical care?

options.A: To deliver oral medications automatically to the patient
options.B: To diagnose complex surgical diseases without a doctor
options.C: To track and transmit health-related data continuously
options.D: To replace traditional laboratory blood testing completely

explanation: Wearables are great because they keep an eye on patient vitals between clinic visits. You've got this! [learn more](GNS212_U4_T11#GNS212_U4_T11_h1)

question: Which wearable device is best for continuous, medical-grade heart rhythm monitoring?

options.A: A standard consumer fitness wristband
options.B: A basic smartphone pedometer app
options.C: An adhesive medical-grade patch
options.D: A smart textile running t-shirt

explanation: Medical patches stick securely and are specifically designed to catch every beat of critical heart rhythms accurately. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T11#GNS212_U4_T11_h1)

question: How do optical sensors in regular fitness wristbands usually measure your heart rate?

options.A: By measuring electrical currents through the skin
options.B: By detecting changes in blood flow using light
options.C: By listening to heart valve closures via tiny microphones
options.D: By calculating body temperature shifts on the wrist

explanation: Think of how a flashlight shines through your fingers—these sensors use light to catch the pulse of blood moving underneath your skin! [learn more](GNS212_U4_T11#GNS212_U4_T11_h2)

question: What fluid do continuous glucose monitors sample to check a patient's sugar levels?

options.A: Epidermal sweat
options.B: Interstitial fluid
options.C: Capillary whole blood
options.D: Venous plasma

explanation: The tiny sensor sits right under the skin, swimming in the fluid surrounding your cells (interstitial fluid) to estimate blood sugar. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T11#GNS212_U4_T11_h2)

question: Why is tracking data over time with a wearable better than a single blood pressure check at the clinic?

options.A: It prevents nurses from having to manually record any vital signs
options.B: It completely eliminates the need for any laboratory blood tests
options.C: It guarantees that the patient will take all prescribed medications
options.D: It captures daily trends and avoids single-visit anxiety spikes

explanation: Ever get nervous seeing a doctor in a white coat? Wearables show real everyday trends without hospital stress getting in the way. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T11#GNS212_U4_T11_h3)

question: A heart failure patient uses a wearable at home. Which trend should make a nurse step in early?

options.A: Gradual upward trends in daily weight and decreasing physical activity
options.B: Stable resting heart rates recorded consistently throughout the night
options.C: Occasional reminders to stand up and stretch during sedentary hours
options.D: A slight increase in daily step counts reported over the weekend

explanation: When activity drops and weight creeps up from fluid, it's often an early warning sign that heart failure symptoms are worsening. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T11#GNS212_U4_T11_h3)

question: What is an important nursing duty when giving a wearable device to a patient?

options.A: Writing custom software code to link the device to the hospital
options.B: Calibrating the internal microchips using a sterile surgical kit
options.C: Teaching the patient how to wear, charge, and sync the device
options.D: Replacing the device hardware components whenever the battery dies

explanation: As a nurse, your guidance is key! Patients need to know how to handle, charge, and sync their devices so the data keeps flowing. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T11#GNS212_U4_T11_h4)

question: Why do nurses set specific alert limits (thresholds) on patient wearables?

options.A: To ensure the device battery never runs out of power unexpectedly
options.B: To stop patients from looking at their own heart rate data
options.C: To comply with government laws regarding smartphone manufacturing
options.D: To prevent alert fatigue from minor, harmless data fluctuations

explanation: Setting smart limits stops alarms from ringing over tiny movements, keeping nurses focused on actual emergencies. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T11#GNS212_U4_T11_h4)

question: Why is data encryption so important for health wearable devices?

options.A: To increase the physical durability of the wristband strap
options.B: To protect sensitive patient health records from unauthorized interception
options.C: To ensure the step counter measures distance more accurately
options.D: To make the device battery last much longer during daily use

explanation: Encryption scrambles personal health details so hackers can't read or steal confidential patient information. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T11#GNS212_U4_T11_h5)

question: Which of these is NOT an ethical concern when using health wearables?

options.A: Ensuring equal access for patients regardless of income
options.B: Obtaining proper informed consent for data sharing
options.C: Protecting personal health information from data breaches
options.D: Increasing the physical battery weight of the wristband

explanation: Battery weight is just hardware design, while privacy, consent, and equal access are major ethical issues in nursing informatics. [learn more](GNS212_U4_T11#GNS212_U4_T11_h5)

question: What is a major challenge when using wearable health devices in some Nigerian communities?

options.A: Excessive availability of high-speed fiber optic cables
options.B: Strict government bans on all digital wristwatches
options.C: A complete lack of patients suffering from chronic illnesses
