options.C: Clear and colorless like water
options.D: Cloudy yellow like thin milk

explanation: Spot on! Normal CSF is transparent and looks just like clean water because it lacks blood cells or excess protein. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T9#GNS221_U2_T9_h8)

question: What does a significantly low glucose level in the cerebrospinal fluid usually suggest?

options.A: Recent physical exercise
options.B: A normal healthy patient
options.C: A bacterial infection
options.D: Viral meningitis illness

explanation: You got it! Bacterial germs consume glucose rapidly within the spinal fluid, making the lab numbers drop below normal. [learn more](GNS221_U2_T9#GNS221_U2_T9_h8)

question: What is the main difference between a medical emergency and a surgical emergency?

options.A: Surgical emergencies never involve internal bleeding
options.B: Medical emergencies always require immediate surgery
options.C: Medical emergencies only happen outside the hospital
options.D: Surgical emergencies usually require an operation to fix

explanation: You've got this! Surgical emergencies involve physical trauma or acute organ trouble that typically needs an operation to fix, while medical emergencies usually stem from internal illnesses. Think surgery vs. medicine! [learn more](GNS221_U3_T1#GNS221_U3_T1_h1)

question: Why is the first sixty minutes after a major injury famously called the 'golden hour'?

options.A: Patients are most cooperative during this time
options.B: Surgeons only perform operations during this timeframe
options.C: Lab results take exactly one hour to return
options.D: Treatment during this window gives the highest chance of survival

explanation: Spot on! That first hour is precious. Getting prompt care during this window dramatically lowers the risk of death or lasting damage after a severe trauma. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T1#GNS221_U3_T1_h1)

question: What is the main goal of emergency triage in the hospital?

options.A: To collect payment information from patients
options.B: To complete a detailed family medical history
options.C: To assign a private room to every arriving patient
options.D: To sort patients based on the severity of their condition

explanation: Great thinking! Triage is simply sorting patients by how sick they are, making sure the most critical, life-threatening cases get seen first. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T1#GNS221_U3_T1_h2)

question: A patient rushes in with severe chest pain, while another has a minor finger cut. According to triage rules, what should you do first?

options.A: Ask both patients to sit in the waiting room together
options.B: Treat the chest pain patient immediately
options.C: Treat the finger cut patient because it will take less time
options.D: Register the finger cut patient first to clear the desk

explanation: You nailed it! Chest pain and trouble breathing point to a high-risk emergency. They always take top priority over minor cuts and scrapes. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T1#GNS221_U3_T1_h2)

question: In the ABCDE emergency assessment, what does the letter 'C' stand for?

options.A: Coma
options.B: Circulation
options.C: Cardiac
options.D: Comfort

explanation: Well done! In the ABCDE routine, C stands for Circulation. It's all about checking pulses, blood pressure, and stopping any heavy bleeding. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T1#GNS221_U3_T1_h3)

question: Why must a nurse check the airway before breathing and circulation during an emergency?

options.A: A blocked airway will cause death regardless of heart function
options.B: Doctors only look at the airway during emergencies
options.C: It is a hospital rule with no medical reason
options.D: Airway assessment takes the least amount of time

explanation: Makes total sense! If air can't get through, nothing else matters because the body gets zero oxygen. Clearing the airway is always step number one. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T1#GNS221_U3_T1_h3)

question: In the FAST mnemonic used to spot a stroke, what does the letter 'T' stand for?

options.A: Tremor check
options.B: Temperature
options.C: Total paralysis
options.D: Time to call

explanation: You got it! T stands for Time—meaning it's time to call for emergency help right away if you notice any stroke signs. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T1#GNS221_U3_T1_h4)

question: A patient having a severe allergic reaction has wheezing, swollen lips, and crashing blood pressure. What medication is given first?

options.A: Intramuscular epinephrine
options.B: Oral diphenhydramine
options.C: Subcutaneous insulin
options.D: Intravenous paracetamol

explanation: Brilliant! Epinephrine is a lifesaver in anaphylaxis because it quickly opens up the airways and brings blood pressure back up. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T1#GNS221_U3_T1_h4)

question: What do we mean by an 'acute abdomen' in clinical practice?

options.A: Chronic indigestion caused by spicy food
options.B: Sudden, severe abdominal pain that often requires urgent surgery
options.C: A normal feeling of fullness after a large meal
options.D: A mild muscle cramp after heavy exercise

explanation: Spot on! An 'acute abdomen' is a red flag for sudden, severe belly pain that usually means trouble inside, like appendicitis or a perforation, needing quick surgical eyes. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T1#GNS221_U3_T1_h5)

question: Why are doctors and nurses careful about giving strong pain relief right away to someone with undiagnosed, severe belly pain?

options.A: Analgesics always cure appendicitis without an operation
options.B: Patients with stomach pain cannot swallow pills
options.C: Pain medicines cause immediate kidney failure
options.D: It can mask important physical signs and delay necessary surgery

explanation: Good clinical thinking! Masking the pain can hide how the illness is progressing, making it tricky for surgeons to figure out what's really wrong inside. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T1#GNS221_U3_T1_h5)

question: Why is an unconscious patient who is still breathing placed in the recovery position?

options.A: To make it easier to start an intravenous line
options.B: To prevent the tongue from blocking the airway and allow drainage
options.C: To lower the patient's blood pressure safely
options.D: To prepare the patient for immediate surgery

explanation: You got it! This position keeps the airway safe by stopping the tongue from sliding back, and lets any saliva or vomit drain safely out of the mouth. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T1#GNS221_U3_T1_h6)

question: What is the best immediate action to control heavy bleeding from a wound on someone's arm?

options.A: Giving the patient large amounts of oral fluids
options.B: Elevating the arm above the level of the heart only
options.C: Applying direct pressure with a clean dressing
options.D: Pouring rubbing alcohol directly into the open cut

explanation: Awesome! Direct pressure is your best friend here. It squeezes the bleeding vessels against the bone so a clot can quickly form. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T1#GNS221_U3_T1_h6)

question: What does the SBAR acronym stand for during a patient handover?

options.A: Symptoms, Breathing, Activity, Recovery
options.B: Situation, Background, Assessment, Recommendation
options.C: Safety, Blood, Airway, Respiration
options.D: Staff, Beds, Ambulances, Reports

explanation: Easy peasy! SBAR stands for Situation, Background, Assessment, and Recommendation. It keeps your shift handovers clear and professional. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T1#GNS221_U3_T1_h7)

question: Why is a structured handover so important when transferring an emergency patient to intensive care?

options.A: It replaces the need to write patient chart notes
options.B: It allows the receiving nurse to avoid reading past history
options.C: It prevents critical clinical details from being missed
options.D: It reduces the financial cost of hospital admission

explanation: You're spot on! Handovers are vital communication bridges. A structured format makes sure nothing important gets forgotten when passing care to a new team. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T1#GNS221_U3_T1_h7)

question: What is a poultice primarily made of?

options.A: A dry powder swallowed with plenty of water
options.B: A clear liquid injected directly into a vein
options.C: A soft, moist mass spread on a cloth
options.D: A hard plastic shell strapped onto a broken bone

explanation: A poultice consists of a moist, soft mixture applied externally using a piece of cloth or gauze. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T10#GNS221_U3_T10_h1)

question: Why should a hospital nurse understand traditional poultice remedies used by patients?

options.A: To legally fine patients who use herbs at home
options.B: To safely integrate patient habits with modern medical care
options.C: To replace all prescription drugs with local leaves
options.D: To prove that traditional methods never work

explanation: Knowing what patients apply at home helps nurses prevent harmful skin reactions and manage treatments safely. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T10#GNS221_U3_T10_h1)

question: What is the primary local physical effect of applying warmth via a poultice?

options.A: Permanent darkening of the skin
options.B: Immediate freezing of skin cells
options.C: Complete blockage of local blood flow
options.D: Vasodilation of local blood vessels

explanation: Warmth causes local blood vessels to widen, bringing more blood and immune cells to the area. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T10#GNS221_U3_T10_h2)

question: How does increased blood flow help an infected, swollen area under a poultice?

options.A: It dries out all body fluids completely
options.B: It cools down the fever instantly
options.C: It brings white blood cells to fight the infection
options.D: It stops the heart from pumping too fast

explanation: Extra blood circulation delivers necessary white blood cells and nutrients to heal inflamed or infected tissue. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T10#GNS221_U3_T10_h2)

question: Which type of poultice is commonly used to retain heat for deep inflammation and boils?

options.A: Kaolin poultice
options.B: Salt crystal poultice
options.C: Dry cotton poultice
options.D: Ice water poultice

explanation: Kaolin is a heavy clay substance known for holding heat well to treat deep-seated swelling and boils. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T10#GNS221_U3_T10_h3)

question: A patient uses crushed fresh leaves on a swollen joint. What kind of poultice is this?

options.A: An herbal poultice
options.B: A surgical poultice
options.C: A chemical poultice
options.D: A synthetic poultice

explanation: Using fresh plants or leaves directly falls under the category of traditional herbal poultices. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T10#GNS221_U3_T10_h3)

question: Which condition is a clear indication for using a warm poultice?

options.A: A widespread whole-body viral fever
options.B: A brand new ankle sprain with active bleeding
options.C: A localized boil or deep muscle ache
options.D: An area of skin with complete loss of sensation

explanation: Poultices work best on localized aches, stiffness, and closed infections like boils. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T10#GNS221_U3_T10_h4)

question: Why should a nurse NOT apply a warm poultice to a fresh injury that happened ten minutes ago?

options.A: It turns the skin completely white permanently
options.B: It freezes the tissue and causes gangrene
options.C: It cures the injury too fast for proper charting
options.D: It increases local blood flow and worsens bleeding

explanation: Heat causes blood vessels to open up, which increases bleeding and swelling immediately after a fresh trauma. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T10#GNS221_U3_T10_h4)

question: What tool should the nurse use to check if a warm poultice is safe to apply?

options.A: A heavy weight pressed onto the mixture
options.B: A metal needle poked into the patient's arm
options.C: Their own inner wrist or a thermometer
options.D: A bright flashlight held close to the paste

explanation: Testing the temperature on the sensitive inner wrist helps verify the poultice is warm, not burning hot. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T10#GNS221_U3_T10_h5)

question: Why is a clean cloth or gauze used between the skin and the poultice paste?

options.A: To keep the application neat and hold the paste together
options.B: To cure the infection without using any medicine
options.C: To completely block all heat from reaching the patient
options.D: To prevent the nurse from wearing clean gloves

explanation: The cloth acts as a barrier that contains the messy paste while allowing warmth and medicinal properties to pass through. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T10#GNS221_U3_T10_h5)

question: What is the very first practical safety step before applying a prepared warm poultice to a patient?

options.A: Wrap the entire body in thick blankets
options.B: Test the temperature of the mixture
options.C: Leave the room for thirty minutes
options.D: Scrub the skin hard with stiff wire wool

explanation: Always test the temperature to prevent accidental burns before the substance touches the patient's skin. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T10#GNS221_U3_T10_h6)

question: A nurse has just placed a warm poultice on a patient's leg. When is the best time to check the skin underneath for irritation?

options.A: Only when the patient is discharged home
options.B: Never, once it is tied down it must stay
options.C: After twenty-four hours have passed completely
options.D: Within the first five minutes of application

explanation: Checking the skin early helps catch burning or allergic reactions before severe tissue damage occurs. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T10#GNS221_U3_T10_h6)

question: What should the nurse do immediately if a patient complains of severe burning under a poultice?

options.A: Wait another hour to see if it stops
options.B: Tie the bandage tighter to stop the burning
options.C: Tell the patient to endure the pain
options.D: Remove the poultice and wash the skin

explanation: Severe burning means the application is too hot or irritating, requiring immediate removal to prevent skin injury. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T10#GNS221_U3_T10_h7)

question: Why is regular skin monitoring necessary while a poultice is in place?

options.A: To catch early signs of thermal burns or irritation
options.B: To measure how much weight the patient gained
options.C: To see if the bandages can be sold again
options.D: To check if the patient is sleeping soundly

explanation: Frequent checks ensure that heat or active ingredients do not damage or blister the skin. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T10#GNS221_U3_T10_h7)

question: What is maceration in the context of skin care?

options.A: Skin becoming completely numb to all touch
options.B: Skin turning completely black from cold temperatures
options.C: Skin growing extra thick layers like a hard shell
options.D: Skin becoming soft and broken down from too much moisture

explanation: Maceration happens when moisture stays on the skin too long, making the tissue weak and prone to damage. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T10#GNS221_U3_T10_h8)

question: Which complication can happen if an unsterile herbal poultice is placed over a minor skin scratch?

options.A: Instant healing of all body aches
options.B: Complete numbness of the limb
options.C: A secondary bacterial infection
options.D: A permanent change in eye color

explanation: Unclean mixtures can carry germs straight into breaks in the skin, causing new infections instead of curing them. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T10#GNS221_U3_T10_h8)

question: Why are human bites often more prone to severe infections than animal bites?

options.A: The human mouth contains a dense mixture of dangerous bacteria
options.B: Human teeth are sharper and longer than dog teeth
options.C: People rarely wash human bite wounds immediately
options.D: Human saliva contains a powerful natural venom

explanation: Human mouths harbor loads of aggressive bacteria that love to multiply in closed spaces like bite wounds. Keep this in mind when caring for bite injuries in the clinical ward! [learn more](GNS221_U3_T11#GNS221_U3_T11_h1)

question: Why do cat bites easily cause deep joint or tendon infections?

options.A: Cats secrete a local anesthetic that hides the pain of the bite
options.B: Cat saliva naturally resists all standard antibiotic treatments
options.C: Cat teeth are sharp and slender, pushing bacteria deep into tight tissues
options.D: Cats possess venom glands located near their salivary ducts

explanation: Think of a cat's teeth like tiny needles. They puncture deep beneath the skin, depositing bacteria right into sterile spaces like joints and tendons. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T11#GNS221_U3_T11_h1)

question: Which bacteria is most famous for causing fast, painful infections after a cat or dog bite?

options.A: Pasteurella multocida
options.B: Clostridium tetani
options.C: Pseudomonas aeruginosa
options.D: Escherichia coli

explanation: Pasteurella lives happily in cat and dog mouths. Once introduced through a bite, it quickly causes sharp pain, redness, and swelling. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T11#GNS221_U3_T11_h2)

question: What happens right away to the tissue when teeth pierce the skin?

options.A: The body instantly creates a permanent protective scar barrier
options.B: The immune system seals the puncture wound with sterile fluid
options.C: All surrounding blood vessels dilate to neutralize the foreign saliva
options.D: Oral bacteria are pushed directly into sterile tissue planes

explanation: The sheer mechanical action of a bite breaks the skin barrier and inoculates mouth germs straight into the vulnerable underlying tissue. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T11#GNS221_U3_T11_h2)

question: What is the most crucial piece of history to gather first when assessing an animal bite?

options.A: The exact weight and age of the bitted patient
options.B: The color and breed of the animal involved
options.C: The insurance and home address of the owner
options.D: The exact time of the bite and tetanus status

explanation: Timing tells us about infection risks, while checking the patient's tetanus status lets us know if a booster shot is urgently needed. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T11#GNS221_U3_T11_h3)

question: A patient arrives with a deep dog puncture on their hand. After checking the ABCs, what should the nurse assess first?

options.A: The patient's current insurance and employment details
options.B: Distal pulses, motor function, and finger sensation
options.C: Whether the patient prefers oral or intravenous medication
options.D: The exact monetary value of any damaged clothing

explanation: Always check circulation, movement, and feeling early on! Deep punctures can easily cause hidden damage to nearby blood vessels and tendons. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T11#GNS221_U3_T11_h3)

question: Why do we irrigate a fresh bite wound with plenty of sterile fluid?

options.A: To dissolve all the surrounding dead skin cells
options.B: To physically wash away bacteria and loose debris
options.C: To permanently freeze the nerve endings to stop pain
options.D: To stimulate rapid production of new blood cells

explanation: Using fluid force is one of our best nursing tools to physically rinse out contaminating microbes and dirt left behind by the bite. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T11#GNS221_U3_T11_h4)

question: Why are deep animal bites often left open instead of being stitched tightly right away?

options.A: To prevent trapping bacteria inside a closed space and causing an abscess
options.B: Because sutures dissolve too quickly when exposed to animal saliva
options.C: To allow the patient to apply their own herbal ointments at home
options.D: Because closed wounds take longer to form a dry scab

explanation: If you seal a dirty bite closed, you trap bacteria inside a warm, cozy pocket where they can easily form a nasty abscess. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T11#GNS221_U3_T11_h4)

question: Which antibiotic is commonly prescribed first-line for animal and human bite injuries?

options.A: Erythromycin ointment
options.B: Ciprofloxacin drops
options.C: Amoxicillin-clavulanate
options.D: Vancomycin syrup

explanation: Amoxicillin-clavulanate is a great choice because it covers the wide variety of bacteria typically found lurking in human and animal mouths. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T11#GNS221_U3_T11_h5)

question: When is rabies post-exposure prophylaxis necessary after an animal bite?

options.A: Only if the human victim shows signs of neurological confusion
options.B: If the patient has not received a tetanus shot within the past year
options.C: When the animal is high-risk and unavailable for observation or testing
options.D: Whenever any household pet breaks the skin during playful activity

explanation: If a high-risk animal cannot be tested or watched for signs of rabies, we don't take chances—rabies prophylaxis is started right away. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T11#GNS221_U3_T11_h5)

question: What is the medical term for a deep bone infection that can happen if a bite goes all the way down to the bone?

options.A: Cellulitis
options.B: Tenosynovitis
options.C: Fasciitis
options.D: Osteomyelitis

explanation: Osteomyelitis means an infection has reached the bone and bone marrow. It's a serious complication we try to prevent with prompt wound care and antibiotics. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T11#GNS221_U3_T11_h6)

question: Which of these is NOT a classic sign of a localized wound infection that nurses look out for?

options.A: Purulent or foul-smelling drainage from the puncture
options.B: Worsening throbbing pain days after the initial event
options.C: Increasing redness and warmth around the injury site
options.D: Gradual shrinking and drying of the wound edges

explanation: Wound shrinking and drying means healing is going well! Spreading redness, foul pus, and worsening pain are the warning signs of infection. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T11#GNS221_U3_T11_h6)

question: What health education should a nurse give a patient taking antibiotics for a bite wound?

options.A: Stop taking the medication as soon as the pain disappears
options.B: Double the dose if redness starts to spread around the edges
options.C: Crush the pills and mix them directly into the open wound
options.D: Finish every single pill, even if the wound looks completely healed

explanation: Always remind patients to complete their full antibiotic course so the infection is wiped out completely and resistance doesn't develop. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T11#GNS221_U3_T11_h7)

question: A discharged patient calls saying they notice red streaks spreading up their arm from a dog bite. What should the nurse advise?

options.A: Apply an ice pack and wait another forty-eight hours
options.B: Stop taking the antibiotics because the red streaks are normal
options.C: Wash the arm with scented soap and increase fluid intake
options.D: Return to the emergency department immediately for evaluation

explanation: Spreading red streaks suggest a fast-moving infection like lymphangitis. This requires prompt medical re-evaluation right away! [learn more](GNS221_U3_T11#GNS221_U3_T11_h7)

question: Which stinging insect leaves its barbed stinger and venom sac behind in human skin?

options.A: Hornet
options.B: Wasp
options.C: Honeybee
options.D: Fire ant

explanation: Great job! The honeybee's stinger is barbed like a hook, so it anchors firmly into the skin and tears away from the bee's body along with the venom sac. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T12#GNS221_U3_T12_h1)

question: Why can wasps sting a person multiple times while honeybees cannot?

options.A: Wasps carry much less venom per sting than bees
options.B: Honeybees die immediately upon encountering human skin
options.C: Wasp stingers are smooth and do not detach from their bodies
options.D: Wasps possess multiple stingers on their abdomens

explanation: You've got this! Unlike honeybees, wasp stingers are smooth without heavy barbs, allowing them to pull the stinger right out and sting again. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T12#GNS221_U3_T12_h1)

question: Which chemical released in the body causes the rapid swelling and itching after an insect sting?

options.A: Amylase
options.B: Hemoglobin
options.C: Insulin
options.D: Histamine

explanation: Spot on! Venom triggers mast cells to release histamine, which makes local blood vessels open up and leak fluid into the skin, causing swelling and itchiness. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T12#GNS221_U3_T12_h2)

question: How does a large local reaction differ from a normal insect sting reaction?

options.A: It indicates that bacteria have entered the wound and caused pus
options.B: It involves swelling greater than ten centimeters that peaks after a couple of days
options.C: It always causes immediate closing of the airway and low blood pressure
options.D: It means the patient is having a systemic IgE-mediated allergic response

explanation: Correct! A large local reaction is just a bigger, exaggerated inflammatory response at the site—it looks scary and spreads past 10cm, but it is not a true whole-body allergy. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T12#GNS221_U3_T12_h2)

question: Which sign tells you a patient is having a full-body (systemic) allergic reaction to a sting, rather than a normal local reaction?

options.A: Generalized hives and itching
options.B: A small red welt around the stinger
options.C: Mild warmth of the skin near the wound
options.D: Pain directly at the puncture site

explanation: Well done! When hives and itching spread all over the body, it's a clear warning that the immune system is reacting systemically to the venom circulating in the blood. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T12#GNS221_U3_T12_h3)

question: A patient arrives at the clinic 30 minutes after multiple wasp stings complaining of throat tightness and dizziness. What is your very first assessment?

options.A: Airway patency and respiratory status
options.B: Size of the redness at each sting site
options.C: Temperature of the extremities
options.D: History of previous childhood illnesses

explanation: Excellent clinical thinking! Throat tightness and dizziness are early signs of dangerous anaphylaxis, making airway and breathing your absolute priority. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T12#GNS221_U3_T12_h3)

question: Why should you avoid using tweezers to pull out a honeybee stinger?

options.A: Tweezers are too sharp and will cut the patient's epidermis
options.B: Squeezing can push more venom from the attached sac into the skin
options.C: It causes the stinger to dissolve inside the wound
options.D: Metal reacts chemically with insect venom to cause burns

explanation: Spot on! Pinching with tweezers squeezes the attached venom sac like a bulb syringe, pumping even more toxin straight into the patient. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T12#GNS221_U3_T12_h4)

question: What is the main reason for putting a cold compress on a fresh insect sting?

options.A: It kills any bacteria introduced by the insect's mouthparts
options.B: It triggers immediate local histamine destruction
options.C: It completely neutralizes the chemical structure of the acid
options.D: It constricts blood vessels to slow down venom absorption

explanation: Correct! Cold causes the local blood vessels to narrow (vasoconstriction), slowing down how quickly the venom travels into the rest of the body. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T12#GNS221_U3_T12_h4)

question: What is the frontline, life-saving medication for treating a patient in anaphylactic shock from a sting?

options.A: Paracetamol
options.B: Amoxicillin
options.C: Hydrocortisone
options.D: Epinephrine

explanation: You got it! Epinephrine is the gold standard because it quickly fixes dangerously low blood pressure and opens up closed airways. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T12#GNS221_U3_T12_h5)

question: Where is the best place on the body to give an emergency intramuscular shot of epinephrine?

options.A: Dorsal gluteal muscle
options.B: Anterolateral thigh
options.C: Deltoid muscle of the arm
options.D: Subcutaneous abdominal fat

explanation: Spot on! The outer-front part of the thigh (anterolateral thigh) absorbs medications into the bloodstream much faster and more reliably than other sites. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T12#GNS221_U3_T12_h5)

question: Which of these is NOT a feature of anaphylactic shock?

options.A: Bronchospasm
options.B: Severe hypertension
options.C: Profound hypotension
options.D: Laryngeal edema

explanation: Correct! Anaphylaxis causes blood vessels to dilate widely and leak fluid, leading to severe *hypotension* (low blood pressure), not high blood pressure. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T12#GNS221_U3_T12_h6)

question: A patient in anaphylactic shock gets an epinephrine shot, but after 10 minutes they are still wheezing and have low blood pressure. What is your next nursing action?

options.A: Discontinue oxygen therapy to calm the patient down
options.B: Wait another hour to see if the first dose takes effect
options.C: Give oral antihistamines instead of further injections
options.D: Administer a second dose of intramuscular epinephrine

explanation: Well done! If symptoms don't clear up, it is completely safe and necessary to give a repeat dose of epinephrine every 5 to 15 minutes while waiting for advanced help. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T12#GNS221_U3_T12_h6)

question: Why are patients who suffer massive insect stings at risk for sudden kidney injury?

options.A: Profound low blood pressure and direct venom toxicity compromise renal perfusion
options.B: Patients refuse to drink water due to fear of swallowing
options.C: Venom causes direct physical blockage of the ureters by crystals
options.D: The kidneys work overtime to filter out oral antihistamine pills

explanation: Spot on! Severe shock starves the kidneys of blood flow, and heavy venom toxins can directly damage the delicate kidney tubules. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T12#GNS221_U3_T12_h7)

question: What delayed complication of a sting can show up days later with fever, joint pain, and a skin rash?

options.A: Hyperglycemia
options.B: Serum sickness
options.C: Cellulitis
options.D: Anaphylactic shock

explanation: Correct! Serum sickness is an immune system reaction that can pop up several days after exposure, causing fever, aching joints, and rashes. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T12#GNS221_U3_T12_h7)

question: What type of clothing is best for someone working outdoors in areas with lots of stinging insects?

options.A: Brightly colored floral shirts that blend with nature
options.B: Shorts and sleeveless tops to stay cool in the heat
options.C: Light-colored, long-sleeved clothing that fits smoothly
options.D: Dark wool garments to absorb sweat effectively

explanation: You got it! Smooth, light-covered, long clothes protect your skin and help you avoid attracting insects that love dark colors and floral patterns. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T12#GNS221_U3_T12_h8)

question: A patient with a history of severe bee sting allergies is preparing for rural fieldwork in Nigeria. What essential item must you ensure they carry before they leave?

options.A: Prescribed epinephrine autoinjector
options.B: Traditional herbal mud for wound dressing
options.C: A bottle of strong perfume for protection
options.D: A pair of dark-colored gardening gloves

explanation: Excellent! Anyone with a history of severe stings must always have their epinephrine autoinjector on hand to treat accidental stings instantly. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T12#GNS221_U3_T12_h8)

question: What is the medical definition of a fracture?

options.A: A stretching injury to the ligaments surrounding a joint
options.B: A complete break or crack in the continuity of a bone
options.C: An infection located deep inside the bone marrow
options.D: A sudden tear in the muscle fibers attached to bone

explanation: A fracture simply means the physical structure of the bone has cracked or broken due to stress or trauma. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T13#GNS221_U3_T13_h1)

question: How does an open fracture differ from a closed fracture?

options.A: Open fractures have a skin wound communicating with the break
options.B: Closed fractures involve multiple pieces of shattered bone
options.C: Closed fractures always require immediate surgical metal plating
options.D: Open fractures only occur in elderly patients with weak bones

explanation: The defining feature of an open fracture is a break in the skin that exposes the bone directly to the outside air. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T13#GNS221_U3_T13_h1)

question: What is a pathologic fracture?

options.A: A break occurring in a bone weakened by an underlying disease
options.B: A minor hairline crack caused by repetitive athletic training
options.C: A clean break resulting from a high-speed motor vehicle crash
options.D: A fracture caused strictly by a direct blow from a blunt object

explanation: Pathologic fractures happen because an existing disease like cancer or osteoporosis has already made the bone fragile. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T13#GNS221_U3_T13_h2)

question: Which patient has the highest risk for developing a fragility fracture?

options.A: A healthy young adult who plays competitive contact football
options.B: An elderly woman with long-standing postmenopausal osteoporosis
options.C: A middle-aged man with a history of mild muscular sprains
options.D: A teenage athlete recovering from a minor hamstring strain

explanation: Osteoporosis severely decreases bone mass, making minor movements or low-impact falls sufficient to cause a severe break. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T13#GNS221_U3_T13_h2)

question: What is the term for the grating sound heard when broken bone ends rub together?

options.A: Cyanosis
options.B: Contracture
options.C: Crepitus
options.D: Clonus

explanation: Crepitus is the distinctive crunchy sound or sensation produced when rough ends of fractured bone rub together. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T13#GNS221_U3_T13_h3)

question: Why must a nurse check the pulse and skin color below a fractured limb?

options.A: To check for signs of blood vessel or nerve damage
options.B: To calculate the exact date when the bone will heal
options.C: To prevent the development of a systemic bone infection
options.D: To determine how much calcium the patient's body needs

explanation: Swelling or displaced bone fragments can pinch nearby arteries and nerves, cutting off blood supply and sensation to the fingers or toes. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T13#GNS221_U3_T13_h3)

question: What is the primary goal of immediate first aid for a suspected fracture?

options.A: Push any protruding bone ends back inside the skin
options.B: Apply hot packs to the injury site to reduce swelling
options.C: Straighten the deformed limb immediately by pulling hard
options.D: Immobilize the bone to prevent further tissue damage

explanation: Keeping the broken bone still stops sharp edges from tearing nearby blood vessels, nerves, and muscle tissue. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T13#GNS221_U3_T13_h4)

question: A patient has an open fracture with a small piece of bone sticking out of the skin. What is the correct initial nursing action?

options.A: Wash the exposed bone vigorously with strong antiseptic soap and water
options.B: Straighten the limb forcefully to hide the bone before taking an X-ray
options.C: Push the bone back inside the wound quickly and apply a tight tourniquet
options.D: Cover the wound loosely with a sterile dressing without pushing the bone in

explanation: Manipulating or pushing exposed bone back inside introduces deep infection, so the area must be covered loosely and left for the surgical team. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T13#GNS221_U3_T13_h4)

question: What does the term 'reduction' mean in the management of fractures?

options.A: Gradual shrinking of local soft tissue swelling using ice packs
options.B: Lowering the patient's blood pressure prior to orthopedic surgery
options.C: Surgical removal of dead bone tissue from an infected site
options.D: Realignment of the broken bone fragments into their normal position

explanation: Reduction is the process of putting displaced bone ends back into their correct anatomical alignment so they can heal properly. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T13#GNS221_U3_T13_h5)

question: Why might a surgeon choose external fixation over a standard internal plate for a severe open fracture?

options.A: It allows the patient to remove the metal pins at home every evening
options.B: It avoids placing metal hardware directly into a contaminated wound area
options.C: It completely eliminates any need for follow-up X-ray imaging
options.D: It guarantees that the bone will heal twice as fast as internal surgery

explanation: External frames hold bones securely from the outside, minimizing the risk of trapping bacteria and deep infection inside a dirty open wound. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T13#GNS221_U3_T13_h5)

question: Which symptom is the earliest and most reliable indicator of developing compartment syndrome?

options.A: Complete lack of any pulse felt in the foot or hand
options.B: Blue discoloration of the skin spreading rapidly over the toes
options.C: Severe, relentless pain that is not relieved by opioid pain medication
options.D: Total paralysis of all the fingers and toes on the affected limb

explanation: Intense, out-of-proportion pain that fails to respond to strong painkillers is the hallmark early warning sign of rising pressure inside a muscle compartment. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T13#GNS221_U3_T13_h6)

question: What is the primary mechanism behind a fat embolism following a long bone fracture?

options.A: Immobility causes fat cells under the skin to melt into the bloodstream
options.B: Infection at the fracture site turns local soft tissues into fatty deposits
options.C: The body stores extra dietary fat in broken bones during the healing phase
options.D: Fat droplets from the bone marrow enter open blood vessels and travel to the lungs

explanation: When a large long bone breaks, yellow bone marrow fat can escape into damaged blood vessels, creating emboli that block small vessels in the lungs and brain. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T13#GNS221_U3_T13_h6)

question: What is the correct way to handle a newly applied plaster cast while it is still drying?

options.A: Lift the cast using only the fingertips
options.B: Support the cast using the palms of the hands
options.C: Rest the damp cast on a narrow, hard metal bar
options.D: Wrap the cast tightly in thick plastic sheeting

explanation: Fingertips create flat pressure spots on a drying plaster cast, which can indent the plaster and cause skin breakdown underneath. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T13#GNS221_U3_T13_h7)

question: A patient with a leg cast complains of severe itching deep inside the cast. What is the best nursing response?

options.A: Tell the patient to pour warm water down the cast to wash away the itchy skin cells
options.B: Cut the cast off immediately because itching means a severe infection is present
options.C: Instruct the patient never to insert objects inside and suggest using a cool hair dryer setting
options.D: Provide a long knitting needle wrapped in cotton gauze so they can scratch safely

explanation: Foreign objects can break fragile skin inside the cast and introduce bacteria, while cool air safely relieves itching without harming the skin. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T13#GNS221_U3_T13_h7)

question: What is the simple definition of poisoning in a clinical setting?

options.A: A chronic vitamin deficiency caused by poor dietary intake
options.B: Any substance that interferes with normal body functions after entering the body
options.C: An infection resulting from bacterial contamination in food
options.D: An allergic reaction to a newly prescribed antibiotic medication

explanation: You've got this! Think of poisoning simply as anything—a chemical, a drug, or a toxin—that disrupts how the body normally works once it gets inside. Great job! [learn more](GNS221_U3_T14#GNS221_U3_T14_h1)

question: How do accidental and intentional poisonings usually look different when patients arrive?

options.A: Accidental cases frequently involve children and single agents, while intentional cases often involve adults and multiple drugs
options.B: Intentional poisonings are completely untreatable compared to accidental exposures
options.C: Intentional poisonings only occur through inhalation, whereas accidental poisonings always involve swallowing
options.D: Accidental exposures never require medical attention, unlike all intentional exposures

explanation: Spot on! Little ones often accidentally swallow just one household item, whereas intentional adult cases more often involve multiple medications. Knowing this helps you prepare for what to expect! [learn more](GNS221_U3_T14#GNS221_U3_T14_h1)

question: What is the most common way people get poisoned right inside their own homes?

options.A: Ingestion
options.B: Injection
options.C: Inhalation
options.D: Absorption

explanation: Well done! Swallowing things—like accidental medications or household cleaners—is by far the top way poisoning happens at home. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T14#GNS221_U3_T14_h2)

question: Why do toxins breathed into the lungs (inhalation) affect the body so quickly?

options.A: The stomach acid breaks down inhaled gases faster than swallowed solids
options.B: Skin pores open wider when toxic fumes are breathed into the room
options.C: Inhaled toxins must first pass through the liver before reaching the brain
options.D: Gases pass directly from the lung alveoli into the rich capillary blood supply

explanation: Think about the tiny air sacs (alveoli) in our lungs—they have a massive blood supply, letting gases jump straight into the bloodstream almost instantly! [learn more](GNS221_U3_T14#GNS221_U3_T14_h2)

question: What is your very first priority when a poisoned patient arrives in the emergency unit?

options.A: Asking family members about the patient's financial history
options.B: Stabilizing vital functions using the ABCDE approach
options.C: Administering a broad-spectrum antidote immediately
options.D: Inducing vomiting to empty the stomach contents

explanation: Safety first! Always check Airway, Breathing, and Circulation (ABCDE) before trying to figure out exactly what poison was swallowed. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T14#GNS221_U3_T14_h3)

question: A patient is rushed in unconscious, with very tiny pupils (pinpoint) and slow, shallow breathing. What type of poison do you suspect?

options.A: Stimulants
options.B: Anticholinergics
options.C: Opioids
options.D: Household bleach

explanation: You nailed it! Pinpoint pupils combined with depressed breathing are the classic textbook signs of an opioid overdose. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T14#GNS221_U3_T14_h3)

question: Why is it a big mistake to make someone vomit after they swallow a corrosive chemical (like strong acid)?

options.A: It always causes permanent paralysis of the vocal cords
options.B: It forces the poison directly into the urinary bladder
options.C: It neutralizes all antidote medications given later in the hospital
options.D: It can cause additional severe burns to the esophagus as the chemical comes back up

explanation: Brilliant thinking! Corrosive chemicals burn on the way down, and forcing them back up means they burn the throat a second time. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T14#GNS221_U3_T14_h4)

question: What should you do immediately if a patient gets a chemical splashed into both eyes?

options.A: Flush the eyes continuously with clean water or normal saline for at least fifteen minutes
options.B: Rub the eyes firmly with a dry towel to remove solid particles
options.C: Put neutral cooking oil directly into the eyes to coat the chemical
options.D: Apply tight gauze patches over both eyes and wait for an ophthalmologist

explanation: Water is your best friend here! Long, continuous flushing washes away caustic chemicals before they can damage the cornea. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T14#GNS221_U3_T14_h4)

question: How does activated charcoal help treat someone who swallowed a poison?

options.A: It dilates blood vessels to speed up renal excretion
options.B: It coats the lungs to block toxic gas inhalation
options.C: It binds to toxins in the gut to prevent their absorption into the bloodstream
options.D: It neutralizes stomach acid to prevent chemical ulcers

explanation: Activated charcoal acts like a microscopic sponge, holding onto the toxins in the stomach and gut so they don't enter the bloodstream. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T14#GNS221_U3_T14_h5)

question: Why is stomach pumping (gastric lavage) rarely done if a patient seeks help hours after swallowing a poison?

options.A: Gastric lavage only works on poisons that were inhaled
options.B: The poison has already passed from the stomach into the small intestines
options.C: Activated charcoal neutralizes the need for any washing
options.D: The stomach lining becomes too tough for tubes to pass safely

explanation: Makes total sense, right? If hours have passed, the poison has already moved past the stomach, making pumping ineffective. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T14#GNS221_U3_T14_h5)

question: Which specific medication is the go-to emergency antidote for an opioid overdose?

options.A: Vitamin K
options.B: Atropine
options.C: Naloxone
options.D: Digoxin immune fab

explanation: Fantastic! Naloxone quickly blocks opioids and helps the patient breathe normally again. Keep this one locked in your memory! [learn more](GNS221_U3_T14#GNS221_U3_T14_h6)

question: A patient recovering from an intentional overdose is now awake and stable. What nursing action is most important?

options.A: Restricting all family visits to punish the patient for the suicide attempt
options.B: Providing continuous observation and psychological support while keeping the environment safe
options.C: Avoiding any conversation about the incident to prevent embarrassment
options.D: Discharging the patient immediately with a prescription for sedatives

explanation: You've got this. Emotional support and a safe, watch-careful environment are vital for anyone recovering from self-harm. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T14#GNS221_U3_T14_h6)

question: What is a common long-term problem for a patient who survives swallowing a corrosive chemical?

options.A: Chronic swelling of the lower limbs
options.B: Esophageal strictures and scarring
options.C: Permanent hearing loss in both ears
options.D: Total loss of skin pigmentation

explanation: When caustic burns heal, they form scar tissue. In the esophagus, this scarring narrows the tube, making swallowing difficult later on. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T14#GNS221_U3_T14_h7)

question: How can community nurses best help parents prevent accidental poisoning in toddlers?

options.A: Advising families to transfer all cleaning chemicals into empty soda bottles
options.B: Recommending that households avoid buying any chemical products entirely
options.C: Encouraging parents to induce vomiting in children at the first sign of illness
options.D: Teaching parents to store medications and cleaning agents in locked cabinets out of reach

explanation: Prevention is key! Keeping dangerous items locked away out of a toddler's curious reach is the best way to keep them safe. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T14#GNS221_U3_T14_h7)

question: What is the primary physiological problem in clinical shock?

options.A: Inadequate blood flow and oxygen to tissues
options.B: An excessive buildup of red blood cells
options.C: A sudden drop in core body temperature
options.D: Severe localized pain in the chest

explanation: Shock happens when the circulatory system fails to deliver enough blood and oxygen to meet the basic needs of body tissues. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T2#GNS221_U3_T2_h1)

question: Why does cellular damage occur during prolonged shock?

options.A: Blood vessels expand and physically crush nearby organs
options.B: Cells lack oxygen to produce energy and waste builds up
options.C: Excess water floods the cells and causes them to burst
options.D: White blood cells mistakenly attack healthy body tissue

explanation: Without a steady supply of oxygen, cells cannot make normal energy, causing harmful waste products to accumulate and damage cellular structures. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T2#GNS221_U3_T2_h1)

question: Which hormone is released by the adrenal glands to help raise heart rate and blood pressure during shock?

options.A: Estrogen
options.B: Insulin
options.C: Thyroxine
options.D: Adrenaline

explanation: The sympathetic nervous system releases adrenaline and noradrenaline to quickly boost heart rate and tighten blood vessels during a crisis. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T2#GNS221_U3_T2_h2)

question: Why does the body redirect blood away from the skin and intestines during early shock?

options.A: To prevent the kidneys from producing urine
options.B: To prioritize blood supply for the heart and brain
options.C: To increase the absorption of oral fluids
options.D: To cool down the body temperature quickly

explanation: Shunting redirects scarce blood from less vital areas like the skin and gut to vital organs that cannot survive without constant perfusion. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T2#GNS221_U3_T2_h2)

question: Which type of shock is caused by a massive loss of blood or body fluids?

options.A: Obstructive shock
options.B: Neurogenic shock
options.C: Hypovolemic shock
options.D: Cardiogenic shock

explanation: Hypovolemic shock directly stems from a low volume of circulating blood or fluid inside the vascular system. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T2#GNS221_U3_T2_h3)

question: A patient develops severe fluid loss following massive burns over 40 percent of their body. Which classification of shock should the nurse anticipate?

options.A: Neurogenic shock
options.B: Septic shock
options.C: Hypovolemic shock
options.D: Cardiogenic shock

explanation: Severe burns cause massive plasma loss through damaged skin, leading directly to a shortage of circulating fluid volume. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T2#GNS221_U3_T2_h3)

question: What is one of the earliest psychological signs that a patient is entering shock?

options.A: Extreme euphoria
options.B: Deep, heavy snoring
options.C: Sudden memory loss
options.D: Restlessness and anxiety

explanation: As oxygen delivery to the brain decreases, patients often become restless, anxious, or confused before losing consciousness. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T2#GNS221_U3_T2_h4)

question: Why is hourly urine output a reliable way to monitor a patient in shock?

options.A: The bladder relaxes completely when blood pressure falls too low
options.B: Fluid intake must match output within a strict ten-minute window
options.C: Kidneys shut down urine production early to save fluid when perfusion drops
options.D: Urine turns dark because red blood cells break down rapidly

explanation: Because the kidneys receive lower priority during shunting, urine production drops quickly when overall perfusion is failing. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T2#GNS221_U3_T2_h4)

question: Why should a nurse avoid raising the legs of a patient experiencing cardiogenic shock?

options.A: It immediately causes a dangerous drop in blood pressure
options.B: It restricts the movement of the diaphragm and causes choking
options.C: It can overload a failing heart with too much venous return
options.D: It prevents the administration of intravenous medications

explanation: Raising the legs dumps blood back toward the core, which strains a damaged heart muscle that cannot pump effectively. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T2#GNS221_U3_T2_h5)

question: Which of the following is NOT a standard immediate action when caring for a patient in shock?

options.A: Providing high-flow oxygen
options.B: Administering a large oral meal
options.C: Establishing large-bore IV access
options.D: Applying warm blankets

explanation: Patients in shock have poor gut perfusion and are at high risk for aspiration, so oral food and fluids are strictly withheld. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T2#GNS221_U3_T2_h5)

question: What is the primary action of vasopressor medications like norepinephrine in shock?

options.A: Dissolve blood clots in the coronary arteries
options.B: Dilate the bronchial tubes in the lungs
options.C: Slow down a rapid heart rate
options.D: Constrict blood vessels to raise blood pressure

explanation: Vasopressors cause blood vessels to tighten, which increases vascular resistance and helps raise blood pressure when fluids are not enough. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T2#GNS221_U3_T2_h6)

question: Why is dobutamine often prescribed for a patient with cardiogenic shock?

options.A: It strengthens the pumping action of the heart muscle
options.B: It prevents dangerous allergic reactions in the blood
options.C: It removes excess fluid directly through the kidneys
options.D: It lowers the patient's body temperature to rest the heart

explanation: Dobutamine is an inotrope that increases the force of myocardial contraction, helping a weak heart pump more blood forward. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T2#GNS221_U3_T2_h6)

question: What condition involves widespread, abnormal blood clotting followed by severe bleeding due to used-up clotting factors?

options.A: Chronic venous insufficiency
options.B: Pulmonary hypertension
options.C: Disseminated intravascular coagulation
options.D: Acute respiratory distress syndrome

explanation: DIC is a serious complication where small clots form throughout the body, eventually exhausting clotting proteins and causing severe bleeding. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T2#GNS221_U3_T2_h7)

question: What does Multiple Organ Dysfunction Syndrome (MODS) represent in a patient treated for shock?

options.A: A temporary nervous system shock caused by emotional stress
options.B: An allergic reaction to intravenous fluid administration
options.C: Failure of two or more organ systems due to prolonged lack of perfusion
options.D: The normal recovery phase after successful blood pressure stabilization

explanation: MODS occurs when prolonged cellular starvation causes multiple major organs to break down and stop functioning. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T2#GNS221_U3_T2_h7)

question: Which part of the brain acts as the body's internal thermostat?

options.A: Hypothalamus
options.B: Cerebellum
options.C: Medulla oblongata
options.D: Thalamus

explanation: The hypothalamus is the specific brain region responsible for monitoring and regulating core body temperature. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T3#GNS221_U3_T3_h1)

question: How does the body primarily generate heat when exposed to cold environments?

options.A: By increasing sweat production
options.B: Through muscle activity and shivering
options.C: Through rapid blood vessel expansion
options.D: By decreasing cellular metabolism

explanation: Shivering and physical muscle movement increase cellular work, which quickly generates heat to warm the body. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T3#GNS221_U3_T3_h1)

question: What is the medical term for a fever?

options.A: Hyperkalemia
options.B: Hypothermia
options.C: Pyrexia
options.D: Hypovolemia

explanation: Pyrexia is the official medical term used to describe an elevated body temperature or fever. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T3#GNS221_U3_T3_h2)

question: What's the main difference between a regular fever and hyperthermia?

options.A: Hyperthermia responds to antipyretic drugs, while fever never does.
options.B: Fever only occurs in children, while hyperthermia only occurs in adults.
options.C: Fever involves the brain raising its temperature target, while hyperthermia is a failure to cool down.
options.D: Hyperthermia is caused by infections, while fever is caused by weather.

explanation: Think of it this way: a fever happens because your brain's thermostat is intentionally turned up (like fighting an infection). Hyperthermia happens when the body is overwhelmed by heat and can't cool itself down, and normal fever meds won't fix that thermostat setting! [learn more](GNS221_U3_T3#GNS221_U3_T3_h2)

question: Which route for measuring body temperature is generally considered the most accurate reflection of core temperature?

options.A: Tympanic
options.B: Rectal
options.C: Oral
options.D: Axillary

explanation: Rectal measurements closely approximate core body temperature because the site is protected from external environmental influences. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T3#GNS221_U3_T3_h3)

question: A confused elderly patient is admitted to the ward. Which temperature route is safest and most appropriate for initial assessment?

options.A: Axillary or tympanic
options.B: Sublingual
options.C: Rectal
options.D: Oral

explanation: Confused patients cannot safely hold a thermometer in their mouth or cooperate with rectal insertion, making non-invasive routes much safer. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T3#GNS221_U3_T3_h3)

question: How do common antipyretic drugs like paracetamol primarily lower a fever?

options.A: By blocking prostaglandin synthesis in the brain
options.B: By destroying bacteria in the bloodstream
options.C: By forcing the blood vessels in the skin to constrict
options.D: By directly cooling the skin through evaporation

explanation: Antipyretics stop the production of prostaglandins in the hypothalamus, which allows the body's internal thermostat to drop back down. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T3#GNS221_U3_T3_h4)

question: Which organ is at the greatest risk of damage during an overdose of paracetamol?

options.A: Liver
options.B: Heart
options.C: Kidneys
options.D: Lungs

explanation: Paracetamol is metabolized in the liver, and excessive amounts overwhelm the organ's pathways, leading to severe cellular injury. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T3#GNS221_U3_T3_h4)

question: Which age group is most commonly affected by febrile seizures?

options.A: Adolescence to early adulthood
options.B: Advanced old age
options.C: Birth to three months
options.D: Six months to five years

explanation: Febrile seizures typically occur in young children whose developing nervous systems react strongly to rapid temperature increases. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T3#GNS221_U3_T3_h5)

question: Why does a high fever place extra stress on the heart?

options.A: Red blood cells stop carrying oxygen during a fever.
options.B: The heart muscle weakens from direct bacterial invasion.
options.C: The body's increased metabolic rate forces the heart to beat faster and work harder.
options.D: Blood pressure drops to dangerously low levels immediately.

explanation: Think of your body like an engine running hot: when you have a fever, your metabolic rate speeds up, meaning your heart has to pump faster to supply all that extra oxygen! [learn more](GNS221_U3_T3#GNS221_U3_T3_h5)

question: Which of the following is NOT a recommended home care practice for managing a mild fever?

options.A: Giving prescribed doses of antipyretic medication safely
options.B: Monitoring the patient for unusual symptoms or confusion
options.C: Dressing the patient in heavy, thick blankets to trap body heat
options.D: Encouraging frequent oral intake of fluids and water

explanation: Trapping body heat with heavy blankets prevents natural cooling and can cause the temperature to rise even higher. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T3#GNS221_U3_T3_h6)

question: A mother calls the clinic because her child has a fever and a stiff neck. What advice should the nurse give?

options.A: Give a double dose of paracetamol and wait until morning.
options.B: Bring the child to the hospital immediately for evaluation.
options.C: Place the child in an ice bath to cool the skin rapidly.
options.D: Reassure the mother that stiff necks are normal with viral colds.

explanation: A stiff neck combined with a fever is a classic warning sign of serious infections like meningitis, which requires urgent medical care. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T3#GNS221_U3_T3_h6)

question: What is the clinical term for when blood escapes from the blood vessels?

options.A: Hemostasis
options.B: Haemorrhage
options.C: Hypovolemia
options.D: Hemolysis

explanation: Haemorrhage is simply the medical word for bleeding. You've got this! Think of it as blood escaping its normal highway. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T4#GNS221_U3_T4_h1)

question: What is the main danger of a massive, uncontrolled bleed?

options.A: It drops blood volume and stops oxygen flow to organs
options.B: It blocks normal clotting completely
options.C: It triggers overproduction of red blood cells
options.D: It causes an immediate spike in blood pressure

explanation: When too much blood is lost, there isn't enough volume left to pump oxygen to vital organs, which can lead to shock. Great job thinking through patient safety! [learn more](GNS221_U3_T4#GNS221_U3_T4_h1)

question: What does arterial bleeding usually look like?

options.A: A steady, continuous dark red stream
options.B: Clear fluid mixed with tiny blood flecks
options.C: Dark red blood oozing out slowly
options.D: Bright red blood spurting out in pulses

explanation: Arteries carry oxygen-rich blood straight from the heart under high pressure, which is why it spurts rhythmically with each heartbeat! [learn more](GNS221_U3_T4#GNS221_U3_T4_h2)

question: Why is capillary bleeding usually less dangerous than arterial bleeding?

options.A: Capillary blood carries no oxygen
options.B: Capillaries carry blood under very low pressure, causing a slow ooze
options.C: Capillaries only exist in the dead outer skin layer
options.D: The body instantly clots capillaries without platelets

explanation: Because tiny capillaries have very low pressure, any bleeding from them usually trickles slowly rather than gushing out fast. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T4#GNS221_U3_T4_h2)

question: During early blood loss, what is the body's main goal to protect itself?

options.A: Slower heart rate to save energy
options.B: Increase urine production to flush toxins
options.C: Maintain blood supply to the brain and heart
options.D: Keep the skin warm and well-perfused

explanation: In early shock, the body smartly shunts blood away from less critical areas to protect VIP organs like the brain and heart. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T4#GNS221_U3_T4_h3)

question: Which sign shows that the body can no longer compensate for blood loss?

options.A: A slow and steady decrease in heart rate
options.B: An increase in urine output by the kidneys
options.C: A sharp and sudden drop in blood pressure
options.D: A sudden return of normal skin color

explanation: When compensation fails, the blood pressure crashes. Recognizing this shift is a key nursing skill! [learn more](GNS221_U3_T4#GNS221_U3_T4_h3)

question: Why is waiting for low blood pressure a risky way to spot early internal bleeding in a young adult?

options.A: Strong compensatory mechanisms keep blood pressure normal until shock is severe
options.B: Internal bleeding actually makes blood pressure rise first
options.C: Young adults never get low blood pressure
options.D: Cuffs cannot measure pressure accurately during shock

explanation: Young bodies work overtime to hide blood loss by tightening blood vessels and racing the heart, so blood pressure can stay normal even when they're in trouble. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T4#GNS221_U3_T4_h4)

question: What is typically one of the earliest physical signs of significant blood loss?

options.A: Slow, deep breathing
options.B: Warm, flushed skin
options.C: High blood pressure
options.D: Fast heart rate

explanation: Tachycardia (fast heart rate) is the body's quick fix to keep blood moving when total volume starts to dip. You're mastering trauma basics! [learn more](GNS221_U3_T4#GNS221_U3_T4_h4)

question: What is the very first thing a nurse should do for active bleeding from an arm wound?

options.A: Elevate the arm and wait
options.B: Wash the open wound thoroughly with cold water
options.C: Apply firm, direct pressure with a clean dressing
options.D: Tie a tight tourniquet above the elbow

explanation: Direct pressure is always your go-to first step! It helps mechanical clotting do its job right away. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T4#GNS221_U3_T4_h5)

question: Blood is soaking right through the gauze on a leg wound you are pressing. What should you do next?

options.A: Remove the soaked gauze to inspect the cut
options.B: Stop pressing entirely and prep for surgery
options.C: Rinse the wound with sterile saline
options.D: Add more gauze pads right on top of the old ones and keep pressing

explanation: Never take off the first layer of gauze—you'll tear away the tiny new clots trying to form. Just pile more on top and keep holding pressure! [learn more](GNS221_U3_T4#GNS221_U3_T4_h5)

question: Why is internal bleeding much harder to spot immediately than external bleeding?

options.A: Patients don't feel any pain or discomfort
options.B: The blood collects inside body cavities and cannot be seen directly
options.C: Lab tests can never detect red blood cell drops
options.D: Internal bleeding never changes vital signs

explanation: Out of sight, out of mind! Because it pools inside, you have to watch closely for signs of shock instead of seeing the blood directly. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T4#GNS221_U3_T4_h6)

question: Which bedside tool is commonly used in emergencies to quickly check for internal belly bleeding?

options.A: Electrocardiogram
options.B: FAST ultrasound
options.C: Magnetic resonance imaging
options.D: Barium swallow study

explanation: The FAST exam is a quick ultrasound used right at the bedside to spot hidden fluid or blood in trauma patients. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T4#GNS221_U3_T4_h6)

question: Why can giving too much normal saline be harmful to a patient with uncontrolled internal bleeding?

options.A: It lowers the patient's heart rate to dangerous levels
options.B: It causes severe dehydration
options.C: It dilutes essential clotting factors and washes away fragile new clots
options.D: It destroys all existing red blood cells instantly

explanation: Pumping in too much plain IV fluid dilutes the blood's natural clotting proteins, making it harder for the body to stop the bleeding. Balance is key! [learn more](GNS221_U3_T4#GNS221_U3_T4_h7)

question: What size of IV catheter is preferred for fast fluid replacement in a severe trauma patient?

options.A: Midline catheter with dual lumens
options.B: Large-bore catheter like 16 or 18 gauge
options.C: Small-bore catheter like 24 gauge
options.D: Peripherally inserted central catheter

explanation: Think of an IV line like a pipe: a wider pipe (16 or 18 gauge) lets fluids and blood flow in much faster during an emergency. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T4#GNS221_U3_T4_h7)

question: What three conditions make up the dangerous 'lethal triad' in severe trauma?

options.A: Hypotension, hypoxia, and polyuria
options.B: Tachycardia, alkalosis, and dehydration
options.C: Hyperglycemia, fever, and hypertension
options.D: Hypothermia, acidosis, and coagulopathy

explanation: Low body temperature, acid buildup, and poor clotting form a vicious, deadly cycle in major trauma cases. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T4#GNS221_U3_T4_h8)

question: How does severe body cooling (hypothermia) directly harm a bleeding patient?

options.A: It speeds up platelet production too fast
options.B: It causes blood vessels to clamp shut permanently
options.C: It prevents kidneys from producing acidic urine
options.D: It slows down the chemical reactions needed for blood to clot

explanation: Clotting enzymes are like workers in a factory—when the patient gets too cold, those workers slow down and can't get the job done! [learn more](GNS221_U3_T4#GNS221_U3_T4_h8)

question: Which part of the brain is the main control center for keeping a person awake and alert?

options.A: Basal ganglia
options.B: Cerebellum
options.C: Reticular activating system
options.D: Medulla oblongata

explanation: Great job! The reticular activating system in the brainstem acts like the brain's alarm clock, controlling wakefulness and your sleep-wake cycle. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T5#GNS221_U3_T5_h1)

question: Why is checking blood sugar one of the first things to do when caring for an unresponsive patient?

options.A: Hypoglycemia is a metabolic cause of altered consciousness that can be quickly reversed
options.B: Glucose checks replace the need for a neurological exam
options.C: High blood sugar directly damages the brainstem within minutes
options.D: Diabetes mellitus is the primary cause of all neurological trauma

explanation: Spot on! Low blood sugar starves the brain of energy, causing unconsciousness that can fix itself almost instantly once glucose is given. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T5#GNS221_U3_T5_h1)

question: What are the three main behaviors checked when scoring the Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS)?

options.A: Reflexes, muscle tone, and pupil size
options.B: Heart rate, breathing rate, and blood pressure
options.C: Sensory touch, pain, and temperature
options.D: Eye opening, verbal response, and motor response

explanation: You've got this! The GCS looks at these three simple reactions to quickly check how well the brain is functioning. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T5#GNS221_U3_T5_h2)

question: How would you describe a patient who is in a state of stupor?

options.A: The patient sleeps constantly unless spoken to softly
options.B: The patient cannot be awakened by any stimulus at all
options.C: The patient is fully awake but confused about the current date
options.D: The patient responds only to vigorous and painful stimuli

explanation: Spot on! A stupor means the person is deeply asleep and will only wake up if you give them strong or painful stimuli. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T5#GNS221_U3_T5_h2)

question: In the emergency ABCDE primary survey, what does the letter 'A' stand for?

options.A: Antibiotic
options.B: Anxiety
options.C: Airway
options.D: Activity

explanation: Easy and essential! Checking and clearing the airway is always the number one priority in any emergency. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T5#GNS221_U3_T5_h3)

question: You notice an unresponsive patient has noisy, gurgling breathing. What should be your very first nursing action?

options.A: Administer a dose of intravenous glucose
options.B: Document the Glasgow Coma Scale score
options.C: Suction the airway to clear secretions
options.D: Apply warm blankets to prevent shivering

explanation: Well done! Gurgling means fluid or spit is blocking the airway, so clearing it out takes priority over everything else. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T5#GNS221_U3_T5_h3)

question: At what Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) score do doctors usually decide to insert an artificial airway (intubation) to protect the patient?

options.A: 8 or lower
options.B: 12 or lower
options.C: 15 exactly
options.D: 3 only

explanation: Remember the golden rule in trauma: 'less than 8, intubate!' A score of 8 or lower means the patient can no longer protect their own airway. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T5#GNS221_U3_T5_h4)

question: Why do nurses place an unconscious, breathing patient into the lateral recovery position?

options.A: To stop the patient from experiencing painful muscle spasms
options.B: To prevent the tongue from blocking the airway and reduce the risk of aspiration
options.C: To increase blood flow directly to the frontal lobes of the cerebrum
options.D: To make it easier for nurses to check blood pressure every hour

explanation: Great thinking! Gravity helps pull saliva or vomit away from the airway when they lie safely on their side. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T5#GNS221_U3_T5_h4)

question: Which set of vital sign changes makes up the classic warning sign known as Cushing's triad?

options.A: Low temperature, slow pulse, and normal blood pressure
options.B: High fever, rapid heart rate, and low blood pressure
options.C: Widening pulse pressure, bradycardia, and irregular respirations
options.D: Narrow pulse pressure, tachycardia, and deep breathing

explanation: You're getting the hang of it! Cushing's triad is a serious late warning sign that pressure inside the skull has risen to a dangerous level. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T5#GNS221_U3_T5_h5)

question: Why must nurses apply lubricating eye drops to an unconscious patient who cannot close their eyelids?

options.A: To test the corneal blink reflex every hour
options.B: To prevent corneal drying, ulceration, and infection
options.C: To decrease pressure inside the eyeball
options.D: To stimulate the optic nerve and improve brain activity

explanation: Spot on! Without natural blinking, the eye surface dries out quickly, so artificial tears protect the eyes from painful ulcers. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T5#GNS221_U3_T5_h5)

question: What is a major lung complication that often happens to patients who are unconscious and immobile for a long time?

options.A: Hypostatic pneumonia
options.B: Pulmonary hypertension
options.C: Asthma exacerbation
options.D: Spontaneous pneumothorax

explanation: Keep learning! When patients stay still, fluids pool at the back of their lungs, making it easy for bacteria to grow and cause pneumonia. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T5#GNS221_U3_T5_h6)

question: How does elevating the head of the bed to about 30 degrees help an unconscious patient?

options.A: It lowers intracranial pressure and reduces the risk of aspiration
options.B: It increases the effectiveness of oral medication administration
options.C: It stops the patient from rolling out of bed
options.D: It completely cures any underlying brain hemorrhage

explanation: Fantastic! Raising the head helps blood drain easily from the brain to lower pressure while keeping stomach contents safely down. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T5#GNS221_U3_T5_h6)

question: What happens to oxygen and carbon dioxide levels in the body during asphyxia?

options.A: High nitrogen and low carbon dioxide
options.B: Low nitrogen and high oxygen
options.C: High oxygen and low carbon dioxide
options.D: Low oxygen and high carbon dioxide

explanation: Think of asphyxia as a double hit: oxygen drops while carbon dioxide builds up rapidly in the blood because the body cannot get rid of it. You've got this! [learn more](GNS221_U3_T6#GNS221_U3_T6_h1)

question: Why is the brain hit the hardest when someone experiences asphyxia?

options.A: It has a high metabolic rate and constant oxygen demand
options.B: It produces its own oxygen through cellular division
options.C: It stores large reserves of backup oxygen
options.D: It is protected by cerebrospinal fluid that blocks toxins

explanation: The brain is a busy organ that constantly demands oxygen. When that supply cuts off, brain cells start struggling almost immediately. Great job reviewing this! [learn more](GNS221_U3_T6#GNS221_U3_T6_h1)

question: How does a person usually breathe right at the start of an asphyxia event?

options.A: Total absence of breathing
options.B: Slow and shallow breathing
options.C: Rapid and deep breathing
options.D: Completely irregular gasping

explanation: At first, the body's control center panics and tries to pull in as much air as possible, resulting in fast, deep breaths to fight off the lack of oxygen. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T6#GNS221_U3_T6_h2)

question: What causes a patient to start having convulsions as asphyxia gets worse?

options.A: Sudden infection spreading to the spinal cord
options.B: Severe lack of oxygen affecting brain function
options.C: A massive release of digestive enzymes
options.D: Rapid cooling of the skin surface

explanation: When brain cells are starved of oxygen for too long, they start misfiring wildly. This erratic electrical activity leads to muscle twitching and convulsions. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T6#GNS221_U3_T6_h2)

question: Which of these is a common situation that can lead to asphyxia?

options.A: Consuming too much salty food
options.B: Confinement in an airtight space
options.C: Sudden loss of blood from a wound
options.D: A mild viral throat infection

explanation: Being trapped in a tiny, unventilated box or room quickly uses up all the oxygen, leading to suffocation. Always keep safety in mind! [learn more](GNS221_U3_T6#GNS221_U3_T6_h3)

question: Why does a person trapped in a smoke-filled room suffer from asphyxia?

options.A: Severe dehydration and low blood volume
options.B: Toxic gas inhalation replacing ambient oxygen
options.C: Allergic reaction to dust particles
options.D: Sudden paralysis of the heart muscle

explanation: Thick smoke and poisonous gases take up all the space in the air, pushing out the good oxygen your lungs need to function. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T6#GNS221_U3_T6_h3)

question: What is the medical name for the bluish color you see on a patient's skin when they lack oxygen?

options.A: Jaundice
options.B: Pallor
options.C: Cyanosis
options.D: Erythema

explanation: Cyanosis comes from 'cyano' (blue). It happens when red blood cells lacking oxygen circulate near the skin surface. A classic clinical sign to remember! [learn more](GNS221_U3_T6#GNS221_U3_T6_h4)

question: Why do patients in the early stages of asphyxia often look restless and confused?

options.A: Their digestive system has shut down
options.B: The brain is not receiving enough oxygen
options.C: Their blood pressure is abnormally high
options.D: They are having an allergic skin reaction

explanation: The brain is very sensitive to oxygen levels. When it starts running low, the patient often gets anxious, confused, or restless before losing consciousness. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T6#GNS221_U3_T6_h4)

question: As a nurse or rescuer, what is the very first thing you must check at an emergency scene?

options.A: Ensure the safety of the surrounding environment
options.B: Check the patient's blood pressure
options.C: Administer intravenous medications
options.D: Begin chest compressions immediately

explanation: Safety first! Always check for dangers (like live wires or smoke) so you don't become a second victim needing rescue. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T6#GNS221_U3_T6_h5)

question: Why should you avoid sticking your fingers blindly into a choking patient's mouth to clear an airway?

options.A: They interfere with heart rhythm monitors
options.B: They always cause permanent bleeding of the gums
options.C: They can push the object further down the throat
options.D: They make the patient vomit large amounts of blood

explanation: Blind finger sweeps are dangerous because you might accidentally jam a loose object deeper into the windpipe. Only clear what you can actually see! [learn more](GNS221_U3_T6#GNS221_U3_T6_h5)

question: Which airway maneuver should you use if you think your patient has a neck or spine injury?

options.A: Jaw-thrust maneuver
options.B: Lateral neck rotation
options.C: Rapid neck hyperextension
options.D: Head-tilt, chin-lift maneuver

explanation: The jaw-thrust opens the airway without bending or moving the neck, keeping the cervical spine safe from further harm. Brilliant nursing judgment! [learn more](GNS221_U3_T6#GNS221_U3_T6_h6)

question: What is the main goal of passing an endotracheal tube during resuscitation?

options.A: To secure a direct passage for oxygen into the lungs
options.B: To remove fluid directly from the stomach
options.C: To prevent the patient from speaking to staff
options.D: To measure the exact weight of the patient

explanation: An endotracheal tube creates a safe, clear highway straight into the lungs, bypassing any blockages in the upper airway. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T6#GNS221_U3_T6_h6)

question: What is a top priority in nursing care right after a patient is revived from asphyxia?

options.A: Discharging the patient home within one hour
options.B: Continuous monitoring of breathing and oxygen levels
options.C: Encouraging the patient to eat a large meal
options.D: Removing all intravenous lines immediately

explanation: Just because a patient is revived doesn't mean they are out of the woods. Close watch on their vitals helps catch any sudden crashes early. [learn more](GNS221_U3_T6#GNS221_U3_T6_h7)

question: Why are frequent neurological checks so important after an asphyxial episode?

options.A: To detect brain injury caused by lack of oxygen
options.B: To test the function of the cranial nerves in the stomach
options.C: To check if the patient remembers their home address
options.D: To see if the patient is ready to walk unassisted
